tabs.title: Overview
tabs.html:
Contoso, Ltd. is a US-based health supplements company. Contoso has two divisions named Sales and Research. The Sales division contains two

departments named Online Sales and Retail Sales. The Research division assigns internally developed product lines to individual teams of researchers and analysts.

tabs.title: Existing Environment
tabs.html:
Identity Environment

Contoso has a Microsoft Entra tenant named contoso.com. The tenant contains two groups named ResearchReviewersGroup1 and ResearchReviewersGroup2.

Data Environment

Contoso has the following data environment:

The Sales division uses a Microsoft Power BI Premium capacity.

The semantic model of the Online Sales department includes a fact table named Orders that uses Import made. In the system of origin, the OrderID value represents the sequence in which orders are created.

The Research department uses an on-premises, third-party data warehousing product.

Fabric is enabled for contoso.com.

An Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 storage account named storage1 contains Research division data for a product line named Productline1. The data is in the delta format.

A Data Lake Storage Gen2 storage account named storage2 contains Research division data for a product line named Productline2. The data is in the CSV format.

tabs.title: Requirements
tabs.html:
Planned Changes

Contoso plans to make the following changes:

Enable support for Fabric in the Power BI Premium capacity used by the Sales division.

Make all the data for the Sales division and the Research division available in Fabric.

For the Research division, create two Fabric workspaces named Productline1ws and Productine2ws.

In Productline1ws, create a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

In Lakehouse1, create a shortcut to storage1 named ResearchProduct.

Data Analytics Requirements

Contoso identifies the following data analytics requirements:

All the workspaces for the Sales division and the Research division must support all Fabric experiences.

The Research division workspaces must use a dedicated, on-demand capacity that has per-minute billing.

The Research division workspaces must be grouped together logically to support OneLake data hub filtering based on the department name.

For the Research division workspaces, the members of

ResearchReviewersGroup1 must be able to read lakehouse and warehouse data and shortcuts by using SQL endpoints.

For the Research division workspaces, the members of

ResearchReviewersGroup2 must be able to read lakehouse data by using Lakehouse explorer.

All the semantic models and reports for the Research division must use version control that supports branching.

Data Preparation Requirements

Contoso identifies the following data preparation requirements:

The Research division data for Productline1 must be retrieved from Lakehouse1 by using Fabric notebooks.

All the Research division data in the lakehouses must be presented as managed tables in Lakehouse explorer.

Semantic Model Requirements

Contoso identifies the following requirements for implementing and managing semantic models:

The number of rows added to the Orders table during refreshes must be minimized.

The semantic models in the Research division workspaces must use Direct Lake mode.

General Requirements

Contoso identifies the following high-level requirements that must be considered for all solutions:

Follow the principle of least privilege when applicable.

Minimize implementation and maintenance effort when possible.

tabs.title: Overview
tabs.html: Litware, Inc. is a manufacturing company that has offices throughout North America. The analytics team at Litware contains data engineers, analytics engineers, data analysts, and data scientists.

tabs.title: Existing Environment
tabs.html:
Fabric Environment

Litware has been using a Microsoft Power BI tenant for three years. Litware has NOT enabled any Fabric capacities and features.

Available Data

Litware has data that must be analyzed as shown in the following table.

The Product data contains a single table and the following columns.

The customer satisfaction data contains the following tables:

  • Survey
  • Question
  • Response

For each survey submitted, the following occurs:

One row is added to the Survey table.

One row is added to the Response table for each question in the survey.

The Question table contains the text of each survey question. The third question in each survey response is an overall satisfaction score. Customers can submit a survey after each purchase.

User Problems

The analytics team has large volumes of data, some of which is semi-structured. The team wants to use Fabric to create a new data store.

Product data is often classified into three pricing groups: high, medium, and low. This logic is implemented in several databases and semantic models, but the logic does NOT always match across implementations.

tabs.title: Requirements
tabs.html:
Planned Changes

Litware plans to enable Fabric features in the existing tenant. The analytics team will create a new data store as a proof of concept (PoC). The remaining Liware users will only get access to the Fabric features once the PoC is complete. The PoC will be completed by using a Fabric trial capacity The following three workspaces will be created:

AnalyticsPOC: Will contain the data store, semantic models, reports pipelines, dataflow, and notebooks used to populate the data store

DataEngPOC: Will contain all the pipelines, dataflows, and notebooks used to populate OneLake

DataSciPOC: Will contain all the notebooks and reports created by the data scientists

The following will be created in the AnalyticsPOC workspace:

A data store (type to be decided)

  • A custom semantic model
  • A default semantic model
  • Interactive reports

The data engineers will create data pipelines to load data to OneLake either hourly or daily depending on the data source. The analytics engineers will create processes to ingest, transform, and load the data to the data store in the AnalyticsPOC workspace daily. Whenever possible, the data engineers will use low-code tools for data ingestion. The choice of which data cleansing and transformation tools to use will be at the data engineers’ discretion.

All the semantic models and reports in the Analytics POC workspace will use the data store as the sole data source.

Technical Requirements

The data store must support the following:

Read access by using T-SQL or Python

Semi-structured and unstructured data

Row-level security (RLS) for users executing T-SQL queries

Files loaded by the data engineers to OneLake will be stored in the Parquet format and will meet Delta Lake specifications.

Data will be loaded without transformation in one area of the AnalyticsPOC data store. The data will then be cleansed, merged, and transformed into a dimensional model

The data load process must ensure that the raw and cleansed data is updated completely before populating the dimensional model

The dimensional model must contain a date dimension. There is no existing data source for the date dimension. The Litware fiscal year matches the calendar year. The date dimension must always contain dates from 2010 through the end of the current year.

The product pricing group logic must be maintained by the analytics engineers in a single location. The pricing group data must be made available in the data store for T-SOL. queries and in the default semantic model. The following logic must be used:

List prices that are less than or equal to 50 are in the low pricing group.

List prices that are greater than 50 and less than or equal to 1,000 are in the medium pricing group.

List prices that are greater than 1,000 are in the high pricing group.

Security Requirements

Only Fabric administrators and the analytics team must be able to see the Fabric items created as part of the PoC.

Litware identifies the following security requirements for the Fabric items in the AnalyticsPOC workspace:

Fabric administrators will be the workspace administrators.

The data engineers must be able to read from and write to the data store. No access must be granted to datasets or reports.

The analytics engineers must be able to read from, write to, and create schemas in the data store. They also must be able to create and share semantic models with the data analysts and view and modify all reports in the workspace.

The data scientists must be able to read from the data store, but not write to it. They will access the data by using a Spark notebook

The data analysts must have read access to only the dimensional model objects in the data store. They also must have access to create Power BI reports by using the semantic models created by the analytics engineers.

The date dimension must be available to all users of the data store.

The principle of least privilege must be followed.

Both the default and custom semantic models must include only tables or views from the dimensional model in the data store. Litware already has the following Microsoft Entra security groups:

FabricAdmins: Fabric administrators

AnalyticsTeam: All the members of the analytics team

DataAnalysts: The data analysts on the analytics team

DataScientists: The data scientists on the analytics team

DataEngineers: The data engineers on the analytics team

AnalyticsEngineers: The analytics engineers on the analytics team

Report Requirements

The data analysts must create a customer satisfaction report that meets the following requirements:

Enables a user to select a product to filter customer survey responses to only those who have purchased that product.

Displays the average overall satisfaction score of all the surveys submitted during the last 12 months up to a selected dat.

Shows data as soon as the data is updated in the data store.

Ensures that the report and the semantic model only contain data from the current and previous year.

Ensures that the report respects any table-level security specified in the source data store.

Minimizes the execution time of report queries.

q001.stem:
You need to ensure that Contoso can use version control to meet the data analytics requirements and the general requirements.

What should you do?
options: Store at the semantic models and reports in Data Lake Gen2 storage.
Modify the settings of the Research workspaces to use a GitHub repository.
Modify the settings of the Research division workspaces to use an Azure Repos repository.
Store all the semantic models and reports in Microsoft OneDrive.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Modify the settings of the Research division workspaces to use an Azure Repos repository.

Why it is correct: The case study requires that "all the semantic models and reports for the Research division must use version control that supports branching", and the general requirements ask for minimal implementation and maintenance effort. Fabric has a built-in feature for this: Git integration at the workspace level. You connect each Research workspace (Productline1ws and Productline2ws) to a Git repository in Azure DevOps (Azure Repos), and the semantic models and reports in the workspace are serialized to the repo, where you get commits, history and branches (the Git integration is designed so that developers can "collaborate using Git branches", and Fabric lets you check out and create branches from the workspace). Nothing has to be built or maintained: it is a workspace setting.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but Fabric Git integration now supports both Azure DevOps and GitHub (including GitHub Enterprise), both with branching, so the GitHub option could also be argued on a current exam; Azure Repos was the only provider when the question was written. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Overview of Fabric Git integration and Manage Git branches in Microsoft Fabric workspaces.
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Store the semantic models and reports in Data Lake Gen2 storage.

Why it is incorrect: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 is a storage service, not a version control system. It has no commits, no branches and no merge capability, and Fabric Git integration does not use it as a source-control target. Saving items there would also be manual work, which goes against the "minimize implementation and maintenance effort" requirement.

  • Official documentation: Overview of Fabric Git integration (supported Git providers)

B. Modify the settings of the Research workspaces to use a GitHub repository.

Why it is incorrect: Fabric Git integration does support GitHub today, so technically this would also give you branching. It is, however, not the expected answer for this question: when the question was written, Azure DevOps was the only provider Fabric supported, so the expected answer is Azure Repos.

  • Official documentation: Overview of Fabric Git integration (supported Git providers)

D. Store all the semantic models and reports in Microsoft OneDrive.

Why it is incorrect: OneDrive offers file version history (a linear list of previous versions), not Git-style version control with branching and merging. It is also not a supported Git integration provider for Fabric workspaces, so it does not satisfy the branching requirement.

  • Official documentation: Get started with Git integration

q002.stem:
You need to recommend a solution to group the Research division workspaces.

What should you include in the recommendation? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Grouping method: Domain
  • Tool: The Fabric Admin portal

Why it is correct: the requirement is to logically group the Research workspaces so they can be filtered in the OneLake data hub by department; in Fabric a domain does that, and it is created and assigned from the admin portal.

  • Grouping method, Domain: a domain logically groups workspaces by business area and their items receive the domain attribute, which can be filtered in the OneLake data hub.
  • Tool, The Fabric Admin portal: domains are created and configured in the Fabric admin portal (governance → Domains), where workspaces are also assigned.

Incorrect options:

  • Grouping method, Capacity — Why it is incorrect: a capacity is the set of compute resources (and billing unit); it does not logically group workspaces in the data hub.
  • Grouping method, Tenant — Why it is incorrect: the tenant is the whole organization: too broad and with no filtering function in the data hub.
  • Tool, OneLake data hub — Why it is incorrect: the OneLake data hub is for discovering and filtering items already grouped; domains are not created or assigned from it.
  • Tool, The Microsoft Entra admin center — Why it is incorrect: the Microsoft Entra admin center manages identities, groups and licenses, not the grouping of Fabric workspaces.
  • Official documentation: Domains in Microsoft Fabric (create and configure domains) and Configure domain settings

q003.stem:
You need to refresh the Orders table of the Online Sales department. The solution must meet the semantic model requirements.

What should you include in the solution?
options: an Azure Data Factory pipeline that executes a Stored procedure activity to retrieve the maximum value of the OrderID column in the destination lakehouse
an Azure Data Factory pipeline that executes a Stored procedure activity to retrieve the minimum value of the OrderID column in the destination lakehouse
an Azure Data Factory pipeline that executes a dataflow to retrieve the minimum value of the OrderID column in the destination lakehouse
an Azure Data Factory pipeline that executes a dataflow to retrieve the maximum value of the OrderID column in the destination lakehouse

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: An Azure Data Factory pipeline that executes a dataflow to retrieve the maximum value of the OrderID column in the destination lakehouse.

Why it is correct: The case states that the Orders fact table uses Import mode, that "the number of rows added to the Orders table during refreshes must be minimized", and that in the source system the OrderID represents the sequence in which orders are created (it only grows). That is the textbook scenario for an incremental load using a watermark: read the maximum OrderID already loaded in the destination and then ingest only the source rows with a higher OrderID. A dataflow (low-code Power Query) can query the destination lakehouse for that maximum value and filter the source accordingly, so only new orders are appended, which also keeps the maintenance effort low.

  • Official documentation: Incremental refresh in Dataflow Gen2 and Decision guide: copy activity, dataflow, or Spark
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. A pipeline that executes a Stored procedure activity to retrieve the maximum value of OrderID in the destination lakehouse.

Why it is incorrect: The maximum value is the right watermark, but a stored procedure is the wrong mechanism here. A lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint is read-only and cannot host stored procedures that you could use for this load logic; stored procedures belong to warehouses or SQL databases. The dataflow option reaches the same result with a low-code tool that can read the lakehouse directly.

  • Official documentation: What is the SQL analytics endpoint for a lakehouse?

B. A pipeline that executes a Stored procedure activity to retrieve the minimum value of OrderID in the destination lakehouse.

Why it is incorrect: It has the same problem as A and a second one: the minimum OrderID in the destination is the oldest order already loaded, so using it as a watermark would make you reload practically all the data on every refresh, the opposite of minimizing the rows added.

  • Official documentation: Incremental refresh in Dataflow Gen2

C. A pipeline that executes a dataflow to retrieve the minimum value of OrderID in the destination lakehouse.

Why it is incorrect: The dataflow is a valid tool, but the minimum is the wrong watermark. Because OrderID is sequential, only values greater than the current maximum are new; filtering from the minimum would re-ingest existing rows and add duplicates or force a full reload.

  • Official documentation: Incremental refresh in Dataflow Gen2

q004.stem: Which syntax should you use in a notebook to access the Research division data for Productline1?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: spark.sql("SELECT * FROM Lakehouse1.ResearchProduct ")

Why it is correct: The case creates a shortcut named ResearchProduct in Lakehouse1 pointing to the Delta data in storage1, and requires that all the data in the lakehouses is "presented as managed tables in Lakehouse explorer". A shortcut to a Delta folder created in the Tables section appears as a table directly under Tables (it is registered in the lakehouse metastore), so a notebook can query it by name with Spark SQL using <lakehouse>.<table>, which is exactly Lakehouse1.ResearchProduct. It is the simplest and most idiomatic syntax in a Fabric notebook.

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. spark.read.format("delta").load("Tables/productline1/ResearchProduct")

Why it is incorrect: The shortcut was created as ResearchProduct directly in the Tables section; no productline1 subfolder exists in the lakehouse (the Tables section does not support that kind of nested folder hierarchy for tables). The path would fail. A correct path-based read would be Tables/ResearchProduct, which is not what is offered.

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts

C. external_table('Tables/ResearchProduct)

Why it is incorrect: external_table() is a Kusto Query Language (KQL) function used in KQL databases/eventhouses to query external tables. It is not valid in a Spark notebook (and the string is not even closed properly).

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts

D. external_table(ResearchProduct)

Why it is incorrect: Same reason as C: it is KQL syntax, not PySpark or Spark SQL, so a Fabric notebook running Spark cannot execute it to read lakehouse data.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse overview

q005.stem:
You need to assign permissions for the data store in the AnalyticsPOC workspace. The solution must meet the security requirements.

Which additional permissions should you assign when you share the data store?

To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • DataEngineers: Read All Apache Spark
  • DataAnalysts: Build Reports on the default dataset
  • DataScientists: Read All Apache Spark

The AnalyticsPOC data store must support semi-structured and unstructured data, T-SQL queries with row-level security (RLS) and access through Python/Spark, so the right item is a lakehouse. When you share it in Fabric you pick additional permissions on top of the base Read access, assigned by least privilege: Read all Apache Spark (read OneLake files and tables from Spark), Read all SQL analytics endpoint data (read tables and views with T-SQL) and Build reports on the default semantic model (create Power BI reports on the default semantic model).

  • DataEngineers, Read All Apache Spark: the data engineers load and process Parquet/Delta files in OneLake with pipelines, dataflows and notebooks from DataEngPOC, and must not get access to datasets or reports. Read All Apache Spark gives direct read access to OneLake files and tables through Spark without granting permissions on the default semantic model or on reports. (Write access to OneLake is completed through OneLake data access roles or workspace permissions.)
  • DataAnalysts, Build Reports on the default dataset: the analysts need to create Power BI reports from semantic models and must read only the dimensional model objects (no access to the raw or cleansed zones). Because the default and custom semantic models contain only dimensional model tables or views, this permission lets them build reports on those objects without exposing the other lakehouse tables.
  • DataScientists, Read All Apache Spark: the case says they read the store data with a Spark notebook and without write permissions. For a user with shared access to read Delta tables and files from a Spark notebook, Read All Apache Spark is required.

Incorrect options:

  • DataEngineers, Build Reports on the default dataset — Why it is incorrect: the requirements forbid giving data engineers access to datasets or reports.
  • DataEngineers, Read All SQL analytics endpoint data — Why it is incorrect: the engineers work with OneLake at the Parquet/Delta file level and Spark notebooks, not with T-SQL queries on the SQL analytics endpoint.
  • DataAnalysts, Read All SQL analytics endpoint data — Why it is incorrect: it grants read on all tables and views of the endpoint, including the raw and cleansed data that coexist in AnalyticsPOC; it violates least privilege.
  • DataAnalysts, Read All Apache Spark — Why it is incorrect: it would let them read every OneLake file (including the untransformed folders), and analysts consume semantic models to build reports rather than using Spark notebooks.
  • DataScientists, Build Reports on the default dataset — Why it is incorrect: it only allows building reports on the default semantic model, not reading files or Delta tables from a notebook.
  • DataScientists, Read All SQL analytics endpoint data — Why it is incorrect: it only enables T-SQL reads, not Spark engines, which is the tool required for the data scientists.
  • Official documentation: How lakehouse sharing works (permissions), Build permission for semantic models and OneLake security

q006.stem:
You need to create a DAX measure to calculate the average overall satisfaction score.

How should you complete the DAX code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First box (aggregation expression inside CALCULATE): AVERAGE('Survey'[Response Value]),
  • Second box (first date filter argument of CALCULATE): Period,

Resulting DAX measure:

Rolling 12 Overall Satisfaction =
VAR NumberOfMonths = 12
VAR LastCurrentDate = MAX ( 'Date'[Date] )
VAR Period = DATESINPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], LastCurrentDate, - NumberOfMonths, MONTH )
VAR Result =
    CALCULATE (
        AVERAGE ( 'Survey'[Response Value] ),
        Period,
        'Survey Question'[Question Title] = "Overall Satisfaction"
    )
RETURN
    Result

Why they are correct:

  • First box — AVERAGE('Survey'[Response Value]), the report requirement is the average overall satisfaction score of all surveys sent in the last 12 months. In the dimensional model, the 'Survey' fact table stores each response's numeric value in [Response Value]. AVERAGE computes the arithmetic mean of those scores, filtered afterwards by the question "Overall Satisfaction". Official documentation: AVERAGE function (DAX) - Microsoft Learn
  • Second box — Period, the Period variable is defined with DATESINPERIOD('Date'[Date], LastCurrentDate, -NumberOfMonths, MONTH), which returns a single-column table with all dates in the rolling 12-month window ending at the maximum selected date. CALCULATE needs filter arguments that are Boolean expressions or filter tables (such as Period) that modify the evaluation context. Official documentation: DATESINPERIOD function (DAX) - Microsoft Learn | Official documentation: CALCULATE function (DAX) - Microsoft Learn

Incorrect options:

  • First box — AVERAGEA(Question[Question Text]), — Why it is incorrect: Question[Question Text] holds the descriptive text of the survey question, not the numeric score given by the customer. Also, AVERAGEA evaluates non-empty text as 0, so it would always return 0. Official documentation: AVERAGEA function (DAX) - Microsoft Learn
  • First box — AVERAGEX(VALUES('Survey'[Customer Key]), — Why it is incorrect: it is syntactically incomplete (AVERAGEX lacks its required second argument, the expression to evaluate per row), and averaging Customer Key values (a surrogate key) makes no analytical sense and does not meet the requirement to average all surveys sent (customers can submit a survey after each purchase). Official documentation: AVERAGEX function (DAX) - Microsoft Learn
  • Second box — LastCurrentDate, — Why it is incorrect: it stores a scalar value (a single date from MAX('Date'[Date])), not a table or Boolean expression; a scalar as a filter argument in CALCULATE causes a DAX error. Official documentation: CALCULATE function (DAX) - Microsoft Learn
  • Second box — NumberOfMonths, — Why it is incorrect: it is just the scalar constant 12, so it is neither a date table nor a valid Boolean predicate for CALCULATE. Official documentation: CALCULATE function (DAX) - Microsoft Learn

q007.stem:
You need to resolve the issue with the pricing group classification.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First dropdown (CREATE ... [dbo].[ProductsWithPricingGroup]): VIEW
  • Second dropdown (conditional expression before WHEN ListPrice <= 50): CASE
  • Third dropdown (intermediate condition for 'medium'): WHEN(ListPrice > 50 AND ListPrice < 1000) THEN 'medium'

Note: the exam screenshot has a typo (the original line lacks the closing parenthesis/equals sign), but this is the only one of the three options that strictly respects the lower bound > 50 and valid block syntax.

Resulting T-SQL:

CREATE VIEW [dbo].[ProductsWithPricingGroup]
AS
SELECT ProductId,
       ProductName,
       ProductCategory,
       ListPrice,
       CASE
           WHEN ListPrice <= 50 THEN 'low'
           WHEN (ListPrice > 50 AND ListPrice < 1000) THEN 'medium'
           WHEN ListPrice > 1000 THEN 'high'
       END AS PricingGroup
FROM dbo.Products

Why they are correct:

  • First dropdown — VIEW: the case study requires that “the product pricing group logic must be maintained by the analytics engineers in a single location” and that “the pricing group data must be available in the data warehouse for T-SQL queries and in the default semantic model”; it also says both default and custom semantic models must include only tables or views from the dimensional model. A view encapsulates the business rule in one centralized T-SQL definition, is directly queryable with T-SQL and can be added to the default semantic model without duplicating data or extra ETL. Official documentation: Views in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse - Microsoft Learn
  • Second dropdown — CASE: the structure with WHEN <condition> THEN <result> clauses closed by END AS <alias> is a searched CASE expression, used to classify values into several discrete ranges ('low', 'medium', 'high'). Official documentation: CASE (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn
  • Third dropdown — WHEN(ListPrice > 50 AND ListPrice < 1000) THEN 'medium': the business rules define disjoint ranges: ≤ 50 → 'low'; > 50 and below 1,000 → 'medium'; > 1,000 → 'high'. Among the available options, this is the only one that correctly excludes 50 (which belongs to 'low') with ListPrice > 50 and keeps valid parenthesis syntax. Official documentation: Comparison operators (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

Incorrect options:

  • First dropdown — FUNCTION — Why it is incorrect: inline table-valued functions exist in T-SQL, but they cannot be added directly as tabular objects of the dimensional model in the default semantic model. Official documentation: T-SQL surface area in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn
  • First dropdown — PROCEDURE — Why it is incorrect: CREATE PROCEDURE does not fit this syntax, and a stored procedure is not an object you can query with SELECT or integrate into the default semantic model. Official documentation: T-SQL surface area in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn
  • First dropdown — TABLE — Why it is incorrect: creating a table from a query in Fabric Data Warehouse requires CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT (CTAS), and a static physical table would need daily reloads to stay in sync with dbo.Products, whereas a VIEW reflects changes immediately and is the object the case study allows in the semantic model. Official documentation: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) in Fabric Data Warehouse - Microsoft Learn
  • Second dropdown — COALESCE and IIF — Why they are incorrect: neither scalar function supports the WHEN ... THEN ... END syntax; COALESCE returns the first non-null argument and IIF(condition, true, false) evaluates a single Boolean expression. Official documentation: CASE (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn
  • Second dropdown — SET — Why it is incorrect: SET assigns values to local variables or configures session options; it is not a column expression within a SELECT clause. Official documentation: CASE (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn
  • Third dropdown — WHEN(ListPrice >= 50 AND ListPrice < 1000) THEN 'medium' — Why it is incorrect: it uses >= 50 instead of > 50, contradicting the requirement that prices of 50 or less belong to 'low'. Official documentation: Comparison operators (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn
  • Third dropdown — WHEN ListPrice BETWEEN 50 AND 1000) THEN 'medium' — Why it is incorrect: BETWEEN 50 AND 1000 is inclusive at both ends (it would wrongly include 50 in 'medium') and it has an orphan closing parenthesis, which is a T-SQL syntax error. Official documentation: Comparison operators (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

q008.stem: What should you recommend using to ingest the customer data into the data store in the AnalyticsPOC workspace?
options: a pipeline that contains a KQL activity

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: A dataflow

Why it is correct: The case states that "whenever possible, the data engineers will use low-code tools for data ingestion", and the data (customer data) is loaded daily into the AnalyticsPOC data store. A Dataflow Gen2 is Fabric's low-code ingestion and transformation tool (Power Query): it connects to many sources and writes to a lakehouse or warehouse destination without code, which fits the requirement and the analytics engineers' skills (Power Query).

  • Official documentation: Decision guide: copy activity, dataflow, or Spark and Data Factory overview
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. A stored procedure

Why it is incorrect: A stored procedure is T-SQL code that runs inside the data store; it is not a low-code ingestion tool and cannot by itself pull data from external sources into OneLake. It also runs counter to the preference for low-code tooling.

  • Official documentation: Decision guide: copy activity, dataflow, or Spark

B. A pipeline that contains a KQL activity

Why it is incorrect: A KQL activity runs Kusto queries against KQL databases (eventhouse). The PoC data store is not a KQL database, and a KQL activity is not an ingestion mechanism for customer data into it.

  • Official documentation: Data Factory overview

C. A Spark notebook

Why it is incorrect: A notebook is a code-first approach (PySpark, Spark SQL). It is powerful, but the case explicitly asks for low-code tools wherever possible, so a notebook is not the recommended choice for the ingestion step.

  • Official documentation: Decision guide: copy activity, dataflow, or Spark

q009.stem:
Which type of data store should you recommend in the AnalyticsPOC

workspace?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: A lakehouse

Why it is correct: The case sets these technical requirements for the AnalyticsPOC data store: read access by using T-SQL or Python, support for semi-structured and unstructured data, and row-level security for users running T-SQL queries. A lakehouse stores structured, semi-structured and unstructured data in OneLake (Delta tables plus files), can be read with Spark/Python, and exposes an automatically created SQL analytics endpoint for T-SQL queries, where RLS can be applied. It is also the store that supports the Spark notebook access required for the data scientists.

  • Official documentation: What is a lakehouse in Microsoft Fabric? and Decision guide: choose a data store
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. A data lake

Why it is incorrect: "Data lake" is a general concept (the Fabric implementation is OneLake and the lakehouse built on it), not a specific Fabric data store item type that you choose to provide T-SQL access with RLS together with Python access.

  • Official documentation: Decision guide: choose a data store

B. A warehouse

Why it is incorrect: A warehouse supports T-SQL (and RLS) well, but it is designed for structured data and does not natively cover the semi-structured and unstructured data requirement; Python/Spark access is also not its primary path. The lakehouse covers every requirement.

  • Official documentation: Decision guide: choose between warehouse and lakehouse

D. An external Hive metastore

Why it is incorrect: An external Hive metastore is a metadata catalog that Spark workloads can be configured to use; it is not a Fabric data store that holds the data or offers a T-SQL endpoint with RLS.

  • Official documentation: Decision guide: choose a data store

q010.stem:
You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Staging.Sales.

Staging.Sales contains the following columns.

You need to write a T-SQL query that will return data for the year 2023 that displays ProductID and ProductName and has a summarized Amount that is higher than 10,000.

Which query should you use?
options:
SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount
FROM Staging.Sales
WHERE DATEPART(YEAR,SaleDate) = '2023'
GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName
HAVING SUM(Amount) > 10000

SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount
FROM Staging.Sales
GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName
HAVING DATEPART(YEAR,SaleDate) = '2023' AND SUM(Amount) > 10000

SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount
FROM Staging.Sales
WHERE DATEPART(YEAR,SaleDate) = '2023' AND SUM(Amount) > 10000

SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount
FROM Staging.Sales
WHERE DATEPART(YEAR,SaleDate) = '2023'
GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName
HAVING TotalAmount > 10000

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: The query that filters the year with WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SaleDate) = '2023', groups by ProductID, ProductName and filters the aggregate with HAVING SUM(Amount) > 10000.
SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount
FROM Staging.Sales
WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SaleDate) = '2023'
GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName
HAVING SUM(Amount) > 10000

Why it is correct: The query must return the data of 2023 only, with ProductID and ProductName and the summed Amount, and keep only the groups whose total is above 10,000. SQL's logical order of evaluation matters: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping (the right place for the 2023 filter), GROUP BY builds the groups by ProductID and ProductName, and HAVING filters the groups after aggregation, so the aggregate condition SUM(Amount) > 10000 goes there. Filtering the year in WHERE also reduces the rows to aggregate, which is more efficient.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - GROUP BY (Transact-SQL) and SELECT - HAVING (Transact-SQL)
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. The query with GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName and HAVING DATEPART(YEAR, SaleDate) = '2023' AND SUM(Amount) > 10000.

Why it is incorrect: SaleDate is neither in the GROUP BY nor inside an aggregate function, so it cannot be used in HAVING; the statement is invalid. Row-level conditions such as the year belong in WHERE.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - HAVING (Transact-SQL)

C. The query with WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SaleDate) = '2023' AND SUM(Amount) > 10000 and no GROUP BY.

Why it is incorrect: Aggregate functions are not allowed in a WHERE clause, because WHERE is evaluated before any aggregation. In addition, the query lacks the GROUP BY needed to return ProductID and ProductName next to a SUM.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - GROUP BY (Transact-SQL)

D. The query with WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SaleDate) = '2023', GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName and HAVING TotalAmount > 10000.

Why it is incorrect: The structure is right, but HAVING is evaluated before the SELECT list, so the alias TotalAmount does not exist yet and cannot be referenced in T-SQL (Spark SQL permits it, T-SQL in a Fabric warehouse does not). You have to repeat the expression: HAVING SUM(Amount) > 10000.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - HAVING (Transact-SQL)

q011.stem:
You have a data warehouse that contains a table named Stage.Customers.

Stage.Customers contains all the customer record updates from a customer relationship management (CRM) system. There can be multiple updates per customer.

You need to write a T-SQL query that will return the customer ID, name. postal code, and the last updated time of the most recent row for each customer ID.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First drop-down (x = ...): ROW_NUMBER()
  • Second drop-down (filter on the CTE): WHERE X = 1

Why it is correct: The requirement is to return, for each customer ID, only the most recent row among many updates. The classic T-SQL pattern is a common table expression (CTE) that numbers the rows of each customer from newest to oldest, followed by an outer query that keeps only the first row of each group.

  • First drop-down (x = ...), ROW_NUMBER(): ROW_NUMBER() assigns a sequential integer starting at 1 within each partition; with ORDER BY LastUpdated DESC, each customer's latest update gets 1.
  • Second drop-down (filter on the CTE), WHERE X = 1: The alias x is the CTE row number; WHERE X = 1 keeps exactly one row per customer: the latest, with all its columns.

Incorrect options:

  • First drop-down (x = ...), LAST_VALUE() — Why it is incorrect: LAST_VALUE() returns an expression value from the last row of the frame, on every row; it produces no marker to filter by (and with the default frame it would not even be the last row).
  • First drop-down (x = ...), NTILE() — Why it is incorrect: NTILE() splits the partition into N groups; it returns group numbers, not a unique marker for the latest row.
  • Second drop-down (filter on the CTE), HAVING MAX(LastUpdated) = 1 — Why it is incorrect: HAVING filters aggregated groups (it needs GROUP BY) and compares a date with the number 1, which makes no sense.
  • Second drop-down (filter on the CTE), WHERE LastUpdated = MAX(LastUpdated) — Why it is incorrect: Aggregate functions cannot be used directly in WHERE; even with a subquery it would give the global latest date, not each customer's.
  • Official documentation: ROW_NUMBER (Transact-SQL), NTILE (Transact-SQL), LAST_VALUE (Transact-SQL)

q012.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.

You plan to create a Fabric notebook that will use Spark DataFrames to generate Microsoft Power BI visuals.

You run the following code.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • The code embeds an existing Power BI report: No
  • The code creates a Power BI report: Yes
  • The code displays a summary of the DataFrame: Yes

Analysis: The code imports QuickVisualize, get_dataset_config and Report from the powerbiclient package and then runs PBI_visualize = QuickVisualize(get_dataset_config(df)) followed by PBI_visualize.

Embeds an existing report: No. Embedding an existing report in a notebook requires the Report class, the report ID, an access token and an embed URL (Report(group_id=..., report_id=..., auth=...)). Although Report is imported, it is never instantiated or rendered, and nothing in the code references an existing report, so nothing is embedded.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Jupyter client - embed a report

Creates a Power BI report: Yes. get_dataset_config(df) builds a dataset configuration from the DataFrame and QuickVisualize uses it to generate and render a new (quick) Power BI report with automatically suggested visuals directly in the notebook cell. The report can then be edited and even saved to the workspace. This is what the statement means by "creates a Power BI report".

Displays a summary of the DataFrame: Yes. The quick visualization is an auto-generated overview of the dataset: it shows the fields of the DataFrame with default visuals and summary aggregations, so the person gets a quick summary of the data. This item is the most debated one (the code does not call describe() or summary()), but within the question the generated quick report is considered a summary of the data, so the statement is Yes.

q013.stem:
You are the administrator of a Fabric workspace that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1. Lakehouse1 contains the following tables:

Table1: A Delta table created by using a shortcut

Table2: An external table created by using Spark

Table3: A managed table -

You plan to connect to Lakehouse1 by using its SQL endpoint.

What will you be able to do after connecting to Lakehouse1?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Read Table3.

Why it is correct: The SQL analytics endpoint of a lakehouse works in read-only mode over Delta tables: you can query them with T-SQL, create views, functions and stored procedures on top of them, but you cannot insert, update or delete data. Table3 is a managed table, which means it is a Delta table stored under the lakehouse's /Tables folder, so it is automatically discovered and exposed by the endpoint. Therefore, after connecting you will be able to read (SELECT from) Table3.

  • Official documentation: What is the SQL analytics endpoint for a lakehouse?
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. Update the data in Table3.

Why it is incorrect: Even though Table3 is visible, the SQL analytics endpoint does not allow data modification (no INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE). To change the data of a lakehouse table you have to use Apache Spark (notebooks, Spark job definitions) or a dataflow/pipeline that writes to the lakehouse. Only a warehouse offers full T-SQL write operations.

  • Official documentation: What is the SQL analytics endpoint for a lakehouse?

C. Read Table2.

Why it is incorrect: Table2 is an external table created with Spark. External Delta tables created with Spark code are not visible to the SQL analytics endpoint, so you cannot query them through it. To make external Delta data visible, you would use a shortcut in the Tables section instead.

  • Official documentation: What is the SQL analytics endpoint for a lakehouse? (external tables and shortcuts)

D. Update the data in Table1.

Why it is incorrect: Table1 is a Delta table created via a shortcut. Shortcuts in the Tables section are exposed in the SQL analytics endpoint, so you can read it, but, as with any table, the endpoint is read-only, so it cannot be updated through T-SQL. In addition, the data of a shortcut lives in the target location, which is not modified through the endpoint.

  • Official documentation: What is the SQL analytics endpoint for a lakehouse?

q014.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse.

You use a dataflow to load a new dataset from OneLake to the warehouse.

You need to add a PowerQuery step to identify the maximum values for the numeric columns.

Which function should you include in the step?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Table.Profile

Why it is correct: in the Power Query M formula language (used in Fabric Dataflows Gen2), Table.Profile(table as table, optional additionalAggregates as nullable list) automatically analyzes all columns of a table and returns a summary table where each row represents a source column with its profiling statistics:

  • Min: the minimum value of the column.
  • Max: the maximum value of every column (numeric, date, text, etc.) in a single operation, with no need to write column-by-column transformations.
  • Other indicators such as Average, StandardDeviation, Count, NullCount and DistinctCount.

Official documentation: Table.Profile (Power Query M) - Microsoft Learn | Data profiling tools in Power Query - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Table.MaxN — Why it is incorrect: Table.MaxN(table, comparisonCriteria, countOrCondition) returns the N largest whole rows of a table according to a comparison criterion on a column or condition. It does not calculate or summarize the maximum values of multiple numeric columns. Official documentation: Table.MaxN (Power Query M) - Microsoft Learn
  • Option B — Table.Max — Why it is incorrect: Table.Max(table, comparisonCriteria, optional default) returns a single record (one whole row) matching the maximum value according to the comparison criterion (e.g. the row with the highest amount in a single column), instead of identifying the maximum values of all numeric columns in the dataset. Official documentation: Table.Max (Power Query M) - Microsoft Learn
  • Option C — Table.Range — Why it is incorrect: Table.Range(table, offset, optional count) extracts a positional subset of rows starting at the given offset, like paging or trimming by row index. It performs no aggregation or statistical profiling of maximum values. Official documentation: Table.Range (Power Query M) - Microsoft Learn

q015.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a machine learning model registered in a Fabric workspace.

You need to use the model to generate predictions by using the PREDICT function in a Fabric notebook.

Which two languages can you use to perform model scoring? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Spark SQL
  • Option D: PySpark

Why it is correct: In Microsoft Fabric, the PREDICT function is a scalable batch-scoring capability that runs on Apache Spark. You invoke it from a Fabric notebook, which is a Spark environment, by using either the Transformer API / PySpark (for example MLFlowTransformer and model.transform(df), or a PySpark UDF) or Spark SQL (SELECT PREDICT('...', columns) FROM table). Because the question explicitly says the scoring happens in a Fabric notebook, the two supported languages are Spark SQL and PySpark.

  • Official documentation: Machine learning model scoring with PREDICT in Microsoft Fabric / Tutorial: Score a model with PREDICT in a Spark pool
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. T-SQL

Why it is incorrect: The PREDICT feature in Fabric notebooks is executed by the Spark engine. A T-SQL endpoint (warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint) is not a Fabric notebook language option for this scenario, so T-SQL is not one of the languages used for PREDICT-based scoring here.

  • Official documentation: Machine learning model scoring with PREDICT in Microsoft Fabric

B. DAX

Why it is incorrect: DAX is the query and formula language of semantic models. It is not available in Fabric notebooks as a scoring language and cannot call a registered machine learning model through PREDICT.

  • Official documentation: Machine learning model scoring with PREDICT in Microsoft Fabric

q016.stem:
You are analyzing the data in a Fabric notebook.

You have a Spark DataFrame assigned to a variable named df.

You need to use the Chart view in the notebook to explore the data manually.

Which function should you run to make the data available in the Chart view?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: display

Why it is correct: In a Fabric notebook, display(df) renders a Spark (or pandas) DataFrame as an interactive output widget. By default it shows a table view, and from that widget you can switch to the Chart view to build charts manually (chart type, axes, aggregation, legend, and so on), and even show data statistics with display(df, summary=True). This is exactly what is needed to explore the data manually with the Chart view.

  • Official documentation: Notebook visualization in Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. displayHTML

Why it is incorrect: displayHTML() renders raw HTML/JavaScript strings, which is useful for libraries such as D3.js, Bokeh or Plotly. It does not provide the DataFrame table and chart view widget.

  • Official documentation: Notebook visualization in Microsoft Fabric

B. show

Why it is incorrect: df.show() prints a plain-text table of the first rows in the cell output. It does not create the interactive widget, so there is no Chart view. (In the docs, show appears only as plt.show() for Matplotlib figures.)

  • Official documentation: Notebook visualization in Microsoft Fabric

C. write

Why it is incorrect: df.write is the DataFrameWriter used to save data (to Delta tables, files, etc.). It does not display anything and has nothing to do with the Chart view.

  • Official documentation: Notebook visualization in Microsoft Fabric

q017.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a Microsoft Power BI report named Report1. Report1 includes a Python visual.

Data displayed by the visual is grouped automatically and duplicate rows are NOT displayed.

You need all rows to appear in the visual.

What should you do?
options: Reference the columns in the Python code by index.
Modify the Sort Column By property for all columns.
Add a unique field to each row.
Modify the Summarize By property for all columns.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Add a unique field to each row.

Why it is correct: in Power BI, both Python and R visuals receive their input data from the semantic model through a DataFrame (dataset) generated by a grouping DAX query. By the Power BI engine's internal design:

  1. Automatic deduplication of the input DataFrame: before passing the data to the Python script, Power BI automatically groups rows that have identical values in all the fields dragged into the visual's Values well, removing any duplicate row (for example, when two different observations share exactly the same values in the variables to plot in a scatter chart).
  2. Official solution — a unique identifier: to prevent Power BI from collapsing rows with identical values and ensure every row appears in the Python visual, add a column with a unique identifier per row (such as a primary key or a row index generated in Power Query) to the Values well of the Python visual. Since that column's value differs for each record, the engine does not group or deduplicate the rows, even if you never use that column in the Python script.

Official documentation: Create Power BI visuals by using Python (known limitations) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Reference the columns in the Python code by index — Why it is incorrect: grouping and duplicate removal happen before the dataset DataFrame reaches the Python interpreter (while the Power BI DAX query is generated). Referencing columns by position (dataset.iloc[:, 0]) instead of by name inside the script does not recover rows Power BI already deduplicated. Official documentation: Create Power BI visuals by using Python - Microsoft Learn
  • Option B — Modify the Sort by column property for all columns — Why it is incorrect: Sort by column only changes the order in which a column's values are displayed (e.g. sorting month names by month number); it does not affect grouping behavior nor prevent duplicate rows from being removed in a Python visual's dataset. Official documentation: Sort one column by another column in Power BI - Microsoft Learn
  • Option D — Modify the Summarize By property for all columns — Why it is incorrect: in Python (and R) visuals, Power BI sets all columns to "Don't summarize" by default when added to the Values well. Even then, Power BI still runs an implicit SUMMARIZE/grouping over the selected columns, so rows with identical values are still removed unless a unique per-row field exists. Official documentation: Create Power BI visuals by using Python (prepare your script) - Microsoft Learn

q018.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model. The model contains data about retail stores.

You need to write a DAX query that will be executed by using the XMLA endpoint. The query must return a table of stores that have opened since December 1, 2023.

How should you complete the DAX expression? To answer, drag the appropriate values to the correct targets. Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First target: DEFINE
  • Second target: EVALUATE
  • Third target (inside FILTER): TABLE

Why it is correct: A DAX query executed through the XMLA endpoint (SSMS, DAX Studio, etc.) follows the structure DEFINE ... EVALUATE ...: the optional DEFINE section declares query-scoped variables, measures or tables, and every query must contain at least one EVALUATE statement that returns a table.

  • First target, DEFINE: DEFINE is the optional section where query-scoped variables, measures or tables are declared; here it holds VAR _SalesSince.
  • Second target, EVALUATE: EVALUATE is the statement that returns the result of a table expression (here the FILTER over Store); every DAX query needs at least one.
  • Third target (inside FILTER), TABLE: TABLE fills the first argument of FILTER according to the study document (see the note); the result is the table of stores opened since December 1, 2023.

Incorrect options:

  • First target, EVALUATE — Why it is incorrect: EVALUATE returns a table; it does not declare variables.
  • First target, FILTER — Why it is incorrect: FILTER is a table function, not a keyword that opens a variable declaration.
  • First target, SUMMARIZE — Why it is incorrect: SUMMARIZE groups columns; it does not introduce a VAR.
  • First target, TABLE — Why it is incorrect: TABLE is not what introduces a VAR in a query.
  • Second target, DEFINE — Why it is incorrect: DEFINE was already used above to declare the variable and returns no results.
  • Second target, FILTER — Why it is incorrect: FILTER cannot be the query statement keyword; it goes inside EVALUATE.
  • Second target, SUMMARIZE — Why it is incorrect: SUMMARIZE is a table function, not the statement that returns the result.
  • Second target, TABLE — Why it is incorrect: TABLE is not the query statement that returns the table.
  • Third target (inside FILTER), DEFINE — Why it is incorrect: DEFINE declares variables; it cannot be the first argument of FILTER, which must be a table expression.
  • Third target (inside FILTER), EVALUATE — Why it is incorrect: EVALUATE is a query statement, not a table expression for the first argument of FILTER.
  • Third target (inside FILTER), FILTER — Why it is incorrect: FILTER inside FILTER does not provide the base table the argument needs.
  • Third target (inside FILTER), SUMMARIZE — Why it is incorrect: SUMMARIZE does return a table and could be defended (see the note), but the document's answer is TABLE.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but TABLE is not a standard DAX function; the function that actually produces a table from a base table and columns, and fits as the first argument of FILTER here, is SUMMARIZE, which could also be argued for the third box. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: DEFINE statement (DAX), DAX queries, SUMMARIZE function (DAX), FILTER function (DAX)

q019.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a dataflow named Dataflow1. Dataflow1 has a query that returns 2,000 rows.

You view the query in Power Query as shown in the following exhibit.

What can you identify about the pickupLongitude column?
options: All the table rows are profiled.
There are 935 values that occur only once.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: The column has duplicate values.

Why it is correct: The Column statistics of pickupLongitude in the exhibit show Count = 1000, Distinct count = 935 and Unique count = 871. In Power Query, distinct is the number of different values, and unique is the number of values that appear exactly once. If all values were different, the distinct count would equal the count (1000). Since there are only 935 distinct values among 1000 rows profiled, at least some values are repeated, so the column contains duplicates.

  • Official documentation: Using the data profiling tools - Power Query
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. All the table rows are profiled.

Why it is incorrect: The query returns 2,000 rows, but the profile shows Count = 1000. By default Power Query profiles only the top 1,000 rows ("Column profiling based on top 1000 rows"); to profile all rows you must switch to "Column profiling based on entire data set".

  • Official documentation: Using the data profiling tools - Power Query

C. The column has missing values.

Why it is incorrect: In the statistics, Error count = 0, Null count = 0 (and NaN count = 0), so there are no missing values in the profiled rows.

  • Official documentation: Using the data profiling tools - Power Query

D. There are 935 values that occur only once.

Why it is incorrect: 935 is the distinct count (number of different values). The number of values that occur exactly once is the unique count, which is 871.

  • Official documentation: Using the data profiling tools - Power Query

q020.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant named Tenant1 that contains a workspace named WS1.

WS1 uses a capacity named C1 and contains a dataset named DS1.

You need to ensure read-write access to DS1 is available by using XMLA endpoint.

What should be modified first?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: the C1 settings

Why it is correct: The XMLA endpoint is exposed by the capacity that hosts the workspace. Its mode (Off, Read Only or Read Write) is configured in the capacity settings (the XMLA Endpoint option under Power BI workloads in the capacity settings of the admin portal). Read-write access is needed to deploy and modify models with tools such as SSMS, Tabular Editor or ALM Toolkit. If the capacity (C1) is set to Read Only (or Off), nothing else can grant write access, so the capacity setting is the first thing to change. The workspace and the semantic model (dataset) only need to be on that capacity.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. the DS1 settings

Why it is incorrect: The dataset's own settings do not control XMLA endpoint access. The access mode is defined at capacity level and the endpoint is enabled for the tenant; individual semantic model settings cannot enable read-write.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint

B. the WS1 settings

Why it is incorrect: The workspace only needs to be assigned to a capacity that supports the XMLA endpoint. The workspace settings do not contain the XMLA read/write mode.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint

D. the Tenant1 settings

Why it is incorrect: The tenant has an "Allow XMLA endpoints and Analyze in Excel with on-premises datasets" setting that is typically enabled by default and controls whether the feature is permitted, but it does not set the read-write mode. The read-write mode is selected per capacity, which is why the capacity setting is the first thing to modify.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint

q021.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 is assigned to a Fabric capacity.

You need to recommend a solution to provide users with the ability to create and publish custom Direct Lake semantic models by using external tools. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.

Which three actions in the Fabric Admin portal should you include in the recommendation? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
options: From the Tenant settings, set Allow XMLA Endpoints and Analyze in Excel with on-premises datasets to Enabled.
From the Tenant settings, set Allow Azure Active Directory guest users to access Microsoft Fabric to Enabled.
From the Tenant settings, select Users can edit data model in the Power BI service.
From the Capacity settings, set XMLA Endpoint to Read Write.
From the Tenant settings, set Users can create Fabric items to Enabled.
From the Tenant settings, enable Publish to Web.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option A: From the Tenant settings, set Allow XMLA endpoints and Analyze in Excel with on-premises datasets to Enabled.
  • Option D: From the Capacity settings, set XMLA Endpoint to Read Write.
  • Option E: From the Tenant settings, set Users can create Fabric items to Enabled.

Why they are correct: for users to create and publish custom Direct Lake semantic models with external tools (such as Tabular Editor, ALM Toolkit or SQL Server Management Studio) in a workspace assigned to a Fabric capacity (Workspace1), exactly three settings are required in the Fabric admin portal:

  • Option E — Users can create Fabric items = Enabled: a Direct Lake semantic model is a native Microsoft Fabric item (unlike a traditional imported Power BI model). To create and publish it in the workspace, the tenant-level switch allowing creation of Fabric items must be enabled for the relevant users.
  • Option A — Allow XMLA endpoints and Analyze in Excel with on-premises datasets = Enabled: the master tenant-level switch authorizing XMLA connectivity to the tenant's capacities. If it is disabled at tenant level, no external tool can connect through the XMLA endpoint even if the capacity allows it.
  • Option D — XMLA Endpoint = Read Write in Capacity settings: once XMLA is allowed at tenant level, the capacity's XMLA endpoint must be set to Read Write (instead of Off or Read Only), because publishing and modifying semantic model metadata from external tools requires write operations on the tabular engine.

Official documentation: Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint - Microsoft Learn | Enable Microsoft Fabric for your organization - Microsoft Learn | Direct Lake overview - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — From the Tenant settings, set Allow Azure Active Directory guest users to access Microsoft Fabric to Enabled — Why it is incorrect: it enables B2B access for external guest users from other Microsoft Entra ID tenants. The statement does not mention external guests, and enabling it needlessly would violate the principle of least privilege. Official documentation: Tenant settings - Export and sharing (guest users) - Microsoft Learn
  • Option C — From the Tenant settings, select Users can edit data model in the Power BI service — Why it is incorrect: this setting only enables the web editor in the Power BI/Fabric service browser interface; it is not needed to create or publish Direct Lake semantic models with external tools (which work through the XMLA endpoint). Official documentation: Edit data models in the Power BI service - Microsoft Learn
  • Option F — From the Tenant settings, enable Publish to Web — Why it is incorrect: Publish to web generates public, anonymous embed codes for reports on the internet. It has nothing to do with Direct Lake or external tools, and enabling it without need risks public data exposure and breaks least privilege. Official documentation: Publish to web from Power BI - Microsoft Learn

q022.stem:
You are creating a semantic model in Microsoft Power BI Desktop.

You plan to make bulk changes to the model by using the Tabular Model Definition Language (TMDL) extension for Microsoft Visual Studio Code.

You need to save the semantic model to a file.

Which file format should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: PBIP

Why it is correct: A Power BI Project (.pbip) saves the report and the semantic model as a folder of plain-text files instead of a single binary container. The semantic model is stored in a <name>.SemanticModel folder using either TMDL (Tabular Model Definition Language) or TMSL/BIM format, with the TMDL format being the default in current versions. Because TMDL is a human-readable, folder-and-file based representation of the model (one file per table, expressions, roles and so on), you can open the folder in Visual Studio Code with the TMDL extension, make bulk edits (rename many measures, change formatting, refactor), and reopen the project in Power BI Desktop. The same format also works well with Git source control, which is why it is the format for developer scenarios.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects (PBIP) overview and Power BI Desktop project semantic model folder
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. PBIX

Why it is incorrect: A .pbix file is a single compressed binary package containing the report, the model and (in import mode) the data. It cannot be opened or edited as text in VS Code, so the TMDL extension cannot make bulk changes to it.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects (PBIP) overview

C. PBIT

Why it is incorrect: A .pbit file is a Power BI template: it contains the model schema, queries and report definition but no data, and it is also a single packaged file. Its purpose is to create new reports from a template with parameters, not to expose the model as TMDL text files for external editing.

  • Official documentation: Create and use report templates in Power BI Desktop

D. PBIDS

Why it is incorrect: A .pbids file is a small JSON file that stores data source connection information so users can start a new report already connected to a source. It does not contain a semantic model at all.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects (PBIP) overview

q023.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

Warehouse1 contains three schemas named schemaA, schemaB, and schemaC.

You need to ensure that a user named User1 can truncate tables in schemaA only.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First box (permission): ALTER
  • Second box (securable): SCHEMA::schemaA

Why it is correct: The completed statement is GRANT ALTER ON SCHEMA::schemaA TO User1;

  • First box (permission), ALTER: for TRUNCATE TABLE the minimum permission required is ALTER on the table; granted on a schema it is inherited by all of its tables.
  • Second box (securable), SCHEMA::schemaA: SCHEMA::schemaA limits the permission exactly to schemaA, to its current and future tables, and to no other schema (least privilege).

Incorrect options:

  • First box (permission), CONNECT — Why it is incorrect: CONNECT only allows connecting to the database; it grants no rights on any table.
  • First box (permission), EXECUTE — Why it is incorrect: EXECUTE is for running stored procedures and functions; it does not allow TRUNCATE TABLE on tables.
  • Second box (securable), DATABASE::schemaA — Why it is incorrect: DATABASE:: refers to the database, not to a schema; granting ALTER there would give rights over schemaB and schemaC.
  • Second box (securable), OBJECT::schemaA — Why it is incorrect: OBJECT:: points to a specific object (table, view…), not a schema; it would have to be repeated per table and future tables would be missed.

q024.stem:
You plan to deploy Microsoft Power BI items by using Fabric deployment pipelines. You have a deployment pipeline that contains three stages named Development, Test, and Production. A workspace is assigned to each stage.

You need to provide Power BI developers with access to the pipeline. The solution must meet the following requirements:

Ensure that the developers can deploy items to the workspaces for

Development and Test.

Prevent the developers from deploying items to the workspace for Production.

Follow the principle of least privilege.

Which three levels of access should you assign to the developers? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
options: Build permission to the production semantic models
Admin access to the deployment pipeline
Viewer access to the Development and Test workspaces
Viewer access to the Production workspace
Contributor access to the Development and Test workspaces
Contributor access to the Production workspace

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option B: Admin access to the deployment pipeline.
  • Option D: Viewer access to the Production workspace.
  • Option E: Contributor access to the Development and Test workspaces.

Why they are correct: in Microsoft Fabric deployment pipelines, the permission model separates access to the pipeline itself (which has a single role: Admin) from the workspace roles assigned at each stage. To deploy items between two adjacent stages (Development → Test, or Test → Production), the user must be a pipeline admin and have at least the Contributor or Member role in both the source and target workspaces:

  • Option B — Admin access to the deployment pipeline: a mandatory requirement for developers to see the pipeline, access its stages, compare content and run deployments. It is the only permission level that exists at pipeline level.
  • Option E — Contributor access to the Development and Test workspaces: Contributor is the least-privileged workspace role in Fabric that lets users create, edit, delete and deploy content between Development and Test (unlike Member or Admin, which grant unnecessary extra permissions such as resharing items or managing workspace access).
  • Option D — Viewer access to the Production workspace: to compare content between Test and Production (see which items exist or differ in the Production stage) without being able to modify or deploy changes to it, developers only need read access through the Viewer role in the Production workspace. With Viewer (and not Contributor, Member or Admin) in Production, Fabric blocks any deployment attempt to Production, strictly following least privilege.

Official documentation: Deployment pipelines process and permissions in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn | Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Build permission to the production semantic models — Why it is incorrect: Build permission on a semantic model lets users connect to it to create new reports or use Analyze in Excel. It does not grant visibility of the other items in the Production workspace in the pipeline interface and is not part of the stage-to-stage deployment control model. Official documentation: Build permission for shared semantic models - Microsoft Learn
  • Option C — Viewer access to the Development and Test workspaces — Why it is incorrect: Viewer is read-only. With Viewer in Development and Test, developers could not publish or edit items in Development nor deploy changes to Test, failing the first requirement. Official documentation: Deployment pipelines process and permissions in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn
  • Option F — Contributor access to the Production workspace — Why it is incorrect: assigning Contributor in the Production workspace (combined with pipeline admin access) would let developers deploy items directly to Production and modify them, directly violating the requirement to prevent them from deploying there. Official documentation: Deployment pipelines process and permissions in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

q025.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains a DirectQuery semantic model. The model queries a data source that has 500 million rows.

You have a Microsoft Power Bi report named Report1 that uses the model.

Report1 contains visuals on multiple pages.

You need to reduce the query execution time for the visuals on all the pages.

What are two features that you can use? Each correct answer presents a complete solution,

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option A: User-defined aggregations.
  • Option B: Automatic aggregation.

Why they are correct: when a DirectQuery semantic model queries a massive fact table (500 million rows) and a Power BI report (Report1) has several pages with visuals that trigger heavy queries against the source, aggregations let summary-level queries be answered from the ultra-fast in-memory cache (VertiPaq) instead of sending GROUP BY queries over 500 million rows to the underlying source:

  • Option A — User-defined aggregations: lets you design pre-calculated aggregation tables (usually in Import storage mode, with Dual mode for the dimensions) that summarize the data at a higher granularity (e.g. by day/month and product). When Report1 visuals request data at that level or above, Power BI automatically redirects the query to the in-memory aggregation table, drastically reducing query execution time and reserving DirectQuery access to the 500-million-row table for the lowest level of detail.
  • Option B — Automatic aggregation: available in Premium and Microsoft Fabric capacities, it uses machine learning to analyze the actual query logs generated by users in reports (such as Report1) and creates, manages and refreshes in-memory aggregation tables with no manual modeling, speeding up repetitive or expensive DirectQuery queries across all report pages.

Official documentation: User-defined aggregations - Microsoft Learn | Automatic aggregations - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option C — Query caching — Why it is incorrect: query caching in Premium/Fabric capacities stores the results of the initial dashboard and report queries, but it only applies when users first open the report in its default state (no filters or interactive slicers) and it is not supported for DirectQuery semantic models or live connections (where each interaction sends fresh queries to the source). It also does not speed up ad-hoc or filtered queries across the pages of a 500-million-row DirectQuery model. Official documentation: Query caching in Power BI Premium - Microsoft Learn
  • Option D — OneLake integration — Why it is incorrect: OneLake integration for semantic models exports copies of semantic model tables (mainly in Import mode) to Delta folders in OneLake so other Fabric workloads (Spark, SQL, T-SQL) can consume them. It is not a query optimization mechanism and does not reduce the execution time of the DirectQuery queries generated by a Power BI report's visuals. Official documentation: OneLake integration for semantic models - Microsoft Learn
