You have a Spark DataFrame assigned to a variable named df. The DataFrame returns four columns.

You need to change the data type of a string column named Age to integer. The solution must return a DataFrame that includes all the columns.

How should you complete the code? To answer, drag the appropriate values to the correct targets. Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Box 1: withColumn
  • Box 2: col
  • Box 3: cast

Why it is correct: Resulting code: df.withColumn("age", col("age").cast("int")).show()

  • Box 1, withColumn: withColumn adds or replaces a column and keeps all the others, as the requirement states.
  • Box 2, col: col("age") builds a Column reference to the existing column, which is what the second argument of withColumn expects.
  • Box 3, cast: Column.cast("int") converts the values to the target type; it accepts a type name or a DataType.

Incorrect options:

  • Box 1, cast — Why it is incorrect: cast is a Column method, not a DataFrame method.
  • Box 1, col — Why it is incorrect: col is a function that creates a column reference, not a DataFrame method.
  • Box 1, get — Why it is incorrect: get is not a DataFrame method for this purpose.
  • Box 1, select — Why it is incorrect: select would return only the listed columns; the other three would have to be listed too.
  • Box 1, selectExpr — Why it is incorrect: selectExpr returns only the given expressions, not all the columns.
  • Box 1, transform — Why it is incorrect: transform applies a function to a whole DataFrame and does not take a column name plus an expression.
  • Box 2, cast — Why it is incorrect: cast is a column method; it does not create a column reference.
  • Box 2, get — Why it is incorrect: get does not produce a column reference in this position.
  • Box 2, select — Why it is incorrect: select is a DataFrame method; it does not produce a Column in this position.
  • Box 2, selectExpr — Why it is incorrect: selectExpr is a DataFrame method; it does not produce a Column here.
  • Box 2, transform — Why it is incorrect: transform does not produce a column reference in this position.
  • Box 2, withColumn — Why it is incorrect: withColumn is a DataFrame method; it cannot be nested as a column reference.
  • Box 3, col — Why it is incorrect: col creates the column reference; it does not convert types.
  • Box 3, get — Why it is incorrect: get is not the method that changes a column's type.
  • Box 3, select — Why it is incorrect: select is a DataFrame method, not a Column method.
  • Box 3, selectExpr — Why it is incorrect: selectExpr is a DataFrame method, not a Column method.
  • Box 3, transform — Why it is incorrect: transform does not change a column's type with a type name.
  • Box 3, withColumn — Why it is incorrect: withColumn is a DataFrame method, not a Column method.

q072.stem:
-

You have an Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 account named storage1 that contains a Parquet file named sales.parquet.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Using a notebook in Workspace1, you need to load the content of the file to the default lakehouse. The solution must ensure that the content will display automatically as a table named Sales in Lakehouse explorer.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First dropdown (.format(" … ")): delta
  • Second dropdown (.saveAsTable(" … ")): sales

The resulting full PySpark code is:

df = spark.read.parquet("abfss://fs1@storage1.dfs.core.windows.net/files/sales.parquet")

df.write.mode("overwrite").format("delta").saveAsTable("sales")

Why it is correct:

  • First dropdown → delta: in Microsoft Fabric, managed tables in a lakehouse use Delta Lake as the native format (ACID transactions, the SQL analytics endpoint and Power BI Direct Lake mode). Although the source is read from a Parquet file, when writing it as a table you must specify .format("delta") so the _delta_log is registered and it shows up as a managed table in Lakehouse explorer. Official documentation: Lakehouse and Delta Lake tables in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn
  • Second dropdown → sales: .saveAsTable("<table_name>") creates a managed table in the metastore of the default lakehouse attached to the notebook (files end up in Tables/sales in OneLake) and accepts only the logical table identifier ("sales"), not a path. (In the Spanish statement it appears as “Sales”.) Official documentation: Load data into your lakehouse with a notebook - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

First dropdown (.format(" … "))

  • Options csv and parquet — Why they are incorrect: in a Fabric lakehouse explorer, the Tables section only recognizes and automatically exposes Delta-format tables (or explicitly registered external tables). Saving in a non-Delta format does not create a native managed table compatible with Fabric's built-in analytical capabilities. Official documentation: Lakehouse and Delta Lake tables in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

Second dropdown (.saveAsTable(" … "))

  • Option files/sales — Why it is incorrect: for two reasons: .saveAsTable() expects a table name, not a path with a / (it causes a parsing error in Spark SQL); and any data written to the lakehouse Files/ folder is treated as unstructured files and does not appear as a table in the Tables section. Official documentation: Explore data in a lakehouse (Files vs. Tables) - Microsoft Learn
  • Option tables/sales — Why it is incorrect: although Spark physically stores managed tables in Tables/sales, .saveAsTable() handles that path internally. Passing "tables/sales" raises an AnalysisException because / is not valid in a table name in the Spark catalog (for physical paths you would use .save("Tables/sales")). Official documentation: Work with Delta tables in Apache Spark for Fabric - Microsoft Learn

q073.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

In Workspace1, you create a data pipeline named Pipeline1.

You have CSV files stored in an Azure Storage account.

You need to add an activity to Pipeline1 that will copy data from the CSV files to Lakehouse1. The activity must support Power Query M formula language expressions.

Which type of activity should you add?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Dataflow

Why it is correct: Power Query M is the formula language used by Dataflow Gen2. In a Fabric data pipeline, the Dataflow activity runs a Dataflow Gen2 item, and the transformations inside that dataflow (including the source CSV files in the Azure Storage account and the destination Lakehouse1) are authored with Power Query M expressions. So, adding a Dataflow activity is the only option in the list that both moves the CSV data into the lakehouse and supports M expressions.

  • Official documentation: Transform data by using the Dataflow activity - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. Notebook

Why it is incorrect: The Notebook activity runs a Fabric notebook written in PySpark, Scala, Spark SQL or R. It can load CSV files, but it has nothing to do with Power Query M expressions.

  • Official documentation: Transform data by using the Dataflow activity - Microsoft Fabric

C. Script

Why it is incorrect: The Script activity executes SQL statements (queries or DML/DDL) against a supported relational data store. It is not designed to copy CSV files into a lakehouse and it does not use M expressions.

  • Official documentation: Transform data by using the Dataflow activity - Microsoft Fabric

D. Copy data

Why it is incorrect: The Copy data activity can indeed copy CSV files into a lakehouse (see the lakehouse connector), but it is configured through source/destination settings and mapping, and it does not support Power Query M. In the pipeline, the Power Query experience is provided by the Dataflow activity, which is why the Copy data activity does not satisfy the stated requirement.

  • Official documentation: Configure Lakehouse in a copy activity - Microsoft Fabric

q074.stem:
-

You have a Fabric tenant that contains lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

Lakehouse1 contains a Delta table with eight columns.

You receive new data that contains the same eight columns and two additional columns.

You create a Spark DataFrame and assign the DataFrame to a variable named df.

The DataFrame contains the new data.

You need to add the new data to the Delta table to meet the following requirements:

  • Keep all the existing rows.
  • Ensure that all the new data is added to the table.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First dropdown (.mode): ("append")
  • Second dropdown (.option): ("mergeSchema","true")

The resulting full PySpark code is:

df.write.format("delta").mode("append") \
  .option("mergeSchema", "true") \
  .saveAsTable("table")

Why it is correct:

  • First dropdown → ("append"): to keep all existing rows and add only the new records at the end of the Delta table in Lakehouse1, use the append mode, which leaves current data intact and adds the new Parquet files to the Delta Lake transaction log. Official documentation: Table batch reads and writes (Append) - Microsoft Learn
  • Second dropdown → ("mergeSchema","true"): by default Delta Lake enforces the schema and rejects an append whose DataFrame has columns missing from the target table (AnalysisException: A schema mismatch detected). Since df has the 8 original columns plus 2 new ones, .option("mergeSchema", "true") merges both schemas: it adds the two columns to the table definition, fills them with NULL in the existing historical rows and stores the new rows with all their values. Official documentation: Update Delta Lake table schema (Automatic schema evolution) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

First dropdown (.mode)

  • Option ("overwrite") — Why it is incorrect: The overwrite mode completely replaces the target table data, deleting all existing rows and violating the first requirement. Official documentation: Table batch reads and writes (Overwrite) - Microsoft Learn
  • Options ("error") and ("errorifexists") — Why they are incorrect: Both values (synonyms in Apache Spark and the default behavior) make the write fail with an exception if the table "table" already exists in Lakehouse1, preventing the new data from being added. Official documentation: Save modes in Apache Spark DataFrameWriter - Apache Spark documentation
  • Option ("ignore") — Why it is incorrect: The ignore mode silently skips the whole write, without an error, when the target table already exists, so none of the new df data would be added. Official documentation: Save modes in Apache Spark DataFrameWriter - Apache Spark documentation

Second dropdown (.option)

  • Option ("mergeSchema","false") — Why it is incorrect: It disables schema evolution (the Delta Lake default). Appending a 10-column DataFrame to an 8-column Delta table fails with a schema mismatch. Official documentation: Update Delta Lake table schema - Microsoft Learn
  • Options ("overwriteSchema","true") and ("overwriteSchema","false") — Why they are incorrect: overwriteSchema is only supported together with .mode("overwrite") (it replaces schema and data). Combined with .mode("append"), Delta Lake raises an error saying the schema cannot be overwritten during an append. Official documentation: Update Delta Lake table schema (Overwrite schema) - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Update Delta Lake table schema - Azure Databricks
Update Delta Lake table schema - Azure Databricks

q075.stem:
-

You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Sales.Orders.

Sales.Orders contains the following columns.

You need to write a T-SQL query that will return the following columns.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Box 1: COALESCE
  • Box 2: LEAST

Why it is correct: Resulting query: COALESCE(Weight, Quantity, 1) AS ChargedQuantity and LEAST(ListPrice, SalePrice) AS OrderPrice.

  • Box 1, COALESCE: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL expression from left to right: COALESCE(Weight, Quantity, 1) implements Weight → Quantity → 1.
  • Box 2, LEAST: LEAST returns the minimum value across several columns of the same row and ignores NULLs when at least one value is non-null (ListPrice is NOT NULL).

Incorrect options:

  • Box 1, CHOOSE — Why it is incorrect: CHOOSE picks an item from a list by position (its first argument is an index); it does not evaluate nulls.
  • Box 1, IIF — Why it is incorrect: IIF is a two-branch conditional; it cannot express a three-level fallback in a single call.
  • Box 2, COALESCE — Why it is incorrect: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value, not the lowest.
  • Box 2, MIN — Why it is incorrect: MIN is an aggregate across rows of one column, not across columns of the same row.
  • Official documentation: COALESCE (Transact-SQL), LEAST (Transact-SQL)

LEAST (Transact-SQL)

q076.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse.

You plan to use a visual query to merge two tables.

You need to ensure that the query returns all the rows in both tables.

Which type of join should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: full outer

Why it is correct: In a visual query (Merge queries), the join kind defines which rows come back. A full outer join returns all the rows from both tables: matching rows are combined and the rows without a match on either side are kept with nulls in the columns of the other table. This is the only option that guarantees that no row from either table is lost.

  • Official documentation: Full outer join - Power Query
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. inner

Why it is incorrect: An inner join returns only the rows that have a match in both tables, so unmatched rows from either side are dropped.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

C. left outer

Why it is incorrect: A left outer join returns all rows from the first (left) table plus the matching rows of the second one; unmatched rows of the right table are lost.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

D. right anti

Why it is incorrect: A right anti join returns only the rows from the right table that have no match in the left table. It returns neither the matching rows nor the left table rows.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

E. right outer

Why it is incorrect: A right outer join returns all rows from the second (right) table plus the matching rows of the first one; unmatched rows of the left table are lost.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

F. left anti

Why it is incorrect: A left anti join returns only the rows from the left table that have no match in the right table, so it excludes all the matching rows and all the right-table rows.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

q077.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

Lakehouse1 contains a Delta table that has one million Parquet files.

You need to remove files that were NOT referenced by the table during the past 30 days. The solution must ensure that the transaction log remains consistent, and the ACID properties of the table are maintained.

What should you do?
options: From OneLake file explorer, delete the files.
Run the OPTIMIZE command and specify the Z-order parameter.
Run the OPTIMIZE command and specify the V-order parameter.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Run the VACUUM command.

Why it is correct: Delta tables keep old Parquet files that are no longer referenced by the current table version (for example after updates, deletes or OPTIMIZE) so that time travel and concurrent readers keep working. VACUUM removes the files that are no longer referenced by the Delta transaction log and are older than the retention threshold. Because it goes through the Delta engine, the transaction log stays consistent and ACID guarantees are maintained. The requirement of "not referenced during the past 30 days" maps to a retention interval of 30 days (720 hours); the Fabric default retention threshold is 7 days, so you would specify the retention explicitly (and in the lakehouse UI you can run the table maintenance with VACUUM and a custom retention).

  • Official documentation: Delta Lake table optimization and V-Order - Lakehouse table maintenance - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. From OneLake file explorer, delete the files.

Why it is incorrect: Deleting Parquet files by hand bypasses the Delta transaction log, which still references them. This can corrupt the table (queries fail with missing files) and breaks consistency and ACID guarantees. Furthermore, doing it for one million files by hand is impractical and you cannot reliably know which ones are unreferenced.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse table maintenance - Microsoft Fabric

B. Run the OPTIMIZE command and specify the Z-order parameter.

Why it is incorrect: OPTIMIZE compacts many small files into fewer larger ones (and Z-order co-locates related data to improve data skipping). It does not delete the old files; they remain on storage as unreferenced files until VACUUM is run. It can even create more unreferenced files.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse table maintenance - Microsoft Fabric

C. Run the OPTIMIZE command and specify the V-order parameter.

Why it is incorrect: V-Order is a write-time optimization of the Parquet layout that improves read performance. Combined with OPTIMIZE it rewrites files, but it does not remove the unreferenced ones, so it does not meet the requirement.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse table maintenance - Microsoft Fabric

links.t: Delta Lake table optimization and V-Order - Lakehouse table maintenance - Microsoft Fabric

q078.stem:
-

You are implementing two dimension tables named Customers and Products in a Fabric warehouse.

You need to use slowly changing dimension (SCD) to manage the versioning of data. The solution must meet the requirements shown in the following table.

Which type of SCD should you use for each table? To answer, drag the appropriate SCD types to the correct tables. Each SCD type may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Customers: Type 2
  • Products: Type 1

Why it is correct: The requirements table says that for Customers a change must create a new version of the row, and for Products the change must overwrite the existing value in the latest row.

  • Customers, Type 2: SCD Type 2 keeps history by inserting a new row version each time a tracked attribute changes.
  • Products, Type 1: SCD Type 1 overwrites the value in the existing row: only the latest value remains.

Incorrect options:

  • Customers, Type 0 — Why it is incorrect: Type 0 ignores changes; it does not create a new version.
  • Customers, Type 1 — Why it is incorrect: Type 1 overwrites and loses history; it does not create a new row.
  • Customers, Type 3 — Why it is incorrect: Type 3 stores only the previous value in an extra column, not a new row.
  • Products, Type 0 — Why it is incorrect: Type 0 never changes values; it would not overwrite the existing one.
  • Products, Type 2 — Why it is incorrect: Type 2 would add a new row instead of overwriting.
  • Products, Type 3 — Why it is incorrect: Type 3 adds a column with the previous value; it does not simply overwrite.
  • Official documentation: Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Microsoft Fabric, Slowly changing dimension type 1 - Microsoft Fabric, Dimensional modeling: dimension tables - Microsoft Fabric

links.t: Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Microsoft Fabric
Slowly changing dimension type 1 - Microsoft Fabric
Dimensional modeling: dimension tables - Microsoft Fabric

q079.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 and an Azure SQL database.

You plan to create a dataflow that will read data from the database, and then transform the data by performing an inner join.

You need to ignore spaces in the values when performing the inner join. The solution must minimize development effort.

What should you do?
options: Append the queries by using fuzzy matching.
Merge the queries by using fuzzy matching.
Append the queries by using a lookup table.
Merge the queries by using a lookup table.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Merge the queries by using fuzzy matching.

Why it is correct: In a dataflow (Power Query), an inner join between two queries is done with Merge queries (join kind = Inner). To make values match even when they differ in spaces, you enable Use fuzzy matching to perform the merge in the merge dialog. Fuzzy matching has options such as ignoring case and ignoring spaces (and similarity threshold), so no additional transformation steps to clean the data are needed, which minimizes development effort.

  • Official documentation: Fuzzy merge - Power Query
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Append the queries by using fuzzy matching.

Why it is incorrect: Append stacks the rows of one query on top of another (like UNION); it does not perform a join, and there is no fuzzy matching in append.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

C. Append the queries by using a lookup table.

Why it is incorrect: Append does not perform an inner join, so it cannot satisfy the requirement, and a lookup table adds extra work.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Power Query

D. Merge the queries by using a lookup table.

Why it is incorrect: Merge is the right operation, but a lookup table (a mapping of values with and without spaces) would have to be built and maintained manually. That is far more development effort than ticking the fuzzy matching option and its ignore-spaces setting.

  • Official documentation: Fuzzy merge - Power Query

Merge queries overview - Power Query

q080.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

Warehouse1 contains two schemas name schema1 and schema2 and a table named schema1.city.

You need to make a copy of schema1.city in schema2. The solution must minimize the copying of data.

Which T-SQL statement should you run?
options: INSERT INTO schema2.city SELECT * FROM schema1.city;
CREATE TABLE schema2.city AS CLONE OF schema1.city;
CREATE TABLE schema2.city AS SELECT * FROM schema1.city;

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: CREATE TABLE schema2.city AS CLONE OF schema1.city;

Why it is correct: In a Fabric warehouse, CREATE TABLE ... AS CLONE OF creates a zero-copy clone: only the metadata is copied and the clone points to the same underlying Parquet data files in OneLake, so the operation is almost instantaneous and does not duplicate data (storage is only consumed later when the clone or the source change). A clone can be created in a different schema of the same warehouse, which is what is requested.

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. INSERT INTO schema2.city SELECT * FROM schema1.city;

Why it is incorrect: It requires the destination table to already exist and physically copies every row, so data is duplicated.

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric

B. SELECT * INTO schema2.city FROM schema1.city;

Why it is incorrect: It creates the table but also physically copies all the data, writing new files.

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric

D. CREATE TABLE schema2.city AS SELECT * FROM schema1.city;

Why it is incorrect: CTAS reads the source and writes a full new copy of the data, so it does not minimize the copying of data (it works, but the requirement is to minimize data copy).

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric

q081.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

You need to prevent new tables added to Lakehouse1 from being added

automatically to the default semantic model of the lakehouse.

What should you configure?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: the SQL analytics endpoint settings

Why it is correct: Every lakehouse has a SQL analytics endpoint, and the default semantic model of the lakehouse is managed from that endpoint. Its settings contain the Default Power BI semantic model option (called "Sync the default Power BI semantic model"). While it is on, new tables created in the lakehouse are added automatically to the default semantic model. Turning it off stops the automatic sync, so new tables in Lakehouse1 are no longer added and you decide which objects to include manually. The setting is opened from the SQL analytics endpoint item (or the warehouse item in the case of a warehouse), which is exactly what the question asks for.

  • Official documentation: Default Power BI semantic models in Microsoft Fabric - Add or remove objects and Semantic models in Fabric Data Warehouse
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. the semantic model settings

Why it is incorrect: The settings of the semantic model cover things like refresh, credentials, endorsement or permissions. The behavior that automatically adds new lakehouse tables to the default model is not controlled there; it is a property of the SQL analytics endpoint that generates and syncs the model.

  • Official documentation: Default Power BI semantic models in Microsoft Fabric

C. the workspace settings

Why it is incorrect: Workspace settings manage general aspects of the workspace (license mode, Spark settings, OneLake options, and so on). They do not include a switch to stop new lakehouse tables being synced to the default semantic model of one specific lakehouse.

  • Official documentation: Semantic models in Fabric Data Warehouse

D. the Lakehouse1 settings

Why it is incorrect: The lakehouse item settings (name, description, sensitivity and so on) do not expose the sync option. That option sits one level lower, in the settings of the lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint, which is a separate item.

  • Official documentation: Default Power BI semantic models in Microsoft Fabric

q082.stem:
-

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1 and a warehouse named Warehouse1.

You need to create a new table in Warehouse1 named POSCustomers by

querying the customer table in Lakehouse1.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First drop-down (statement): CREATE TABLE dbo.POSCustomers AS SELECT
  • Second drop-down (FROM clause): FROM lakehouse1.dbo.customer

Why it is correct: First selection: CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT (CTAS). The goal is to create a new table in Warehouse1 and populate it with the result of a query over data that lives in Lakehouse1. CTAS does both in one statement: it creates the table and loads it with the rows returned by the SELECT (here SELECT DISTINCT customerid, customer, postalcode, category). A plain CREATE TABLE dbo.POSCustomers would only define a table and would not accept a SELECT after it. CREATE TABLE ... AS CLONE OF is wrong because a clone is a zero-copy, metadata-based copy of an existing table in the same warehouse. It cannot take a column list or a DISTINCT query, and table clones across different warehouses/items in a workspace are not supported, so it cannot copy a lakehouse table into a warehouse.

  • First drop-down (statement), CREATE TABLE dbo.POSCustomers AS SELECT: CTAS creates the table and loads it with the SELECT rows (here SELECT DISTINCT …) in a single statement.
  • Second drop-down (FROM clause), FROM lakehouse1.dbo.customer: Lakehouse1 and Warehouse1 are in the same workspace: the three-part name lakehouse1.dbo.customer allows the cross-database query.

Incorrect options:

  • First drop-down (statement), CREATE TABLE dbo.POSCustomers — Why it is incorrect: CREATE TABLE without AS SELECT only defines the table and does not accept a SELECT afterwards.
  • First drop-down (statement), CREATE TABLE dbo.POSCustomers AS CLONE OF — Why it is incorrect: AS CLONE OF is a metadata copy of a table in the same warehouse; it does not accept a DISTINCT query nor copy between lakehouse and warehouse.
  • Second drop-down (FROM clause), FROM dbo.Customer — Why it is incorrect: FROM dbo.Customer looks for the table in the current database (Warehouse1), where it does not exist.
  • Second drop-down (FROM clause), FROM dbo.POSCustomers — Why it is incorrect: FROM dbo.POSCustomers would reference the table being created, which makes no sense as a source.
  • Official documentation: Ingest data into your Warehouse using Transact-SQL, Clone table in Microsoft Fabric - Limitations, Query the SQL analytics endpoint or Warehouse in Microsoft Fabric (cross-database queries), Tutorial: Create cross-warehouse queries with the SQL query editor

q083.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.

You are creating an Azure Data Factory pipeline.

You have a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales for the current month.

You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream activities of the pipeline.

Which type of activity should you add?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Lookup

Why it is correct: The Lookup activity can retrieve data from a source, and it can also execute a stored procedure and return the result set. Its output (a single row or an array of rows) is exposed through the activity output, so downstream activities can reference it with expressions such as @activity('Lookup1').output.firstRow.ActiveCustomers. Here the stored procedure returns two values (the number of active customers and the average sales), and they must be consumed by later activities, which is the typical use of Lookup.

  • Official documentation: Use the Lookup activity to look up data from a data source - Microsoft Fabric and Lookup activity in Azure Data Factory
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Switch

Why it is incorrect: Switch is a control-flow activity that evaluates an expression and runs one of several branches of activities. It does not call stored procedures and does not return data.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric

B. Copy data

Why it is incorrect: Copy data moves data from a source to a destination. It can use a stored procedure as a source, but its purpose is to write the rows to a sink; its output only contains run metadata (rows read, rows written, duration), not the returned values for use by downstream activities.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric

C. Append variable

Why it is incorrect: Append variable only adds a value to an existing array variable. It cannot execute a stored procedure in a warehouse.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric

q084.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains two workspaces named Workspace1 and Workspace2. Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1. Workspace2 contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse2. Lakehouse1 contains a table named dbo.Sales. Lakehouse2 contains a table named dbo.Customers.

You need to ensure that you can write queries that reference both dbo.Sales and dbo.Customers in the same SQL query without making additional copies of the tables.

What should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: a shortcut

Why it is correct: In Microsoft Fabric, OneLake shortcuts are built-in virtual pointers that reference data in other Fabric items (even in different workspaces such as Workspace1 and Workspace2) or in external storage accounts without copying or duplicating the underlying files:

  • Cross-workspace virtualization without duplication: creating a shortcut in Lakehouse1 (in Workspace1) that points to the dbo.Customers table of Lakehouse2 (in Workspace2) leaves the data physically in Lakehouse2, meeting the requirement of no additional copies.
  • Automatic exposure in the SQL analytics endpoint: when a shortcut points to a valid Delta table in the Tables folder of a lakehouse, the SQL analytics endpoint of Lakehouse1 recognizes it as just another local table. You can then write one T-SQL query that directly combines dbo.Sales and dbo.Customers (for example, with a JOIN) in the same query context.
  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn | Query the SQL analytics endpoint or warehouse in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

Option B: a dataflow

Why it is incorrect: A dataflow (Dataflow Gen2) extracts, transforms and physically writes a copy of the data to the configured destination (for example, loading a copy of dbo.Customers into Lakehouse1). It breaks the requirement of no additional copies and also needs scheduled runs to keep the data in sync.

  • Official documentation: Dataflow Gen2 overview in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

Option C: a view

Why it is incorrect: Cross-database T-SQL queries using three-part names (Lakehouse2.dbo.Customers) are only supported within the same workspace. Since Lakehouse1 is in Workspace1 and Lakehouse2 in Workspace2, you cannot create a view in the SQL endpoint of Lakehouse1 that directly queries Workspace2 without first linking the table through a OneLake shortcut.

  • Official documentation: Cross-database queries in the SQL analytics endpoint and Warehouse - Microsoft Learn

Option D: a managed table

Why it is incorrect: Creating a managed table in Lakehouse1 (for example, with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT or by loading files into Tables) materializes and physically stores a duplicate copy of the data in OneLake within Workspace1, violating the requirement to avoid additional copies.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse and Delta Lake tables in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

q085.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse.

You are designing a star schema model that will contain a customer dimension.

The customer dimension table will be a Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD).

You need to recommend which columns to add to the table. The columns must NOT already exist in the source.

Which three types of columns should you recommend? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
options: an effective end date and time
an effective start date and time

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: an effective end date and time
  • Option D: a surrogate key
  • Option E: an effective start date and time

Why it is correct: A Type 2 slowly changing dimension keeps history by inserting a new row each time a tracked attribute changes, instead of overwriting the old one. That requires columns that the source system does not have:

  • Surrogate key: because the same business entity (customer) now appears in several rows (one per version), the natural key is no longer unique. A warehouse-generated surrogate key uniquely identifies each version and is the key that fact tables reference.

  • Effective start date and time and effective end date and time: they define the period during which each version of the row was valid, so you can find the current version (for example, end date is null or in the far future) and join facts to the version that was valid at the time of the transaction.

  • Official documentation: Dimension tables in dimensional modeling - Microsoft Fabric and Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. a foreign key

Why it is incorrect: In a star schema, foreign keys live in the fact table and point to the dimensions. A dimension table does not need a foreign key to implement SCD Type 2.

  • Official documentation: Dimension tables in dimensional modeling - Microsoft Fabric

B. a natural key

Why it is incorrect: The natural (business) key is the identifier that already comes from the source system, for example the customer number. The question asks for columns that do NOT already exist in the source, so the natural key is not something you add; you keep it and use it to detect changes.

  • Official documentation: Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Microsoft Fabric

links.t: Dimension tables in dimensional modeling - Microsoft Fabric
Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Microsoft Fabric
Dimension tables in dimensional modeling - Microsoft Fabric

q086.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.

You plan to create a data pipeline named Pipeline1. Pipeline1 will include two activities that will execute in sequence.

You need to ensure that a failure of the first activity will NOT block the second activity.

Which conditional path should you configure between the first activity and the second activity?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Upon Completion

Why it is correct: In a Fabric data pipeline, the connection between two activities has a conditional path: Upon success, Upon fail, Upon completion and Upon skip. The Upon completion path runs the next activity once the previous one has finished, regardless of whether it succeeded or failed. This is exactly what is needed so that a failure of the first activity does not block the second.

  • Official documentation: Pipeline canvas experience - Microsoft Fabric and Errors and conditional execution - Azure Data Factory
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Upon Failure

Why it is incorrect: Upon failure runs the second activity only if the first fails. If the first activity succeeds, the second would not run, so it does block the second activity in the success case.

  • Official documentation: Errors and conditional execution - Azure Data Factory

C. Upon Skip

Why it is incorrect: Upon skip runs the second activity only when the first activity was skipped (because one of its own dependencies was not met). It does not cover the normal success or failure outcomes of the first activity.

  • Official documentation: Errors and conditional execution - Azure Data Factory

D. Upon Skip

Why it is incorrect: This option repeats option C (Upon Skip), and it does not meet the requirement. For comparison, Upon success would run only if the first activity succeeded, so a failure would block the second activity.

  • Official documentation: Pipeline canvas experience - Microsoft Fabric

q087.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model.

You need to identify any surrogate key columns in the model that have the Summarize By property set to a value other than to None. The solution must minimize effort.

What should you use?
options: Model explorer in Microsoft Power BI Desktop
Model view in Microsoft Power BI Desktop
Best Practice Analyzer in Tabular Editor

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Best Practice Analyzer in Tabular Editor

Why it is correct: Best Practice Analyzer (BPA) in Tabular Editor scans the whole semantic model against a set of rules and lists every object that breaks a rule. One of the commonly used rules is precisely that key columns (for example, columns ending in "Key" or "ID") should have Summarize By set to None. Running BPA therefore finds all the surrogate key columns with a different Summarize By value in one pass, with almost no manual effort, and the rule can even offer a fix.

  • Official documentation: Optimize a data model by using Best Practice Analyzer - Microsoft Learn and External tools in Power BI Desktop
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. DAX Formatter in DAX Studio

Why it is incorrect: DAX Formatter only reformats the text of DAX expressions to make them readable. It knows nothing about column properties such as Summarize By.

  • Official documentation: Troubleshoot DAX performance by using DAX Studio

B. Model explorer in Microsoft Power BI Desktop

Why it is incorrect: Model explorer lets you browse the tables and columns and edit their properties, but you would have to inspect the columns one by one (or select several manually). It cannot automatically identify the columns that break a rule, so it does not minimize effort.

  • Official documentation: Model explorer - Power BI

C. Model view in Microsoft Power BI Desktop

Why it is incorrect: Model view shows tables and relationships and gives access to the Properties pane, but it has the same limitation as Model explorer: no automated rule-based search for columns with a given property value.

  • Official documentation: Work with Modeling view in Power BI Desktop

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a Microsoft Power BI report named Report1.

Report1 is slow to render. You suspect that an inefficient DAX query is being executed.

You need to identify the slowest DAX query, and then review how long the query spends in the formula engine as compared to the storage engine.

Which five actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers (in order):

  1. From Performance analyzer, capture a recording.
  2. Sort the Duration (ms) column in descending order.
  3. Copy the first query to DAX Studio.
  4. Enable Query Timings and Server Timings. Run the query.
  5. View the Server Timings tab.

Why it is correct: to analyze Report1's performance and compare formula-engine and storage-engine time, follow this sequence:

  • Step 1, From Performance analyzer, capture a recording.: Performance analyzer records, per visual, how long its DAX query and rendering take; you start the recording and refresh the visuals.
  • Step 2, Sort the Duration (ms) column in descending order.: sorting by duration descending shows the slowest operation first, that is, the slowest DAX query.
  • Step 3, Copy the first query to DAX Studio.: Performance analyzer lets you copy a visual's DAX query to analyze it outside the report in DAX Studio.
  • Step 4, Enable Query Timings and Server Timings. Run the query.: DAX Studio only collects timing traces if Query Timings and Server Timings are enabled before running the query.
  • Step 5, View the Server Timings tab.: Server Timings splits the total duration into formula engine (FE) and storage engine (SE) time, which is what the scenario asks for.

Incorrect options:

  • View the Query Timings tab — Why it is incorrect: not used: the FE/SE breakdown appears in the Server Timings tab, not in Query Timings.
  • Sort the Duration (ms) column in descending order by DAX query time — Why it is incorrect: it is a distractor: sorting by duration already identifies the slowest query; this variant is not one of the five correct actions.
  • Official documentation: Use Performance analyzer to examine report element performance and Troubleshoot DAX performance by using DAX Studio

Troubleshoot DAX performance by using DAX Studio

q089.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model. The model contains 15 tables.

You need to programmatically change each column that ends in the word Key to meet the following requirements:

  • Hide the column.
  • Set Nullable to False
  • Set Summarize By to None.
  • Set Available in MDX to False.
  • Mark the column as a key column.

What should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Tabular Editor

Why it is correct: The requirement is to change the same set of properties (Hidden, Nullable, Summarize By, Available in MDX, Is Key) on every column whose name ends in "Key" across 15 tables, programmatically. Tabular Editor supports C# scripts (Advanced Scripting) and the Best Practice Analyzer, with which you can loop through all the columns, filter by name and set all the properties in one run. It connects to a semantic model, including one in a Fabric workspace through the XMLA endpoint, and saves the changes back.

  • Official documentation: External tools in Power BI Desktop and Power BI usage scenarios: Advanced data model management
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Microsoft Power BI Desktop

Why it is incorrect: Power BI Desktop lets you edit column properties in the UI, but only manually (although you can multi-select columns, you still have to find them across 15 tables) and it offers no scripting to apply changes by name pattern. Several of the listed properties are not even exposed there.

  • Official documentation: Work with Modeling view in Power BI Desktop

B. ALM Toolkit

Why it is incorrect: ALM Toolkit is used to compare two semantic model schemas and deploy the differences between them (a diff/merge tool). It is not meant to bulk-edit properties of columns.

  • Official documentation: External tools in Power BI Desktop

D. DAX Studio

Why it is incorrect: DAX Studio is for writing and running DAX queries and analyzing their performance. It is not a model authoring tool and cannot modify column metadata.

You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model.

You plan to implement calculation groups.

You need to create a calculation item that will change the context from the selected date to month-to-date (MTD).

How should you complete the DAX expression? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First drop-down: CALCULATE
  • Second drop-down: SELECTEDMEASURE

Why it is correct: The complete expression is CALCULATE ( SELECTEDMEASURE (), DATESMTD ( 'Date'[Date] ) ).

  • First drop-down, CALCULATE: CALCULATE evaluates the expression in a modified filter context; here the DATESMTD filter moves the context to month-to-date.
  • Second drop-down, SELECTEDMEASURE: SELECTEDMEASURE() is the placeholder for the measure being evaluated in the visual, so the same MTD logic works for every measure.

Incorrect options:

  • First drop-down, GENERATE — Why it is incorrect: GENERATE is a table function (cross join); it does not return the scalar value of a calculation item.
  • First drop-down, MEASURE — Why it is incorrect: MEASURE is the DEFINE MEASURE keyword, not a function to use in an expression.
  • Second drop-down, COMBINEVALUES — Why it is incorrect: COMBINEVALUES concatenates values into a string for multi-column relationships; it is unrelated to the measure.
  • Second drop-down, SELECTEDVALUE — Why it is incorrect: SELECTEDVALUE returns a column value when a single value is in context; it works for columns, not measures.
  • Official documentation: Create calculation groups in Power BI, SELECTEDMEASURE function (DAX), Calculation groups - Analysis Services

q091.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI report named Report1 that uses a Fabric semantic model.

Users discover that Report1 renders slowly.

You open Performance analyzer and identify that a visual named Orders By Date is the slowest to render. The duration breakdown for Orders By Date is shown in the following table.

What will provide the greatest reduction in the rendering duration of Report1?
options: Optimize the DAX query of Orders By Date by using DAX Studio.
Change the visual type of Orders By Date.
Reduce the number of visuals in Report1.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Reduce the number of visuals in Report1.

Why it is correct: The Performance analyzer table splits the time of the slowest visual into three parts: DAX query = 27 ms, Visual display = 39 ms and Other = 1047 ms. Almost the entire duration (about 94%) is in "Other". Microsoft defines "Other" as the time the visual spends preparing queries, waiting for other visuals to finish, and performing other background processing. In other words, Orders By Date is not slow because of its own query or its own drawing; it is slow because it is queued behind the other visuals on the page, which are rendered and queried competitively. The thing that reduces that waiting time the most is to have fewer visuals competing on the page (for example by splitting content into several pages or removing redundant visuals), which lowers the number of concurrent queries and the rendering work for the whole report.

  • Official documentation: Use Performance Analyzer to examine report element performance - Power BI
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Enable automatic page refresh.

Why it is incorrect: Automatic page refresh makes a report re-query its data source at a fixed interval so that the visuals show fresh data. It does not speed anything up; on the contrary, each refresh triggers new queries and more rendering work. It addresses data freshness, not render duration.

  • Official documentation: Use Performance Analyzer to examine report element performance - Power BI

B. Optimize the DAX query of Orders By Date by using DAX Studio.

Why it is incorrect: DAX Studio is a good tool to tune slow queries, but the exhibit shows the DAX query takes only 27 ms. Even if you made it instantaneous you would save at most 27 ms out of roughly 1,113 ms in total. The bottleneck is the "Other" category (1047 ms), which a DAX optimization does not address.

  • Official documentation: Use Performance Analyzer to examine report element performance - Power BI

C. Change the visual type of Orders By Date.

Why it is incorrect: Changing the visual type could only influence the "Visual display" component, which is just 39 ms. It would not reduce the 1047 ms that the visual waits for other visuals and background processing, so the gain would be marginal.

  • Official documentation: Use Performance Analyzer to examine report element performance - Power BI

q092.stem:
You have a custom Direct Lake semantic model named Model1 that has one billion rows of data.

You use Tabular Editor to connect to Model1 by using the XMLA endpoint.

You need to ensure that when users interact with reports based on Model1, their queries always use Direct Lake mode.

What should you do?
options: From Model, configure the Default Mode option.
From Partitions, configure the Mode option.
From Model, configure the Storage Location option.
From Model, configure the Direct Lake Behavior option.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: From Model, configure the Direct Lake Behavior option.

Why it is correct: In a Direct Lake semantic model, queries can fall back to DirectQuery mode when Direct Lake cannot be used efficiently (for example when the table is very large, as with the one billion rows here, or when guardrails of the capacity are exceeded). This behavior is controlled by the model-level DirectLakeBehavior property, which has three values: Automatic (default, fallback allowed), DirectLakeOnly (all queries use Direct Lake mode only; fallback is disabled and an error is returned if the data cannot be loaded into memory) and DirectQueryOnly. Because you are connected to Model1 through the XMLA endpoint with Tabular Editor, you select the Model object and set Direct Lake Behavior to DirectLakeOnly, which guarantees that report queries always use Direct Lake mode.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview - Fallback behavior and Direct Lake: how it works
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. From Model, configure the Default Mode option.

Why it is incorrect: Default Mode is a model property that sets the default storage mode (Import, DirectQuery, Dual) for new tables. It does not control whether a Direct Lake model may fall back to DirectQuery at query time, so it cannot force queries to stay in Direct Lake mode.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview - Fallback behavior

B. From Partitions, configure the Mode option.

Why it is incorrect: A Direct Lake table partition already has its mode set to Direct Lake; changing the partition mode is how you would convert a table to another storage mode, not how you prevent fallback. The fallback is governed by the model-level DirectLakeBehavior property, not by the partition Mode.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview - Fallback behavior

C. From Model, configure the Storage Location option.

Why it is incorrect: Storage Location refers to where the model data is stored (for example large semantic model storage format). It has nothing to do with the query mode or the DirectQuery fallback of a Direct Lake model.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake: how it works

You create a semantic model by using Microsoft Power BI Desktop. The model contains one security role named SalesRegionManager and the following tables:

  • Sales
  • SalesRegion

You need to modify the model to ensure that users assigned the

SalesRegionManager role cannot see a column named Address in SalesAddress.

Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: Open the model in Tabular Editor.
  • Step 2: Select the Address column in SalesAddress.
  • Step 3: Set Object Level Security to None for SalesRegionManager.

Why it is correct: OLS cannot be configured in the Power BI Desktop interface; you must use an external tool such as Tabular Editor and follow this sequence:

  • Step 1, Open the model in Tabular Editor.: object-level security is defined with an external tool such as Tabular Editor.
  • Step 2, Select the Address column in SalesAddress.: OLS is applied per object: first you choose the exact column to protect (Address, not the whole SalesAddress table).
  • Step 3, Set Object Level Security to None for SalesRegionManager.: the None value for the SalesRegionManager role makes the column behave as if it did not exist for its members.

Incorrect options:

  • Open the model in Power BI Desktop — Why it is incorrect: Desktop lets you create roles, but not set table or column permissions.
  • Set the Hidden property to True — Why it is incorrect: it only hides the column in the report view; it is not security: with Build permission it can still be queried with DAX or Analyze in Excel.
  • Set Object Level Security to Default — Why it is incorrect: Default restores the standard behavior (no restriction) for the role; it hides nothing.
  • Official documentation: Object-level security (OLS) - Microsoft Fabric

q094.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model that contains measures. The measures use multiple CALCULATE functions and a FILTER function.

You are evaluating the performance of the measures.

In which use case will replacing the FILTER function with the KEEPFILTERS function reduce execution time?
options: when the FILTER function uses a nested calculate function
when the FILTER function references a measure
when the FILTER function references columns from multiple tables
when the FILTER function references a column from a single table that uses Import mode

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: when the FILTER function references a column of a single table that uses Import mode.

Why it is correct: a common DAX performance mistake is iterating a whole table with FILTER (for example, CALCULATE([Sales], FILTER(Table, Table[Column] = "Value"))) instead of using a Boolean predicate with KEEPFILTERS (CALCULATE([Sales], KEEPFILTERS(Table[Column] = "Value"))).

Storage engine execution: when the condition only references a column of a single table in Import mode, replacing FILTER with KEEPFILTERS and a Boolean expression avoids row-by-row iteration and materializing an intermediate table in the formula engine. Import tables are in-memory column stores optimized for filtering this way, so execution time drops.

Intersection semantics: unlike a plain Boolean filter inside CALCULATE (which overwrites previous filters on that column), KEEPFILTERS intersects the new filter with the existing context, reproducing the behavior of FILTER without the performance penalty.

  • Option A, nested CALCULATE: a Boolean predicate does not support nested CALCULATE functions; in that case an iterator such as FILTER is needed (or precompute with VAR), so KEEPFILTERS cannot directly replace it.
  • Option B, reference to a measure: a Boolean expression in CALCULATE or KEEPFILTERS cannot reference a measure; if the criterion depends on a measure, FILTER is required.
  • Option C, columns from multiple tables: Boolean expressions cannot reference columns from multiple tables in a single condition; in that case FILTER must be kept.
  • Official documentation: KEEPFILTERS function (DAX), Avoid using FILTER as a filter argument, CALCULATE function (DAX)

Avoid using FILTER as a filter argument

q095.stem:
You have a semantic model named Model1. Model1 contains five tables that all use Import mode. Model1 contains a dynamic row-level security (RLS) role named HR. The HR role filters employee data so that HR managers only see the data of the department to which they are assigned.

You publish Model1 to a Fabric tenant and configure RLS role membership. You share the model and related reports to users.

An HR manager reports that the data they see in a report is incomplete.

What should you do to validate the data seen by the HR Manager?
options: Select Test as role to view the data as the HR role.
Filter the data in the report to match the intended logic of the filter for the HR department.
Select Test as role to view the report as the HR manager.
Ask the HR manager to open the report in Microsoft Power BI Desktop.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Select Test as role to view the report as the HR manager.

Why it is correct: Model1 implements dynamic RLS with DAX functions such as USERPRINCIPALNAME() or USERNAME() to identify the signed-in user and filter by their department. To validate exactly which rows a specific user sees in the Fabric / Power BI service:

Open the semantic model security, select the (...) menu next to the HR role and select Test as role.

In the Now viewing as header, select the person and enter the account of the affected HR manager. The engine then evaluates the dynamic DAX expression simulating their identity and shows the report as they see it, letting you check whether an assignment is missing in the users/departments table or the filter has an error.

  • Option A: testing only as the generic role, without specifying the person, works for static RLS; in dynamic RLS USERPRINCIPALNAME() is evaluated with your own identity, not the manager's, so you do not reproduce their department context or find out why they see incomplete data.
  • Option B: manually filtering the report only restricts what is shown on screen; it does not run or validate the role's DAX rules, filter propagation or the role membership configured in the service.
  • Option D: Power BI Desktop is an authoring tool, not a consumption tool. Opening the file locally does not apply the service's RLS role assignments, and handing over the .pbix would expose all imported data without restrictions.
  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI, Row-level security (RLS) guidance in Power BI Desktop, Types of filters in Power BI reports, Test security and manage roles

q096.stem:
You have a Microsoft Fabric tenant that contains a dataflow.

You are exploring a new semantic model.

From Power Query, you need to view column information as shown in the following exhibit.

Which three Data view options should you select? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
options: Show column profile in details pane

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Show column value distribution.
  • Option C: Enable column profile.
  • Option D: Show column quality details.

Why it is correct: in the Power Query Online editor of Fabric dataflows, the profiling tools are configured under View > Data view. Power Query Online separates the statistics calculation from the grid display options, so to reproduce the indicators shown under the column headers (SalesOrderID, OrderDate, CustomerID, LineItem, ProductID and OrderQty) these three options are required:

Enable column profile (C): it is the main switch that turns on the data profile calculation. Without it, the metrics are not computed and the indicators cannot be shown on the columns.

Show column quality details (D): it shows the status bar with the percentage of valid, error and empty rows (Valid 100%, Error 0%, Empty 0%) under each column name.

Show column value distribution (A): it shows the thumbnail chart with value frequency and the count of distinct and unique values (for example, 32 distinct, 4 uniq...) right below the quality details.

  • Option B, enable details pane: it opens the bottom details pane; in the exhibit only the grid headers with their built-in metrics are visible, with no bottom pane.
  • Option E, show column profile in details pane: it shows extended statistics for a single selected column (count, min, max, average, standard deviation and distribution) in the details pane, which does not appear in the question's screenshot.

You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Sales.Products.

Sales.Products contains the following columns.

You need to write a T-SQL query that will return the following columns.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • HighestSellingPrice: GREATEST
  • TradePrice: COALESCE

Why it is correct:

  • HighestSellingPrice, GREATEST: GREATEST returns the maximum value of a list of expressions in the same row and ignores NULLs when at least one value is non-null.
  • TradePrice, COALESCE: COALESCE evaluates its arguments in order and returns the first non-NULL: AgentPrice, otherwise WholesalePrice, otherwise ListPrice (with the arguments in that order).

Incorrect options:

  • HighestSellingPrice, COALESCE — Why it is incorrect: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value, not the largest; with ListPrice first it would always return ListPrice.
  • HighestSellingPrice, IIF — Why it is incorrect: IIF takes one condition and two results; it cannot take three columns.
  • HighestSellingPrice, MAX — Why it is incorrect: MAX is an aggregate across rows of one column; it takes a single expression, not a list of columns.
  • TradePrice, CHOOSE — Why it is incorrect: CHOOSE selects by index position, not through NULL checks.
  • TradePrice, IIF — Why it is incorrect: IIF handles only one condition and does not chain three alternatives.
  • TradePrice, MAX — Why it is incorrect: MAX would return the highest price instead of the first available one.
  • Official documentation: GREATEST (Transact-SQL), COALESCE (Transact-SQL), IIF (Transact-SQL), CHOOSE (Transact-SQL) and MAX (Transact-SQL)

answer.correct:

Why it is correct: The notebook code plots a histogram of the tip amounts of a sampled taxi dataset with Matplotlib and shows the distribution of the values (how many trips fall in each tip range). answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • DayName: weekday

Why it is correct:

  • PeriodDate, DATETRUNC: DATETRUNC(month, OrderDate) truncates the date to the first day of the month and returns a date (2025-03-17 → 2025-03-01).
  • DayName, weekday: DATENAME with weekday returns the weekday name as a string (for example, "Wednesday").

Incorrect options:

  • PeriodDate, DATE_BUCKET — Why it is incorrect: DATE_BUCKET requires an interval width and an origin (DATE_BUCKET(month, 1, OrderDate)); the signature (month, OrderDate) does not fit.
  • PeriodDate, DATEFROMPARTS — Why it is incorrect: DATEFROMPARTS needs year, month and day, not (month, OrderDate).
  • PeriodDate, DATEPART — Why it is incorrect: DATEPART returns an integer with just that part (3), not a date.
  • DayName, day — Why it is incorrect: day would return the day of the month ("17"), not a name.
  • DayName, dayofyear — Why it is incorrect: dayofyear would return the day number in the year ("76"), not a name.

q100.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains JSON files in OneLake. The files have one billion items.

You plan to perform time series analysis of the items.

You need to transform the data, visualize the data to find insights, perform anomaly detection, and share the insights with other business users. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • Use parallel processing.
  • Minimize the duplication of data.
  • Minimize how long it takes to load the data.

What should you use to transform and visualize the data?
options: the PySpark library in a Fabric notebook
the pandas library in a Fabric notebook
a Microsoft Power BI report that uses core visuals

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: the PySpark library in a Fabric notebook

Why it is correct: The scenario has one billion items stored as JSON files in OneLake and three constraints: use parallel processing, minimize duplicating data and minimize load time. A Fabric notebook running PySpark reads the files in place from OneLake (no copy needed) and distributes the transformation across the executors of the Spark cluster, so it meets the parallel processing requirement and scales to this volume. The notebook also lets you visualize the result with built-in charts or libraries and run anomaly detection on the time series, and the results can be shared with business users from the Fabric workspace.

  • Official documentation: What is Apache Spark compute in Microsoft Fabric? and Notebook visualization in Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. the pandas library in a Fabric notebook

Why it is incorrect: pandas runs on a single node and loads the whole dataset in the memory of the driver, so it does not provide distributed (parallel) processing and cannot reasonably handle one billion items. Loading the data would also take much longer.

  • Official documentation: What is Apache Spark compute in Microsoft Fabric?

C. a Microsoft Power BI report that uses core visuals

Why it is incorrect: A Power BI report with core visuals is a visualization layer; it does not by itself transform the JSON files nor perform the anomaly detection on one billion items, and importing that volume would duplicate the data and lengthen the load. It would require a transformation engine such as Spark first.

q101.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains customer churn data stored as Parquet files in OneLake. The data contains details about customer demographics and product usage.

You create a Fabric notebook to read the data into a Spark DataFrame. You then create column charts in the notebook that show the distribution of retained customers as compared to lost customers based on geography, the number of products purchased, age, and customer tenure.

Which type of analytics are you performing?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: descriptive

Why it is correct: Descriptive analytics answers the question "what happened?". It summarizes historical data with counts, distributions and aggregations, typically shown as tables and charts. In the scenario you read the churn Parquet files into a Spark DataFrame and build column charts that show how retained customers compare to lost customers by geography, number of products, age and tenure. You are only describing the existing distribution of the data. You are not investigating the root cause of the churn, you are not training a model to forecast who will leave, and you are not recommending any action. That is exactly the definition of descriptive analytics, and exploratory charting in a Fabric notebook is the typical way to do it.

  • Official documentation: Understand data analytics types - Microsoft Learn and Explore data analytics - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. diagnostic

Why it is incorrect: Diagnostic analytics answers "why did it happen?". It drills down, correlates variables and looks for root causes (for example, testing which factor actually drives customers to leave). Plotting the distribution of retained versus lost customers by several attributes only shows what the data looks like; it does not establish causes. The scenario never asks for an explanation of the churn.

  • Official documentation: Understand data analytics types - Microsoft Learn

C. prescriptive

Why it is incorrect: Prescriptive analytics answers "what should we do?". It recommends actions or decisions, usually on top of predictions and optimization. The notebook produces only charts and recommends nothing, so it is not prescriptive.

  • Official documentation: Overview of data analysis - Microsoft Learn

D. predictive

Why it is incorrect: Predictive analytics answers "what is likely to happen?". It uses statistical or machine learning models trained on historical data to forecast future outcomes, such as the probability that a given customer will churn. The scenario reads data and draws column charts but trains no model and produces no forecast, so it is not predictive.

  • Official documentation: Explore data analytics - Microsoft Learn

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model. The model contains data about retail stores.

You need to write a DAX query that will be executed by using the XMLA endpoint. The query must return the total amount of sales from the same period last year.

How should you complete the DAX expression? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First box (function used in VAR _LYSales =): SUMMARIZE
  • Second box (after RETURN): _LYSales

Why it is correct: Detailed analysis:

  • First box (function used in VAR _LYSales =), SUMMARIZE: the study document marks SUMMARIZE to build the prior-year result (see the note: CALCULATE could also be defended).
  • Second box (after RETURN), _LYSales: after RETURN the newly defined variable _LYSales is returned, holding the prior-year calculation.

Incorrect options:

  • First box (function used in VAR _LYSales =), CALCULATE — Why it is incorrect: CALCULATE fits the arguments (measure + time-intelligence filter) and could be defended (see the note), but it is not the marked option.
  • First box (function used in VAR _LYSales =), CALCULATETABLE — Why it is incorrect: CALCULATETABLE returns a table, not a scalar total.
  • First box (function used in VAR _LYSales =), FILTER — Why it is incorrect: FILTER needs a table and a Boolean condition.
  • First box (function used in VAR _LYSales =), SUMMARIZECOLUMNS — Why it is incorrect: SUMMARIZECOLUMNS builds a grouped table from columns and does not accept a measure plus a filter table this way.
  • Second box (after RETURN), [Total Sales] — Why it is incorrect: [Total Sales] would return the current-period measure and ignore the prior-year calculation.
  • Second box (after RETURN), (_LYSales) — Why it is incorrect: (_LYSales) in parentheses is not the expected form; { _LYSales } would be a valid table constructor, but it is not the expected selection.
  • Second box (after RETURN), VAR — Why it is incorrect: VAR is a keyword, not a value that can be returned.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but the arguments shown (a measure followed by a time-intelligence table function used as a filter) match the signature of CALCULATE, which evaluates an expression in a modified filter context, whereas SUMMARIZE expects a table as its first argument. For the first box, CALCULATE could therefore also be argued. Check it against the linked documentation.

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a dataflow named Dataflow1. Dataflow1 returns 500 rows of data.

You need to identify the min and max values for each column in the query results.

Which three Data view options should you select? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
options: Show column profile in details pane

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Enable column profile.
  • Option C: Show column profile in details pane.
  • Option E: Enable details pane.

Why it is correct: in the Power Query Online editor of a Dataflow Gen2, column profile analyzes the first 1,000 rows by default, so it covers the 500 rows that Dataflow1 returns. The minimum and maximum values come from the column profile statistics, which are shown in the details pane, so all three Data view options must be turned on:

Enable column profile (B): turns on the calculation of detailed column statistics (count, errors, empty, distinct, unique, average, standard deviation, min and max).

Enable details pane (E): shows the details pane in the editor, where information about the selected column is presented.

Show column profile in details pane (C): makes the details pane display the column profile statistics, including min and max, along with the value distribution.

  • Option A, show column value distribution: it only shows a mini histogram with distinct and unique value counts under each column header; it does not show the min or max.
  • Option D, show column quality details: it only shows the quality bar with the percentage of valid, error and empty rows; it provides no range metrics or min and max.

q104.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a Microsoft Power BI report.

You are exploring a new semantic model.

You need to display the following column statistics:

  • Count
  • Average
  • Null count
  • Distinct count
  • Standard deviation

Which Power Query function should you run?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Table.Profile

Why it is correct: Table.Profile(table) returns a table with one row per column of the input table and a set of statistics for it: minimum, maximum, average, standard deviation, count, null count and distinct count (where applicable). That is exactly the list of column statistics required (count, average, null count, distinct count and standard deviation). It is the M function behind the column profiling that Power Query shows when you explore a new dataset.

  • Official documentation: Table.Profile - Power Query M
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Table.schema

Why it is incorrect: Table.Schema returns metadata about the structure of the table (column names, positions, type names, nullability and so on), not statistics computed over the data values such as average or standard deviation.

  • Official documentation: Table.Profile - Power Query M

B. Table.view

Why it is incorrect: Table.View creates a table whose behavior is defined by custom handlers (for query folding and similar scenarios in connector development). It computes no column statistics.

  • Official documentation: Table.Profile - Power Query M

C. Table.FuzzyGroup

Why it is incorrect: Table.FuzzyGroup groups rows whose key values are similar (fuzzy matching) and aggregates them. It is a grouping function, not a profiling function, and it does not return count, null count, distinct count or standard deviation per column.

DESCRIBE DETAIL customer -

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: No

Why it is correct: The goal is to find out whether maintenance tasks (OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and so on) have been run on the Customer table. DESCRIBE DETAIL returns the current metadata of the Delta table: location, format, creation time, number of files, size in bytes, partition columns and table properties. It is a snapshot of the table now, not a log of the operations performed on it. To see whether OPTIMIZE or VACUUM were executed, you need the transaction log history with DESCRIBE HISTORY customer, which lists every operation, its timestamp and its metrics. DESCRIBE DETAIL can hint at fragmentation (a large number of small files), but it cannot prove whether maintenance was performed, so the solution does not meet the goal.

A. Yes

Why it is incorrect: DESCRIBE DETAIL does not expose the operation history of the table, so it cannot tell you whether OPTIMIZE or VACUUM have run. The correct statement is DESCRIBE HISTORY.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named Model1.

You discover that the following query performs slowly against Model1.

You need to reduce the execution time of the query.

Solution: You replace line 4 by using the following code:

ISEMPTY ( RELATEDTABLE ( 'Order Item' ) )

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: No

Why it is correct: The original line 4 is CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( 'Order Item' ) ) > 0, used as the filter condition to keep only the customers that have order items. The proposed replacement, ISEMPTY ( RELATEDTABLE ( 'Order Item' ) ), returns TRUE when the related table has no rows. Therefore it keeps exactly the opposite set of customers (those without order items), which changes the meaning of the query and produces wrong results. A valid rewrite would need a negation, NOT ISEMPTY ( ... ). Since the result of the query would be wrong, the solution does not meet the goal, whatever its performance.

  • Official documentation: ISEMPTY function (DAX), RELATEDTABLE function (DAX)
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Yes

Why it is incorrect: Although ISEMPTY is cheaper than counting rows, it is used here without NOT, so the filter is inverted and the query returns customers without order items. A faster query that returns incorrect results does not satisfy the requirement.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named Model1.

You discover that the following query performs slowly against Model1.

You need to reduce the execution time of the query.

Solution: You replace line 4 by using the following code:

NOT ISEMPTY ( CALCULATETABLE ( 'Order Item ' ) )

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Yes

Why it is correct: The original filter, CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( 'Order Item' ) ) > 0, has to count every related row for each customer just to check whether the count is greater than zero. NOT ISEMPTY ( CALCULATETABLE ( 'Order Item' ) ) expresses the same logic (the customer has at least one order item, with CALCULATETABLE transforming the row context of each customer into a filter context) but ISEMPTY only needs to find out whether at least one row exists and can stop there. It works like EXISTS in T-SQL: it does not enumerate or aggregate all the rows. The result is the same set of customers with lower execution time, so the solution meets the goal.

  • Official documentation: ISEMPTY function (DAX), CALCULATE function (DAX), DAX queries
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. No

Why it is incorrect: The replacement is logically equivalent to the original (rows exist versus count greater than zero) and avoids the full count, so it does reduce execution time. The syntax NOT ISEMPTY(...) is valid DAX, since NOT is a function that takes the Boolean expression returned by ISEMPTY.
