  • Second box (.save("...")): Tables/productline2

Why it is correct: Detailed analysis:

  • First box (.format("...")), delta: only Delta data under Tables is registered as a managed table and works with Direct Lake; the CSVs must be converted by writing as delta.
  • Second box (.save("...")), Tables/productline2: Tables/productline2 creates the managed Delta table directly under Tables, with the least effort.

Incorrect options:

  • First box (.format("...")), csv — Why it is incorrect: csv leaves flat files that are not a managed table.
  • First box (.format("...")), parquet — Why it is incorrect: parquet without a Delta transaction log is not recognized as a table.
  • Second box (.save("...")), productline2 — Why it is incorrect: productline2 (relative path) saves to the Files area, producing files rather than a table.
  • Second box (.save("...")), Tables/research/productline2 — Why it is incorrect: Tables/research/productline2 adds an unnecessary nested subfolder that is not a managed table at the root.

q111.stem: Which syntax should you use in a notebook to access the Research division data for Productline1?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: spark.read.format(“delta”).load(“Files/ResearchProduct”)

Why it is correct: The Contoso case study says that the Research division data for Productline1 sits in the storage1 Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 account in delta format, that Lakehouse1 contains a shortcut named ResearchProduct pointing to it, and that the data must be retrieved from Lakehouse1 by using Fabric notebooks. A shortcut is exposed inside the lakehouse as a folder, so a notebook reads it by using a relative lakehouse path with the Spark DataFrame reader. Because the data is stored in Delta format, the reader must be told so with format("delta") and then pointed to the shortcut path with load(...). Among the options, option A is the only one that is valid PySpark that reads a Delta folder through the lakehouse path of the ResearchProduct shortcut.

Keep in mind that Spark resolves relative paths against the default lakehouse attached to the notebook (Lakehouse1). The path used in this option reads the shortcut through the lakehouse file path.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but the case study also requires all Research data to be presented as managed tables in Lakehouse explorer, which would normally mean the shortcut sits under Tables. In that case spark.sql("SELECT * FROM Lakehouse1.ResearchProduct") (option B) or a Tables/ResearchProduct path would be the natural choice, as in the sibling question on the same case study. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts - Microsoft Fabric and Use a notebook to load data into your lakehouse
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. spark.sql(“SELECT * FROM Lakehouse1.ResearchProduct ”)

Why it is incorrect: Spark SQL can query a table of the lakehouse by name (lakehouse.table) only when the item is registered as a table in the Tables section of the lakehouse. This question expects the file-path approach for the ResearchProduct shortcut instead, so this option is not the expected answer. In a real environment where the shortcut was created under Tables, this statement would work.

C. spark.sql(“SELECT * FROM Lakehouse1.Tables.ResearchProduct ”)

Why it is incorrect: Tables is a folder of the lakehouse, not a schema or namespace in the Spark catalog. The three-part name Lakehouse1.Tables.ResearchProduct is therefore not a valid identifier for a table and the query would fail with an analysis error. The table is addressed as Lakehouse1.ResearchProduct (or Lakehouse1.dbo.ResearchProduct when schemas are enabled).

D. external_table(ResearchProduct)

Why it is incorrect: external_table() is a KQL function used in a KQL database or eventhouse to query an external table (for example one that points to a OneLake shortcut). It is not a PySpark or Spark SQL function, so it cannot be used in a notebook with the Spark engine to read the lakehouse shortcut.

You have a Fabric workspace that uses the default Spark starter pool and runtime version 1.2.

You plan to read a CSV file named Sales_raw.csv in a lakehouse, select columns, and save the data as a Delta table to the managed area of the lakehouse.

Sales_raw.csv contains 12 columns.

You have the following code.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Statement 1 (The Spark engine will read only the SalesOrderNumber, OrderDate, CustomerName and UnitPrice columns from Sales_raw.csv): Yes
  • Statement 2 (The Year column replaces the OrderDate column in the table): No
  • Statement 3 (Adding inferSchema='true' to the options will increase the execution time of the query): Yes

Statement 1 - Yes. Spark evaluates DataFrames lazily: .load() and .select() only build a logical plan, and nothing is read until the .saveAsTable() action runs. The Catalyst optimizer then pushes the projection down to the CSV data source, which applies column pruning, so only the four selected columns are parsed and materialized from the 12-column file.

Statement 2 - No. withColumn("Year", year("OrderDate")) adds a new column called Year derived from OrderDate; it does not drop or replace OrderDate, because the column name used in withColumn is different from the existing one. The resulting table therefore has five columns: SalesOrderNumber, OrderDate, CustomerName, UnitPrice and Year. Only a call with the same name (withColumn("OrderDate", ...)) would replace the original column. The Year column is then used by partitionBy('Year') to partition the Delta table.

Statement 3 - Yes. By default, the CSV reader treats every column as a string (and, here, the header option only names the columns). With inferSchema='true' Spark must make an additional pass over the data to sample/scan the values and infer the data types, so the execution time increases. For large files it is faster and more predictable to provide the schema explicitly.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks statement 1 as Yes, but a CSV file is a row-oriented text format, so every line is still physically scanned from storage even though only the selected columns are parsed; read that way, the statement could be argued as "No". Check it against the linked documentation.

df.describe().show()

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Yes

Why it is correct: The describe() method of a Spark DataFrame computes basic statistics - count, mean, stddev, min and max - for the numeric and string columns of the DataFrame, and .show() prints the result. When it is called without arguments, it automatically includes all the columns that are numeric or string, which is exactly the scope the question asks for ("all the string and numeric columns"). For string columns, min and max are computed lexicographically, and mean and stddev are returned as null because they are not meaningful for text; the goal is therefore satisfied by a single call.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but describe() returns null for mean and standard deviation on string columns, so if real values of those statistics were required for string columns, the goal could be argued as not met (answer "No"). Check it against the linked documentation.

answer.incorrect:

B. No

Why it is incorrect: The solution meets the goal as the question is worded, so "No" is not the expected answer. The only argument for "No" is that mean and standard deviation have no numeric meaning for string columns (they come back as null), and that if you required real values for those columns for string types the goal could not be met by any expression. Since describe() is designed to cover numeric and string columns in one call, the expected answer is "Yes".

You have a Fabric tenant.

You are creating a Fabric Data Factory pipeline.

You have a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales for the current month.

You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream activities of the pipeline.

Which type of activity should you add?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Lookup

Why it is correct: In a Fabric Data Factory pipeline, the Lookup activity can run a stored procedure against a data source, including a Fabric warehouse, and returns the result (the first row or the whole result set) as the activity output. That output can be referenced by downstream activities by using expressions such as @activity('Lookup1').output.firstRow.ActiveCustomers. The scenario requires exactly this: execute a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales and make those values available to the activities that follow in the pipeline.

  • Official documentation: Use the Lookup activity to look up data from a data source
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Switch

Why it is incorrect: The Switch activity is a control flow activity that evaluates an expression and runs one of several branches of activities depending on the value. It does not connect to a warehouse and cannot execute a stored procedure.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric Data Factory

B. KQL

Why it is incorrect: The KQL activity runs Kusto Query Language commands against a KQL database in an eventhouse. A Fabric warehouse is queried by using T-SQL and stored procedures, so a KQL activity cannot execute the procedure in the warehouse.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric Data Factory

C. Append variable

Why it is incorrect: The Append variable activity only adds a value to an existing array variable of the pipeline. It does not run any query or stored procedure, so it cannot obtain the values returned by the warehouse (it could at most store a value that another activity already produced).

  • TransactionKey: Remove the column.
  • SaleDateTime: Split the column.

Why it is correct: TransactionKey - Remove the column. This column holds an incrementing surrogate key with 2,500,350,000 distinct values and a compressed size of 160 GB. The Vertipaq engine of Import mode stores data in a columnar way and compresses it based on repeated values, so a column in which every row is different (cardinality equal to the number of rows) cannot be compressed and is the biggest contributor to model size and to refresh time. The requirement is to reduce the model size and speed up refresh, and the only datetime information that must remain is the sale datetime; a surrogate key of a fact table is not needed for analysis, aggregation or relationships (nothing references it), so the best action is to remove it from the model. Microsoft guidance states that unnecessary high-cardinality columns, such as fact table surrogate keys, should be removed. Alternatives: "Change the data type" would not make the unique values compressible; "Split the column" does not make sense for a key; "Truncate the data" would delete rows or values and is not a modeling optimization for the column.

  • TransactionKey, Remove the column.: TransactionKey is a surrogate key with 2,500,350,000 distinct values (160 GB); its cardinality prevents compression and it is unused in analysis or relationships: remove it.
  • SaleDateTime, Split the column.: SaleDateTime (6,850,273 distinct values) must remain available; splitting it into date and time drastically reduces cardinality and both compress well.

Incorrect options:

  • TransactionKey, Change the data type of the column. — Why it is incorrect: changing the data type does not make unique values compressible.
  • TransactionKey, Split the column. — Why it is incorrect: splitting a surrogate key makes no sense and does not reduce size.
  • TransactionKey, Truncate the data. — Why it is incorrect: truncating would remove rows or values; it is not a column modeling optimization.
  • SaleDateTime, Change the data type of the column. — Why it is incorrect: changing to date loses the time part and changing to text would increase size.
  • SaleDateTime, Remove the column. — Why it is incorrect: removing the column would lose the sale date and time, which must remain available.
  • SaleDateTime, Truncate the data. — Why it is incorrect: truncating (to date or time) loses time precision and does not meet the requirement.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a data warehouse named DW1. DW1 contains a table named DimCustomer. DimCustomer contains the fields shown in the following table.

You need to identify duplicate email addresses in DimCustomer. The solution must return a maximum of 1,000 records.

Which four T-SQL statements should you run in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate statements from the list of statements to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  1. SELECT TOP(1000) CustomerAltKey, COUNT(*)
  2. FROM DimCustomer
  3. GROUP BY CustomerAltKey
  4. HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

Why it is correct: the T-SQL query that returns up to 1,000 duplicate CustomerAltKey values is composed, in this order, of:

  • Step 1, SELECT TOP(1000) CustomerAltKey, COUNT(*): SELECT TOP(1000) CustomerAltKey, COUNT(*) limits the result to 1,000 rows in T-SQL and counts each key.
  • Step 2, FROM DimCustomer: FROM DimCustomer names the source table.
  • Step 3, GROUP BY CustomerAltKey: GROUP BY CustomerAltKey groups the rows by key so they can be counted.
  • Step 4, HAVING COUNT(*) > 1: HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 filters the already aggregated groups, leaving only duplicated keys.

Incorrect options:

  • SELECT CustomerAltKey, COUNT(*) — Why it is incorrect: it would find duplicates, but it does not enforce the 1,000-record maximum unless combined with LIMIT, which does not exist in T-SQL.
  • LIMIT 1000 — Why it is incorrect: it is not supported in T-SQL (it is MySQL/PostgreSQL syntax); T-SQL uses TOP or OFFSET … FETCH.
  • WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 — Why it is incorrect: WHERE is evaluated before grouping and cannot contain aggregate functions; aggregates are filtered with HAVING.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named WH1.

You run the following T-SQL query against WH1.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Statement 1 (Dimension.GetDirectReports is a scalar T-SQL function): Yes
  • Statement 2 (The Dimension.GetDirectReports function will run only once when the query runs): No
  • Statement 3 (The output rows will include at least one row for each row in the Dimension.Employee table): Yes

Statement 1 - Yes. Dimension.GetDirectReports is accepted as a T-SQL user-defined function that is invoked once per employee row and whose returned columns are projected as gdr.[WWI Employee ID] and gdr.Employee.

Statement 2 - No. The APPLY operator invokes the right-side expression once for each row of the left-side table (here Dimension.Employee), passing the employee key as a parameter. It therefore executes many times, once per employee, and not once for the whole query.

Statement 3 - Yes. OUTER APPLY works like a left outer join: when the function returns no rows for an employee (an employee without direct reports), the left row is still returned with NULL values in the function columns. Therefore the result contains at least one row for every row of Dimension.Employee. In contrast, CROSS APPLY would discard the employees for which the function returns an empty result.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks statement 1 as Yes, but the function is used on the right side of OUTER APPLY, which requires a table-valued function (or a derived table), so it more likely behaves as a table-valued function than as a scalar one, which would make statement 1 "No". Check it against the linked documentation.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named Model1.

You discover that the following query performs slowly against Model1.

You need to reduce the execution time of the query.

Solution: You replace line 4 by using the following code:

NOT ( CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( 'Order Item' ) ) < 0)

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: No

Why it is correct: The query evaluates FILTER(VALUES(Customer[Customer Name]), CALCULATE(COUNTROWS('Order Item')) > 0), which returns the customers that have at least one order item. The proposed replacement, NOT(CALCULATE(COUNTROWS('Order Item')) < 0), does not improve the execution and also changes the result:

  1. COUNTROWS never returns a negative number: it returns a positive count or blank. The condition < 0 is therefore always false and NOT(...) is always true, so the filter no longer removes any customer. The query returns all the customers, including those without order items, instead of only those with orders. A tuning change must keep the same results.
  2. The expression still contains a CALCULATE with a context transition evaluated for every customer (row context to filter context), which is the costly part of the original query, so the number of storage engine and formula engine operations is not reduced in any meaningful way.

The solution therefore does not meet the goal of reducing the execution time while keeping the query meaningful.

  • Official documentation: COUNTROWS function (DAX), Filter functions (DAX) and Optimize DAX calculations
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Yes

Why it is incorrect: The replacement NOT(CALCULATE(COUNTROWS('Order Item')) < 0) is always true, because a row count can never be negative, so the filter stops filtering and the result of the query changes (all customers are returned). It also keeps the per-customer CALCULATE evaluation, so it is not a real optimization. Therefore, the solution does not meet the goal.

You have a Microsoft Power BI Premium Per User (PPU) workspace that contains a semantic model.

You have an Azure App Service app named App1 that modifies row-level security (RLS) for the model by using the XMLA endpoint.

App1 requires users to sign in by using their Microsoft Entra credentials to access the XMLA endpoint.

You need to configure App1 to use a service account to access the model.

What should you do first?
options: Add a managed identity to the workspace.
Upgrade the workspace to Premium capacity.
Add a managed identity to App1.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Add a managed identity to App1.

Why it is correct: App1 is an Azure App Service app that currently authenticates to the XMLA endpoint with interactive user sign-in (Microsoft Entra credentials). To make it use a service account instead, the app needs a non-human identity in Microsoft Entra ID that it can use to obtain tokens without storing credentials. For an App Service app this is done by enabling a managed identity on the app itself (the identity is created as a service principal in Microsoft Entra ID and is managed by Azure). This is the first step: once App1 has an identity, you can allow service principals to use the Fabric/Power BI APIs in the tenant settings, add that identity to the workspace with a suitable role (for example Member or Contributor/Admin), and then use it with the XMLA endpoint to change the RLS. Premium Per User workspaces already support XMLA read/write, so no capacity change is needed.

  • Official documentation: How to use managed identities for App Service and Azure Functions and Automate Premium workspace and semantic model tasks with service principals
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Add a managed identity to the workspace.

Why it is incorrect: The identity that must authenticate belongs to the application that calls the XMLA endpoint (App1), not to the workspace. A workspace identity is used for outbound authentication of Fabric items to data sources, not for letting an external app sign in as a service account. Moreover, App1 has no identity yet that could be granted access to the workspace, so creating the identity for App1 comes first.

  • Official documentation: Automate Premium workspace and semantic model tasks with service principals

B. Modify the XMLA Endpoint setting.

Why it is incorrect: The XMLA endpoint is already usable by the app (it currently connects to it with user credentials), and Premium Per User workspaces support read/write operations through the endpoint. Changing the endpoint mode (Read Only / Read Write) does not give the app a service account identity, so it does not solve the requirement.

  • Official documentation: Connect to a semantic model with client applications and tools by using the XMLA endpoint

C. Upgrade the workspace to Premium capacity.

Why it is incorrect: A Premium Per User workspace already provides the XMLA endpoint, and service principals can be used with it, so upgrading to a Premium capacity is not required. It would also add cost without addressing the missing app identity.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named WH1.

You have source data in a CSV file that has the following fields:

  • SalesTransactionID
  • SaleDate
  • CustomerCode

  • CustomerAddress

  • ProductName

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • CustomerCode: Dimension
  • CustomerName: Dimension
  • SaleDate: Dimension

Why it is correct: The source CSV mixes transaction-level facts (SalesTransactionID, Quantity, UnitPrice) with descriptive attributes of customers, products and dates. In a star schema the descriptive attributes go into dimension tables and the measurable events go into a fact table. The question asks only about the three fields that describe who and when, and all three belong to dimension tables.

  • CustomerCode, Dimension: CustomerCode is the customer's business key; in an SCD Type 2 dimension it is kept next to the surrogate key and validity columns, and the fact table only stores the surrogate key.
  • CustomerName, Dimension: CustomerName is a descriptive attribute that changes over time; SCD Type 2 keeps its history by inserting rows in the dimension.
  • SaleDate, Dimension: a date is the classic (role-playing) dimension: the fact table stores a key referencing the date dimension and enables time analysis.

Incorrect options:

  • CustomerCode, Fact — Why it is incorrect: Fact: it is not a numeric measure; a descriptive attribute does not belong in the fact table.
  • CustomerCode, Factless fact — Why it is incorrect: Factless fact: it records events or coverage with foreign keys only, not descriptive attributes.
  • CustomerCode, Junk dimension — Why it is incorrect: Junk dimension: it groups assorted low-cardinality flags (payment type, status…), not a customer or a date.
  • CustomerName, Fact — Why it is incorrect: Fact: it is not a numeric measure; a descriptive attribute does not belong in the fact table.
  • CustomerName, Factless fact — Why it is incorrect: Factless fact: it records events or coverage with foreign keys only, not descriptive attributes.

  • SaleDate, Fact — Why it is incorrect: Fact: it is not a numeric measure; a descriptive attribute does not belong in the fact table.
  • SaleDate, Factless fact — Why it is incorrect: Factless fact: it records events or coverage with foreign keys only, not descriptive attributes.

You have a Fabric tenant.

You have a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales for the current month.

You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream activities of the pipeline.

Which type of activity should you add?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Lookup

Why it is correct: The Lookup activity in a Fabric Data Factory pipeline can run a stored procedure against a data source such as a warehouse and return the result set to the pipeline. The output (for example @activity('Lookup1').output.firstRow.ActiveCustomers) can then be referenced by any downstream activity, such as a Set variable, an If Condition or a Copy data activity. Since the stored procedure returns the number of active customers and the average sales and these values must be consumed later in the pipeline, Lookup is the activity designed for that purpose.

answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Get metadata

Why it is incorrect: Get Metadata retrieves metadata about data (for example the structure, size, last modified date or existence of a file, folder or table). It does not execute a stored procedure or return the rows that a procedure produces.

  • Official documentation: Use the Get Metadata activity to look up data from a data source - Microsoft Fabric

B. Copy data

Why it is incorrect: Copy data moves data from a source to a destination. It can use a stored procedure as a source, but its output only exposes run statistics (rows read, rows written, throughput), not the values returned by the procedure, so the downstream activities cannot consume the customer count or the average sales.

  • Official documentation: How to copy data using copy activity - Microsoft Fabric

D. Append variable

Why it is incorrect: Append variable only adds a value to an existing array variable of the pipeline. It does not connect to a warehouse and cannot execute a stored procedure. At most it could store a value that was previously retrieved by another activity.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

Warehouse1 contains a fact table named FactSales that has one billion rows.

You run the following T-SQL statement.

CREATE TABLE test.FactSales AS CLONE OF dbo.FactSales;

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • A replica of dbo.FactSales is created in the test schema by copying the metadata only: Yes
  • Additional schema changes to dbo.FactSales will also apply to test.FactSales: No
  • Additional data changes to dbo.FactSales will also apply to test.FactSales: No

Analysis: CREATE TABLE test.FactSales AS CLONE OF dbo.FactSales; creates a zero-copy clone of the table in the Fabric warehouse. The statement is fast even for a table with one billion rows because it does not copy data files.

Statement 1, Yes. A table clone is created by copying only the metadata of the source table. The clone points to the same underlying Parquet files in OneLake, so no data is physically duplicated and no extra storage is consumed at creation time. The clone can be placed in a different schema of the same warehouse, which is what happens here (test schema).

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse

Statement 2, No. After the clone is created, it is an independent table. DDL changes applied later to dbo.FactSales (adding a column, for instance) are not propagated to test.FactSales, and the same is true in the other direction.

  • Official documentation: Clone table in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse

Statement 3, No. Data changes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) made to the source after the clone is created are not reflected in the clone, and changes to the clone do not affect the source. Existing data files are shared until one of the tables is modified; new or rewritten files then belong only to the table that was changed. This is why a clone is useful for testing, backups and point-in-time analysis, and it is not a replication or synchronization mechanism.

  • Official documentation: Tutorial: Clone a table using T-SQL in Microsoft Fabric

q125.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a data warehouse.

You need to load rows into a large Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD). The solution must minimize resource usage.

Which T-SQL statement should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: UPDATE AND INSERT

Why it is correct: A Type 2 slowly changing dimension keeps history: when a tracked attribute changes you close the current row (set the end date and the current flag to false) with an UPDATE and add a new version of the row with an INSERT. Applying only the changed or new rows with these two statements touches the minimum amount of data in a large dimension, which minimizes resource usage and preserves history. In the Fabric warehouse the MERGE statement is listed among the T-SQL limitations of the surface area (it was not available), so the supported pattern is the combination of UPDATE and INSERT statements.

  • Official documentation: T-SQL surface area - Microsoft Fabric and Dimensional modeling in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse: Load tables
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. MERGE

Why it is incorrect: MERGE is the statement many people would use for SCD loads in SQL Server, but the T-SQL surface area of Fabric Data Warehouse lists it as a limitation (not supported), so it is not an available choice for this scenario.

  • Official documentation: T-SQL surface area - Microsoft Fabric

C. TRUNCATE TABLE and INSERT

Why it is incorrect: Truncating the dimension and reloading it removes all the historical versions, which defeats the purpose of Type 2 SCD. It also reprocesses the whole large table on each load, which maximizes resource usage rather than minimizing it.

  • Official documentation: Slowly changing dimension type 2 - Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric

D. CREATE TABLE AS SELECT

Why it is incorrect: CTAS creates a new table from a query result. Rebuilding the entire dimension this way rewrites all the data on every load and loses the history that cannot be recomputed from the current source. It is a bulk transformation tool, not an incremental load technique.

  • Official documentation: Dimensional modeling in Microsoft Fabric Warehouse: Load tables

You have a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales for the current month.

You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream activities of the pipeline.

Which type of activity should you add?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Lookup

Why it is correct: The Lookup activity can execute a stored procedure in a warehouse and return its result to the pipeline. The returned values (customer count and average sales) are then available to downstream activities through the activity output (for example firstRow), which is exactly what the scenario requires.

answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Append variable

Why it is incorrect: Append variable only adds a value to an array variable. It cannot connect to a warehouse or run a stored procedure.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric

C. Copy data

Why it is incorrect: Copy data is intended to move data between a source and a sink. Its output exposes copy statistics and not the values returned by the stored procedure, so downstream activities cannot use the results directly.

  • Official documentation: How to copy data using copy activity - Microsoft Fabric

D. KQL

Why it is incorrect: The KQL activity runs Kusto queries against an eventhouse / KQL database. It cannot run a T-SQL stored procedure in a warehouse.

Your network contains an on-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) domain named contoso.com that syncs with a Microsoft Entra tenant by using Microsoft Entra Connect.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model.

You enable dynamic row-level security (RLS) for the model and deploy the model to the Fabric service.

You query a measure that includes the USERNAME() function, and the query returns a blank result.

You need to ensure that the measure returns the user principal name (UPN) of a user.

Solution: You add user objects to the list of synced objects in Microsoft Entra Connect.

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: No

Why it is correct: Adding user objects to the list of synced objects in Microsoft Entra Connect does not change what the USERNAME() function returns, so the solution does not meet the goal. USERNAME() is a DAX information function that reports the identity of the user who is running the query in the current context; it does not look anything up in a directory and it has no dependency on which AD DS object types are in the Entra Connect sync scope. The scenario already says that contoso.com syncs with the Microsoft Entra tenant, so the people who sign in to the Fabric service already have identities in the tenant. A blank result is therefore not fixed by widening the sync scope. If the requirement is explicitly to return the user principal name (UPN), DAX provides a dedicated function, USERPRINCIPALNAME(), whose purpose is exactly that, and the dynamic RLS pattern in Power BI is normally built on the UPN of the signed-in user matched against a column or mapping table in the model.

Changing the sync configuration is an identity-infrastructure change in the on-premises/Entra layer; it is not a change to the semantic model measure, which is where the behavior the question complains about lives.

  • Official documentation: USERNAME function (DAX) and USERPRINCIPALNAME function (DAX). Background on sync scope: Configure object filters for directory synchronization.
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Yes

Why it is incorrect: Answering "Yes" would mean that putting more user objects into the Microsoft Entra Connect sync scope makes the measure return the UPN. It does not: the value produced by USERNAME() depends on how the function is evaluated for the querying principal, not on the list of objects that Entra Connect synchronizes, and in this scenario the AD DS domain already syncs with the tenant. To obtain the UPN deterministically you use USERPRINCIPALNAME() in the model's DAX, which is the function designed to return the UPN.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a PySpark notebook named Notebook1.

You define sas_token as a variable in the first cell of Notebook1 and store a shared access signature (SAS) token in the variable.

In the second cell, you run the following code.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • customers is a pandas DataFrame: No
  • If a delta table named Customers does NOT exist, an error will be generated: No
  • The source data is located in the customers folder in a container named contacts: Yes

Statement 1: "customers is a pandas DataFrame" is No. spark.read.parquet(...) is a method of the SparkSession reader and it returns a Spark DataFrame (pyspark.sql.DataFrame), which is distributed and lazily evaluated. It is not a pandas DataFrame. A pandas DataFrame would only appear if the code used pandas.read_parquet or called .toPandas() on the Spark DataFrame. The follow-on code, customers.write.format("delta")..., is the Spark DataFrameWriter API, which a pandas DataFrame does not have. The Fabric documentation distinguishes the Spark API (used to write Delta tables) from the Pandas API (which works through the default lakehouse mount point).

  • Official documentation: Use a notebook to load data into your lakehouse

Statement 2: "If a delta table named Customers does NOT exist, an error will be generated" is No. saveAsTable("Customers") with .format("delta") and .mode("overwrite") creates the table when it does not exist and replaces its contents when it does. The write mode overwrite does not require a pre-existing target (an error on a missing target would be the behavior of an UPDATE/MERGE or of insertInto, not of saveAsTable). In a Fabric lakehouse Delta is also the default table format, so the table is created in the Tables section of the default lakehouse. The "error" alternative would only be true for the errorifexists mode when the table does exist, which is the opposite case.

  • Official documentation: Use a notebook to load data into your lakehouse and Lakehouse and Delta Lake tables

Statement 3: "The source data is located in the customers folder in a container named contacts" is Yes. The path wasbs://contacts@contoso.blob.core.windows.net/customers?{sas_token} follows the pattern wasbs://<container>@<storage account>.blob.core.windows.net/<path>. The part before the @ is the container (contacts), the host is the storage account contoso, and /customers is the folder (path) inside the container. The ?{sas_token} suffix is the shared access signature appended as the query string to authorize access; it is not part of the folder name. The f-string substitutes the token stored in the sas_token variable defined in the first cell. So the data is read from the customers folder of the contacts container.

  • Official documentation: Use a notebook to load data into your lakehouse (Spark read/write of Parquet and Delta in a notebook).

q133.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named DW1 and a

lakehouse named LH1. DW1 contains a table named Sales.Product. LH1 contains a table named Sales.Orders.

You plan to schedule an automated process that will create a new point-in-time (PIT) table named Sales.ProductOrder in DW1. Sales.ProductOrder will be built by using the results of a query that will join Sales.Product and Sales.Orders. You need to ensure that the types of columns in Sales.ProductOrder match the column types in the source tables. The solution must minimize the number of operations required to create the new table.

Which operation should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS)

Why it is correct: The requirements are: create a new table Sales.ProductOrder in the warehouse DW1, populate it with the result of a query that joins a warehouse table (Sales.Product) with a lakehouse table (Sales.Orders), have the column types match the source types, and use as few operations as possible. CTAS does everything in a single statement: it creates the destination table and loads it with the query result, and the column names and data types of the new table are derived from the SELECT result, so they match the source columns (you only cast when you need a different type). From a warehouse you can reference a lakehouse in the same workspace with a three-part name (LH1.Sales.Orders), so the join between DW1.Sales.Product and LH1.Sales.Orders is possible within the CTAS query. Because it is a plain T-SQL statement it can also be scheduled (for example in a data pipeline) to rebuild the point-in-time table.

  • Official documentation: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (Transact-SQL) and Ingest data into your Warehouse using Transact-SQL
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. INSERT INTO

Why it is incorrect: INSERT INTO ... SELECT only appends rows to a table that already exists. You would first have to run a CREATE TABLE statement defining every column and data type manually (an extra operation, and a chance of mismatching the source types) and then the INSERT. That is two operations instead of one, and the requirement is to minimize them. INSERT is the right tool for incremental loads into a table whose schema you control, not for creating the table.

  • Official documentation: Ingest data into your Warehouse using Transact-SQL / Create tables in Fabric Data Warehouse

C. CREATE TABLE AS CLONE OF

Why it is incorrect: A table clone creates a zero-copy copy of one existing table as of a point in time. It cannot take the result of a query, so it cannot join Sales.Product and Sales.Orders, and it cannot clone a lakehouse table into the warehouse in that way. The requirement is a new table built from a join, which a clone cannot express. (The "point-in-time" wording in the question is about the content being a snapshot of the query result, not about the clone feature.)

  • Official documentation: Tables in data warehousing in Microsoft Fabric (table-creation options available in the warehouse).

D. CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW AS SELECT

Why it is incorrect: The question asks for a table (a point-in-time table) whose data is physically created by an automated process. A materialized view is a view object, not a table, and the supported way to create a table from a query result in a Fabric warehouse is CTAS. A view would also not produce a static point-in-time snapshot the way a scheduled CTAS does.

  • Official documentation: Tables in data warehousing in Microsoft Fabric / CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (Transact-SQL)

You have a Fabric tenant that contains the semantic model shown in the following exhibit.

Use the drop-down menus to select the answer choice that completes each statement based on the information presented in the graphic.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First dropdown: DirectQuery
  • Second dropdown: undefined

Querying SQL views from the warehouse of the model will cause a fallback to DirectQuery mode. Row and column security is undefined.

Why it is correct:

  • First dropdown → DirectQuery: In Direct Lake semantic models, data is read directly from the Delta files in OneLake into the VertiPaq engine without going through the SQL analytics endpoint. However, SQL views defined in a Warehouse or Lakehouse SQL endpoint are not physical Delta tables in OneLake, so Direct Lake cannot read them directly. When a SQL view is queried, the model falls back to the SQL endpoint using DirectQuery mode. (Note on Direct Lake Behavior = Direct Lake Only shown in the left pane: in real models with Direct Lake Only fallback is disabled and a query to a SQL view would return an error, but the exam sentence asks which mode a technical fallback goes to in Direct Lake: DirectQuery.) Official documentation: Direct Lake overview (fallback to DirectQuery) - Microsoft Learn
  • Second dropdown → undefined: In the right pane Data > Model, under the root Semantic model node, the Roles (0) branch shows zero defined roles. Both row-level security (RLS) and object/column-level security (OLS) require at least one role in the semantic model to define access rules. With 0 roles, row and column security is undefined. Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI - Microsoft Learn | Object-level security (OLS) - Microsoft Learn

Incorrect options:

  • First dropdown, Automatic — Why it is incorrect: Automatic is a value of the Direct Lake Behavior property (with Direct Lake Only and DirectQuery Only) that controls whether fallback is allowed, not the storage mode it switches to when fallback occurs. Official documentation: Manage Direct Lake behavior - Microsoft Learn
  • First dropdown, Direct Lake — Why it is incorrect: Direct Lake is the model's primary storage mode, not the fallback mode. Fallback happens when a query cannot be resolved in Direct Lake (for example SQL views) and is delegated to the SQL endpoint in DirectQuery. Official documentation: Direct Lake overview - Microsoft Learn
  • Second dropdown, configured to use object-level security (OLS) — Why it is incorrect: Object-level security is configured by assigning permissions (None or Read) on tables or columns to existing model roles. Since the explorer shows Roles (0), no OLS rule is configured. Official documentation: Object-level security (OLS) - Microsoft Learn
  • Second dropdown, configured to use row-level security (RLS) — Why it is incorrect: Row-level security requires DAX filter expressions tied to roles of the semantic model. With Roles (0) no RLS configuration is active. Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI - Microsoft Learn

Your network contains an on-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) domain named contoso.com that syncs with a Microsoft Entra tenant by using Microsoft Entra Connect.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model.

You enable dynamic row-level security (RLS) for the model and deploy the model to the Fabric service.

You query a measure that includes the USERNAME() function, and the query returns a blank result.

You need to ensure that the measure returns the user principal name (UPN) of a user.

Solution: You create a role in the model.

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: No

Why it is correct: Creating a role in the model does not change what a USERNAME() measure returns. A role in a semantic model is a container for RLS filter expressions and for table/column permissions, and it is evaluated only to restrict which rows or objects the members of that role can see. A measure that calls USERNAME() simply returns the identity of the user running the query; the existence of a role does not alter how that identity is presented, so the blank result is not resolved, and the measure still does not become a function that returns the UPN. The dedicated DAX function for the UPN is USERPRINCIPALNAME(). Roles are the second half of dynamic RLS (the role filter uses USERPRINCIPALNAME() or USERNAME() to compare to a column), not a way to change the function's result.

  • Official documentation: USERNAME function (DAX) and Configure row-level security with the dynamic method
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Yes

Why it is incorrect: Defining a role only adds filter expressions and permissions for the members of the role. It does not change the value returned by USERNAME() in a measure, and it does not convert that value to the UPN. The scenario already enabled dynamic RLS, and the measure still returns blank, so adding a role does not meet the goal; you would replace or complement the expression with USERPRINCIPALNAME().

  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI / USERPRINCIPALNAME function (DAX)

q136.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains two workspaces named Workspace1 and Workspace2 and a user named User1.

You need to ensure that User1 can perform the following tasks:

  • Create a new domain.
  • Create two subdomains named subdomain1 and subdomain2.
  • Assign Workspace1 to subdomain1.
  • Assign Workspace2 to subdomain2.

The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.

Which role should you assign to User1?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Fabric admin

Why it is correct: The first task is to create a new domain, and in Microsoft Fabric only a Fabric admin (tenant-level admin role) can create domains. The documentation states this explicitly: "To create domain, you must be a Fabric admin." The other tasks are also covered by this role: creating subdomains is allowed to Fabric admins (and to the domain admins of the parent domain) and assigning workspaces to a domain or subdomain is available in the admin portal to Fabric admins and domain admins. Since the single role that satisfies all four tasks, including the creation of the domain itself, is Fabric admin, it is also the least-privileged choice that works. A domain admin could manage subdomains and workspace assignments of a domain, but only after a Fabric admin had created that domain, so it cannot cover the first requirement.

  • Official documentation: Fabric domains and Administration overview
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. domain admin

Why it is incorrect: Domain admins can create subdomains, associate workspaces with the domain and define domain contributors, but only for domains they administer, and a domain admin cannot create the domain itself (the role is assigned to a domain that a Fabric admin has created). Because the user must be able to create a new domain, this role is insufficient. This is a tempting choice, but it fails on the first requirement.

  • Official documentation: Fabric domains (roles and permissions)

B. domain contributor

Why it is incorrect: A domain contributor is a workspace admin who has been authorized to assign their own workspaces to a domain (or change an existing assignment) from the workspace settings. Contributors cannot create domains or subdomains and do not have access to the Domains tab in the admin portal.

  • Official documentation: Fabric domains (domain contributors) / Domains best practices

D. workspace Admin

Why it is incorrect: Workspace Admin is a role inside a single workspace. It controls the items and membership of that workspace, but it has no authority over the tenant-level domain structure: it cannot create domains or subdomains, and it can only assign the workspace to a domain if it is also authorized as a domain contributor.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric

You have a Fabric tenant that contains three users named User1, User2, and User3. The tenant contains a security group named Group1. User1 and User3 are members of Group1.

The tenant contains the workspaces shown in the following table.

The tenant contains the domains shown in the following table.

User1 creates a new workspace named Workspace3.

You assign Domain1 as the default domain of Group1.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • User2 is assigned the Contributor role for Workspace3: No
  • User3 is assigned the Viewer role for Workspace3: No
  • User3 is assigned the Contributor role for Workspace1: No

Statement 1: No. User1 creates Workspace3, so User1 is the workspace Admin of Workspace3 (the creator becomes Admin). Nothing in the scenario grants User2 any role in Workspace3. User2 is Admin of Workspace2 and of Domain2, but a role in another workspace, or a domain role, does not carry over to a different workspace. Workspace roles are assigned per workspace.

Statement 2: No. User3 is a member of Group1, and Domain1 is made the default domain of Group1. The default domain only controls the domain assignment of workspaces created by members of the group (a new workspace created by User1, a member of Group1, is assigned to Domain1 automatically) and makes those users domain contributors for those workspaces. It does not add User3 to the access list of Workspace3. Domain assignment and workspace access are independent: workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) must be granted explicitly in the workspace.

Statement 3: No. User1 is the Admin of Workspace1 and no role is given to User3 on that workspace. Being a member of Group1 or having Domain1 as default domain does not grant a workspace role. "Domain contributor" is a domain-level capability to assign workspaces to a domain, not the workspace Contributor role.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric and Fabric domains (default domain and domain contributors)

q138.stem:
You have a Fabric warehouse named Warehouse1 that contains a table named Table1. Table1 contains customer data.

You need to implement row-level security (RLS) for Table1. The solution must ensure that users can see only their respective data.

Which two objects should you create? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: FUNCTION
  • Option E: SECURITY POLICY

Why it is correct: Row-level security in a Fabric warehouse is implemented with two T-SQL objects. First, a predicate function, an inline table-valued function (CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURNS TABLE) that contains the filtering logic, for example comparing a column of the row with USER_NAME() so that each user only qualifies for their own rows. Second, a security policy (CREATE SECURITY POLICY ... ADD FILTER PREDICATE ... ON <table>) that binds the function to Table1 and turns enforcement on. Together they make each user see only their respective customer rows. The function defines which rows are allowed and the security policy defines where and when the predicate is applied.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security in Fabric data warehousing and CREATE SECURITY POLICY (Transact-SQL)
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. DATABASE ROLE

Why it is incorrect: A database role groups principals so that permissions can be granted to them together. It is not part of the RLS mechanism: the Fabric documentation example needs only a predicate function and a security policy, and "users see only their own data" is achieved by the predicate comparing the row to the querying user. Roles can complement RLS (for example to grant SELECT) but are not one of the two required objects.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security in Fabric data warehousing

B. STORED PROCEDURE

Why it is incorrect: A stored procedure is a callable routine, and a user could simply bypass it by querying the table directly. RLS filter predicates must be inline table-valued functions bound through a security policy, so a stored procedure cannot act as the predicate.

  • Official documentation: CREATE SECURITY POLICY (Transact-SQL)

C. CONSTRAINT

Why it is incorrect: Constraints (CHECK, PRIMARY KEY, and so on) enforce data integrity on data that is written; they do not filter the rows that a user reads. A constraint therefore cannot limit each user to their own rows. Row-level access is enforced by a security policy.

  • Official documentation: Implement row-level security (Secure a Microsoft Fabric data warehouse)

q139.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1. Lakehouse1 contains a table named Table1. Table1 contains the following data.

You need to perform the following actions:

  • Load the data from Table1 into a star schema.
  • Create a product dimension table named DimProduct and a fact table named FactSales.

Which three columns should you include in DimProduct?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: ProductColor, ProductID, and ProductName.

Why it is correct: In a star schema, a dimension table describes a business entity (here, the product) and holds a unique key plus descriptive attributes used to filter and group, while a fact table stores the events or observations (the transactions) with the foreign keys to the dimensions and the numeric measures. In Table1, the product entity is described by ProductID (the unique key), ProductName and ProductColor (descriptive attributes). Those three columns therefore belong in DimProduct. TransactionID, Date (which would normally link to a date dimension) and SalesAmount (the measure) belong in FactSales, together with ProductID as the foreign key to DimProduct.

  • Official documentation: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. ProductName, SalesAmount, and TransactionID.

Why it is incorrect: SalesAmount is a numeric measure and TransactionID identifies each transaction, so both are fact-level columns that describe events. Putting them in the product dimension would mix grain and would leave DimProduct without its unique key ProductID.

  • Official documentation: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

C. Date, ProductID, and TransactionID.

Why it is incorrect: Date and TransactionID are attributes of the transaction (the fact grain), not of the product. This set would describe a fact table, and it contains no descriptive product attributes.

  • Official documentation: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

D. ProductID, ProductName, and SalesAmount

Why it is incorrect: It correctly includes the key and the name, but SalesAmount is a measure that varies for each transaction. In a dimension it would not be unique per product and it would not be summarized from the fact table. The product color, a real descriptive attribute, is the column that should be there instead.

q140.stem:

You have a Fabric workspace that contains a Dataflow Gen2 query. The query returns the following data.

You need to filter the results to ensure that only the latest version of each customer’s record is retained. The solution must ensure that no new columns are loaded to the semantic model.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence in Power Query Editor? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: Group by CustomerID and calculate the max version date per customer ID.
  • Step 2: Filter the query where the version date value equals the max version date value.
  • Step 3: Remove duplicates based on CustomerID.
  • Step 4: Remove the max version date column.

Why it is correct: the goal is to keep only each customer's latest version without loading new columns into the semantic model; the order is:

  • Step 1, Group by CustomerID and calculate the max version date per customer ID.: the grouping computes the maximum VersionDate per CustomerID: the reference value to compare each record against.
  • Step 2, Filter the query where the version date value equals the max version date value.: the filter comparing VersionDate with the maximum keeps only each customer's latest row; it must come after the aggregate exists.
  • Step 3, Remove duplicates based on CustomerID.: if two rows share the latest timestamp, removing duplicates by CustomerID guarantees one row per customer.
  • Step 4, Remove the max version date column.: the helper max column is only needed for filtering; it must be removed at the end because no new columns may be loaded.

Incorrect options:

  • Group by CustomerID, use the All Rows operation… — Why it is incorrect: it is an alternative route (group with All Rows and expand) that adds steps and nested tables; the marked sequence uses the simple max aggregation (see the note).
  • Expand the All Rows detail column — Why it is incorrect: it is only needed in the All Rows route, which is not the marked sequence.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this sequence, but a plain Group by in Power Query returns only CustomerID and the max column, so the filter step would not work exactly as described. A technically sound pattern is Group by with All Rows plus the max, filter, expand the All Rows column, and remove the max column (or sort and remove duplicates). Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: For the modelling context (keeping one current row per entity in a dimension) see Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

You have a Microsoft Power Bl project that contains a file named definition.pbir. definition.pbir contains the following JSON.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • definition.pbir is in the PBIR-Legacy format: No
  • The semantic model referenced by definition.pbir is located in the Power BI service: No
  • When the related report is opened, Power BI Desktop will open the semantic model in full edit mode: Yes

Statement 1 - "definition.pbir is in the PBIR-Legacy format": No. The definition.pbir file is the entry-point file of a Power BI Desktop project report: it holds the overall report settings and the pointer to the semantic model. The file itself is part of the current PBIR project structure and is not a "legacy" artifact; the format (PBIR-Legacy or PBIR) is determined by how the report definition is stored next to it, in a report.json file or in the definition folder. The version property controls which report definition formats are allowed: with "version": "1.0" (as in the exhibit) the report definition must be stored as PBIR-Legacy in a report.json file, whereas version 4.0 or higher allows either PBIR-Legacy (report.json) or PBIR (the definition folder).

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop project report folder - definition.pbir

Statement 2 - "The semantic model referenced is located in the Power BI service": No. The datasetReference contains "byPath": { "path": "../Sales.Dataset" } and "byConnection": null. A byPath reference is a relative path to a semantic model folder that lives next to the report folder in the same project (here, the Sales.Dataset folder). A model located in the Power BI service / a Fabric workspace would be referenced with byConnection and a connection string (for example semanticmodelid=...). Because byConnection is null, the model is local, not in the service.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop project report folder - datasetReference (byPath / byConnection)

Statement 3 - "Power BI Desktop will open the semantic model in full edit mode": Yes. The documentation states that when a byPath reference is used, opening the .pbir file in Power BI Desktop also opens the semantic model alongside the report, in full edit mode, so you can edit report and model together. In contrast, with a byConnection reference Power BI Desktop opens the report as a live connection and does not open the model in edit mode.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but the documentation says that "version": "1.0" in definition.pbir requires the report definition to be stored as PBIR-Legacy (report.json), so "Yes" for statement 1 could also be argued. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop project report folder - byPath behavior

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

You plan to deploy a semantic model named Model1 by using the XMLA

endpoint.

You need to optimize the deployment of Model1. The solution must minimize how long it takes to deploy Model1.

What should you do in Workspace1?
options: Select Small semantic model storage format.
Select Users can edit data models in the Power BI service.
Set Enable Cache for Shortcuts to On.
Select Large semantic model storage format.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Select Large semantic model storage format.

Why it is correct: The Large semantic model storage format uses a different, more efficient storage and write path (segment-based, on-demand loading) designed for big models. Microsoft documents that when it is enabled, XMLA write operations (such as deploying or refreshing through tools that use the XMLA endpoint) are faster, and it recommends enabling it whenever you plan to use XMLA-based tools for write operations, even if the model is not strictly "large". Since the requirement is to minimize deployment time through the XMLA endpoint, enabling the Large format in the workspace/model settings is the right action.

  • Official documentation: Large semantic models in Power BI Premium
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Select Small semantic model storage format.

Why it is incorrect: The small storage format is the default and it does not give the XMLA write-performance benefit of the large format. It also caps models at a limited size. Choosing it would not minimize deployment time.

  • Official documentation: Large semantic models in Power BI Premium

B. Select Users can edit data models in the Power BI service.

Why it is incorrect: This workspace setting enables web-based data modeling for users (editing the model in the browser). It is a permission/authoring feature and has no effect on how fast a deployment through the XMLA endpoint runs.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model modes in the Power BI service

C. Set Enable Cache for Shortcuts to On.

Why it is incorrect: Caching for OneLake shortcuts reduces egress cost and latency when reading external shortcut data (for example, S3 or GCS). It does not influence the deployment of a semantic model metadata/definition through XMLA.

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts

You have a Microsoft Power BI project that contains a semantic model.

You plan to use Azure DevOps for version control.

You need to modify the .gitignore file to prevent the data values from the data sources from being pushed to the repository.

Which file should you reference?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: cache.abf

Why it is correct: in a Power BI Desktop project (.pbip), the semantic model folder separates declarative metadata from cached data to make source control in Git (Azure DevOps) easier.

cache.abf (Analysis Services Backup File) is the binary file that stores a local copy of the tabular database, including the data values loaded from the data sources. It must be excluded in .gitignore to avoid pushing real or sensitive data to the repository and bloating the Git history with heavy binary files; the .gitignore generated by Power BI Desktop already excludes it by default.

  • Option A, unappliedChanges.json: it contains Power Query editor changes not yet applied to the model; it is part of the definition under development and does not store data extracted from the sources.
  • Option C, localSettings.json: it stores local user or Power BI Desktop session preferences; it is also usually ignored, but it does not contain data values from the sources.
  • Option D, model.bim: it is the TMSL-format file that defines the model metadata (tables, columns, relationships, measures and roles). It is precisely the one that is versioned in Git and it does not contain the imported data records.
  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects: semantic model folder, Power BI Desktop projects and Git integration

Workspace1 uses Pro license mode and contains a semantic model named Model1.

Which setting should modify?
options: Users can edit data models in the Power BI service

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

Why it is correct: The XMLA endpoint is a feature of Power BI Premium, Premium Per User and Embedded workspaces (and Fabric capacities). A workspace in Pro license mode runs on shared capacity and does not expose an XMLA endpoint. To make Model1 accessible through XMLA you must change the workspace License mode (called workspace type in newer UI) to Premium per-user, Premium capacity or a Fabric capacity (also making sure the capacity's XMLA Endpoint setting is Read Write if you need write operations). You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named LH1.

You need to deploy a new semantic model. The solution must meet the

following requirements:

  • Support complex calculated columns that include aggregate functions, calculated tables, and Multidimensional Expressions (MDX) user hierarchies.
  • Minimize page rendering times.

How should you configure the model? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Mode: Import
  • Query Caching: On

Why it is correct: Mode - Import. The requirements are calculated columns that use aggregate functions, calculated tables and MDX user hierarchies. Import mode keeps the data in the in-memory VertiPaq engine and supports the full set of DAX modeling features, including calculated columns, calculated tables and user hierarchies. Direct Lake is the wrong choice here: a Direct Lake table cannot have calculated columns/tables that reference Direct Lake columns, and Direct Lake table user-defined hierarchies are not supported (the documented limitations). DirectQuery also restricts calculated columns and tables (and sends queries to the source, making rendering slower), so it fails the performance requirement as well.

  • Mode, Import: Import keeps the data in VertiPaq and supports calculated columns with aggregations, calculated tables and user hierarchies.
  • Query Caching, On: On enables query caching (available for Import models on Premium/Fabric capacities), which speeds up opening the report's landing page.

Incorrect options:

  • Mode, Direct Lake — Why it is incorrect: Direct Lake does not support calculated columns/tables over its columns nor user hierarchies (documented limitations).
  • Mode, DirectQuery — Why it is incorrect: DirectQuery restricts calculated columns and tables and sends queries to the source, which slows rendering.
  • Query Caching, Capacity default — Why it is incorrect: Capacity default equals Off unless the capacity admin has changed it; it does not guarantee the benefit.
  • Query Caching, Off — Why it is incorrect: Off disables the cache and does not help minimize rendering time.
  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview - considerations and limitations, Semantic model modes in the Power BI service, Query caching in Power BI Premium

q147.stem:
-

You have the following KQL query.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • The query excludes sales that have a Status of Cancelled: Yes
  • The query calculates the total sales of each product category for the last 30 days: Yes
  • The query includes product categories that have had zero sales during the last 30 days: No

Statement 1 - Yes. | where Status != "Cancelled" is a filter predicate: only rows whose Status is different from "Cancelled" continue down the pipeline, so cancelled sales are excluded before aggregation.

Statement 2 - Yes. where OrderDate >= ago(30d) keeps only orders from the last 30 days, and summarize TotalSales = sum(SalesAmount) by ProductCategory groups the remaining rows by category and sums SalesAmount. The result is therefore the total sales per product category for the last 30 days (excluding cancelled ones).

Statement 3 - No. summarize ... by only produces groups that exist in the input rows. A category with no sales in the last 30 days has no rows after the where filters, so it never appears in the output. Furthermore, the final | where TotalSales > 0 removes any group whose total is zero or negative, which would also remove categories whose sales net to zero. Both effects mean zero-sales categories are not included.

  • Official documentation: KQL quick reference (where, summarize, ago)

q148.stem:
You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named SalesOrderDetail, SalesOrderDetail contains three columns named OrderQty, ProductID and SalesOrderlD. SalesOrderDetail contains one row per combination of

SalesOrderlD and ProductID.

You need to calculate the proportion of the total quantity of each sales order represented by each product within the sales order.

Which T-SQL statement should you run?
options:
SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty
  ,CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(PARTITION BY ProductID) * 100
  AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty
  ,CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(ORDER BY SalesOrderID) * 100
  AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty
  ,CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(ORDER BY ProductID) * 100
  AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty
  ,CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER(PARTITION BY SalesOrderID) * 100
  AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProductID
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: the statement that computes SUM(OrderQty) OVER (PARTITION BY SalesOrderID)
SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty
  ,CAST(1. * OrderQty / SUM(OrderQty) OVER (PARTITION BY SalesOrderID) * 100
   AS DECIMAL(5,2)) AS PercentbyProduct
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail;

Why it is correct: The goal is the share of each product's quantity within its own sales order. The window function SUM(OrderQty) OVER (PARTITION BY SalesOrderID) returns, on every row, the total quantity of that order (rows are not collapsed, as they would be with GROUP BY). Dividing the row's OrderQty by that total (multiplying by 1. forces decimal division instead of integer division) and by 100 gives the percentage each product represents within the order. Partitioning by SalesOrderID restarts the total for every order.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - OVER clause (Transact-SQL)
  • Official documentation: T-SQL surface area in Fabric Data Warehouse
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. SUM(OrderQty) OVER (PARTITION BY ProductID)

Why it is incorrect: It partitions by product, so the denominator is the total quantity of that product across all orders. The result is each order line's share of the product's total, not the product's share of its order.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - OVER clause (Transact-SQL)

B. SUM(OrderQty) OVER (ORDER BY SalesOrderID)

Why it is incorrect: With no PARTITION BY, the whole result set is a single partition, and with an ORDER BY the aggregate becomes a running (cumulative) total ordered by SalesOrderID. The denominator would be a growing cumulative quantity across orders, not the order's total.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - OVER clause (Transact-SQL)

C. SUM(OrderQty) OVER (ORDER BY ProductID)

Why it is incorrect: Same problem as B, ordered by ProductID: a running total over the whole table rather than the total per sales order.

  • Official documentation: SELECT - OVER clause (Transact-SQL)

answer.correct:

A shortcut that points to Delta data is created at the top level of the Tables section, so it is recognized as a table. From a notebook with Lakehouse1 as default lakehouse, the relative path Tables/ResearchProduct plus the delta format reads it. Shortcuts under Tables can only be created at the top level, so there is no sub-folder.

q150.stem:

You have a Fabric lakehouse named Lakehouse1 that contains the following data.

You need build a T-SQL statement that will return the total sales amount by OrderDate only for the days that are holidays in Australia. The total sales amount must sum the quantity multiplied by the price on each row in the dbo.sales table.

How should you complete the statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Aggregate expression: Sum(s.Quantity * s.UnitPrice)
  • Join type: Inner

Why it is correct: Aggregate expression - Sum(s.Quantity * s.UnitPrice). The total sales amount must be the sum of quantity multiplied by price per row, grouped by OrderDate. Therefore the multiplication happens inside the aggregate. s.Quantity * s.UnitPrice without SUM would be a non-aggregated expression and fail with GROUP BY s.OrderDate. Sum(s.Quantity) * s.UnitPrice multiplies a total by a single, non-grouped price column (invalid under GROUP BY and not the sum of row amounts), and Sum(s.Quantity) * Sum(s.UnitPrice) multiplies two totals, which gives a different (wrong) number.

  • Aggregate expression, Sum(s.Quantity * s.UnitPrice): the multiplication must happen inside the aggregate (quantity × price per row) and then be summed, grouped by OrderDate.
  • Join type, Inner: INNER JOIN returns only sales whose OrderDate matches a holiday date; the WHERE filters Australia.

Incorrect options:

  • Aggregate expression, s.Quantity * s.UnitPrice — Why it is incorrect: s.Quantity * s.UnitPrice without SUM is not aggregated and would fail with GROUP BY s.OrderDate.
  • Aggregate expression, Sum(s.Quantity) * s.UnitPrice — Why it is incorrect: Sum(s.Quantity) * s.UnitPrice multiplies a total by an ungrouped column: invalid with GROUP BY and not a sum of per-row amounts.
  • Aggregate expression, Sum(s.Quantity) * Sum(s.UnitPrice) — Why it is incorrect: Sum(s.Quantity) * Sum(s.UnitPrice) multiplies two totals and yields a different number.
  • Join type, Cross — Why it is incorrect: Cross produces a Cartesian product.
  • Join type, Full outer — Why it is incorrect: Full outer keeps unmatched rows (holidays without sales, sales on non-holiday days).
  • Join type, Right outer — Why it is incorrect: Right outer keeps holidays without sales, which does not meet the requirement.
  • Official documentation: T-SQL surface area in Fabric Data Warehouse, FROM clause plus JOIN (Transact-SQL)

links.t: T-SQL surface area in Fabric Data Warehouse
FROM clause plus JOIN (Transact-SQL)

q151.stem:
-

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains a warehouse named DW1. DW1 contains two tables named Employees and Sales. All users have read access to Dw1.

You need to implement access controls to meet the following requirements:

  • For the Sales table, ensure that the users can see only the sales data from their respective region.
  • For the Employees table, restrict access to all Personally Identifiable Information (PII).
  • Maintain access to unrestricted data for all the users.

What should you use for each table? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Employees: Column-level security
  • Sales: Row-level security (RLS)

Why it is correct: Employees: Column-level security. The requirement is to hide the Personally Identifiable Information (PII) columns (for example name, national ID, phone, salary) while every user keeps access to the non-sensitive columns of the same table. That is exactly what column-level security (CLS) does in a Fabric warehouse: you use T-SQL GRANT SELECT ON Employees(<allowed columns>) TO <user or role> so that the PII columns are simply not included. A query that touches a restricted column fails with a "SELECT permission was denied on the column" error, while queries over the permitted columns work. Because all users already have read access to DW1, CLS lets you narrow it at column granularity without creating extra views or duplicating the table.

  • Employees, Column-level security: CLS hides the PII columns (GRANT SELECT on the allowed columns) and keeps access to the rest of the table's columns.
  • Sales, Row-level security (RLS): RLS filters rows with a predicate (table-valued function + CREATE SECURITY POLICY): each user sees only their own region's sales.

Incorrect options:

  • Employees, Item permissions — Why it is incorrect: item permissions act on the whole warehouse; they do not restrict individual columns.
  • Employees, Row-level security (RLS) — Why it is incorrect: RLS removes rows: it would hide whole employees instead of only the PII columns.
  • Employees, Workspace permissions — Why it is incorrect: workspace roles apply to every item; they cannot separate PII columns.
  • Sales, Column-level security — Why it is incorrect: CLS hides whole columns; it cannot make each user see only their own region's rows.
  • Sales, Item permissions — Why it is incorrect: item permissions work at the whole-item level; they do not restrict rows.
  • Sales, Workspace permissions — Why it is incorrect: workspace roles are even more general; they cannot filter rows by region.
  • Official documentation: Column-level security in Fabric data warehousing, Row-level security in Fabric data warehousing, Security for data warehousing in Microsoft Fabric, Permission model - Microsoft Fabric
