q152.stem:
You need to create a Microsoft Power BI file that will be used to create multiple reports. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • The file must include predefined data source connections.
  • The file must include the report structure and formatting.
  • The file must NOT contain any data.

Which file format should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: PBIT

Why it is correct: A Power BI template file (.pbit) is designed precisely for this scenario. It stores the report definition (pages, visuals, formatting, theme), the data model (tables, relationships, measures) and the queries, including the data source connections, but it does not contain any data. When someone opens the template, Power BI Desktop prompts for the required parameters or credentials and loads the data from the sources, creating a new .pbix report. That satisfies the three requirements: predefined data source connections, report structure and formatting, and no data in the file. It can be reused to create as many reports as needed.

  • Official documentation: Create and use report templates in Power BI Desktop
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. PBIDS

Why it is incorrect: A Power BI data source file (.pbids) is a small JSON file that only holds the connection information for a single data source (server, database, connection type). When opened, Power BI Desktop starts the Get Data experience against that source. It contains no report pages, visuals or formatting, so it fails the requirement to include the report structure and formatting.

  • Official documentation: Data sources in Power BI Desktop

C. PBIX

Why it is incorrect: A .pbix file is the regular Power BI Desktop file. It includes the report, the model and the connections, but it also stores the imported data (the compressed model cache). This violates the requirement that the file must not contain any data. Exporting the report as a template (.pbit) is what removes the data.

  • Official documentation: Create and use report templates in Power BI Desktop

D. PBIP

Why it is incorrect: A Power BI Project (.pbip) saves a report and a semantic model as a folder of plain-text definition files, mainly for source control, CI/CD and programmatic edits. It is a development format, not a distributable template: it is not opened by a user to spawn new reports with prompted parameters, and the project can include a local data cache that is only excluded through .gitignore. It is not the file format intended for creating multiple reports from a predefined structure.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects overview

q153.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains a single semantic model that has two Microsoft Power BI reports.

You have a Microsoft 365 subscription that contains a data loss prevention (DLP) policy named DLP1.

You need to apply DLP1 to the items in Workspace1.

What should you do?
options: Apply a certified endorsement to the semantic model.
Apply sensitivity labels to the semantic model and reports.
Apply a master data endorsement to the semantic model.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Apply sensitivity labels to the semantic model and reports.

Why it is correct: Data loss prevention (DLP) policies for Fabric and Power BI are defined in the Microsoft Purview portal and evaluate items based on conditions such as sensitivity labels and sensitive information types. A policy such as DLP1 therefore takes effect on the items in Workspace1 when those items carry the label (or contain the sensitive content) that the policy's conditions target. Applying the appropriate sensitivity labels to the semantic model and to the two reports is the way to make DLP1 apply to them, and the semantic model is one of the item types that DLP policies evaluate (on publish, refresh, and so on).

  • Official documentation: Get started with data loss prevention policies for Fabric and Power BI and Information protection in Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Create a workspace identity.

Why it is incorrect: A workspace identity is an automatically managed service principal that the workspace uses to authenticate to resources protected by Microsoft Entra ID, such as firewall-enabled storage accounts through trusted workspace access. It has nothing to do with Microsoft Purview DLP policies.

  • Official documentation: Workspace identity in Microsoft Fabric

B. Apply a certified endorsement to the semantic model.

Why it is incorrect: Certification is a governance badge that tells users the item is reliable and meets the organization's quality standards. It affects discoverability and trust, not security: DLP policy conditions do not use endorsement, and it only covers the semantic model, not the reports.

  • Official documentation: Endorsement overview - Microsoft Fabric

D. Apply a master data endorsement to the semantic model.

Why it is incorrect: Master data is another endorsement badge that marks an item as a core, single source of truth. Like certification, it is only a label for discovery and trust; it does not trigger or scope DLP policies.

  • Official documentation: Endorsement overview - Microsoft Fabric

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1 and a user named User1. User1 is assigned the Contributor role for Workspace1.

You plan to configure Workspace1 to use an Azure DevOps repository for version control.

You need to ensure that User1 can commit items to the repository.

Which two settings should you enable for User1? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
options: Users can sync workspace items with GitHub repositories
Users can create and use Data workflows
Users can synchronize workspace items with their Git repositories

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option C: Users can create Fabric items
  • Option D: Users can synchronize workspace items with their Git repositories

Why it is correct: Git integration is controlled by tenant settings, and the ones needed here are listed in the Git prerequisites. "Users can synchronize workspace items with their Git repositories" is the core switch that allows users to sync a workspace with an Azure DevOps repository (it is enabled by default and can be limited to specific security groups). "Users can create Fabric items" is also required so that users can work with Fabric items (lakehouses, warehouses, notebooks, and so on) that are saved to and committed from the repository. User1 already has the Contributor role, so the role is not the missing piece; the tenant switches must apply to User1 (for example by being a member of the security group they are scoped to).

answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Users can sync workspace items with GitHub repositories

Why it is incorrect: This switch is only needed when the workspace is connected to a GitHub repository. The scenario uses an Azure DevOps repository, so this setting is not required.

  • Official documentation: Git integration tenant settings

B. Users can create and use Data workflows

Why it is incorrect: This tenant setting relates to Data workflows (Apache Airflow-based orchestration in Data Factory). It is not part of the Git integration prerequisites, and committing items to a repository does not depend on it.

q155.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains a data pipeline named Pipeline1 and a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

You perform the following actions:

  • Create a workspace named Workspace2.
  • Create a deployment pipeline named DeployPipeline1 that will deploy items from Workspace1 to Workspace2.
  • Add a folder named Folder1 to Workspace1.
  • Move Lakehouse1 to Folder1.
  • Run DeployPipeline1.

Which structure will Workspace2 have when DeployPipeline1 is complete?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: \Pipeline1 \Folder1\Lakehouse1

Why it is correct: When you deploy to a stage whose workspace is empty (Workspace2 is new), deployment pipelines copy all the supported items from the source and create them in the target. Pipeline1 is in the root of Workspace1, so it is created in the root of Workspace2. Lakehouse1 was moved to Folder1 before the deployment; deployment pipelines apply the folder hierarchy of the deployed items, and if the folder does not exist in the target it is created first. Therefore Workspace2 ends up with \Pipeline1 and \Folder1\Lakehouse1. Folder structure is only deployed because an item inside the folder is deployed, and the data pipeline in the root is not placed inside Folder1.

  • Official documentation: Understand the deployment process - Microsoft Fabric and Introduction to deployment pipelines
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. \Folder1\Pipeline1 \Folder1\Lakehouse1

Why it is incorrect: Only Lakehouse1 was moved to Folder1. Pipeline1 stays in the root of Workspace1, and the deployment preserves each item's own path, so Pipeline1 is not placed in Folder1.

  • Official documentation: Understand the deployment process - Microsoft Fabric

B. \Pipeline1 \Lakehouse1

Why it is incorrect: This ignores the folder. Deployment pipelines apply the folder hierarchy of the deployed items, creating the folder in the target workspace if it does not exist, so Lakehouse1 does not land in the root.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to deployment pipelines

D. \Folder1\Lakehouse1

Why it is incorrect: It omits Pipeline1. A data pipeline is a supported item type for deployment pipelines, and the run deploys all the supported items from Workspace1 (not only those in the folder), so Pipeline1 must also appear in Workspace2.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to deployment pipelines

q156.stem:
Your company has a finance department.

You have a Fabric tenant, an Azure Storage account named storage1, and a Microsoft Entra group named Group1. Group1 contains the users in the finance department.

You need to create a new workspace named Workspace1 in the tenant. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • Ensure that the finance department users can create and edit items in Workspace1.
  • Ensure that Workspace1 can securely access storage1 to read and write data.
  • Ensure that you are the only admin of Workspace1.
  • Minimize administrative effort.

You create Workspace1.

Which two actions should you perform next? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
options: Assign the Contributor role to Group1.
Assign the Admin role to yourself.
Assign the Contributor role to each finance department user.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option A: Assign the Contributor role to Group1.
  • Option B: Create a workspace identity.

Why it is correct: Two things are needed after creating the workspace.

  1. Finance users can create and edit items, with minimal effort: The Contributor role allows creating and modifying content. Assigning it to the Microsoft Entra group Group1 (instead of to each user) minimizes administrative effort, because membership changes are handled in Entra and not in the workspace.
  2. Secure access to storage1 for reading and writing: A workspace identity is a managed service principal tied to the workspace. Once created, you grant that identity an Azure RBAC role on the storage account (for example Storage Blob Data Contributor) and use trusted workspace access, so items in the workspace can securely read and write the firewall-protected storage without managing keys or secrets.

The Admin requirement needs no action: the person who creates a workspace is automatically its Admin, and nobody else receives that role.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric, Workspace identity in Microsoft Fabric and Trusted workspace access
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

C. Assign the Admin role to yourself.

Why it is incorrect: It is redundant. The user who creates a workspace already holds the Admin role in it, so there is nothing to assign, and this action does not address either the finance access or the storage requirement.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric

D. Assign the Contributor role to each finance department user.

Why it is incorrect: It gives the right permission level, but it is not the most efficient way: each user would have to be added and maintained individually. The requirement to minimize administrative effort is met by assigning the role once to Group1.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric

q157.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains the workspaces shown in the following table.

You have a deployment pipeline named Pipeline1 that deploys items from Workspace_DEV to Workspace_TEST. In Pipeline1, all items that have matching names are paired.

You deploy the contents of Workspace_DEV to Workspace_TEST by using

Pipeline1.

What will the contents of Workspace_TEST be once the deployment is complete?
options: Lakehouse1 - Lakehouse2 - Notebook1 - Notebook2 - Pipeline1 - SemanticModel1

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Lakehouse1 - Lakehouse2 - Notebook1 - Notebook2 - Pipeline1 - SemanticModel1

Why it is correct: Deployment pipelines work with paired items. Workspace_TEST was populated independently, so Lakehouse2 and Notebook2 have no counterpart in Workspace_DEV and are not paired with anything. During deployment:

  • Lakehouse1, Notebook1 and Pipeline1 exist only in Workspace_DEV, so they are new items and are copied to Workspace_TEST.
  • SemanticModel1 exists in both workspaces with the same name and, as the question states, the items with matching names are paired, so the DEV version overwrites the TEST one (a single SemanticModel1 remains).
  • Lakehouse2 and Notebook2 exist only in the target. Items that do not exist in the source stage remain as they are; deployment never deletes them.

The result is the union of both sets: Lakehouse1, Lakehouse2, Notebook1, Notebook2, Pipeline1 and SemanticModel1.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to deployment pipelines and Understand the deployment process
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. Lakehouse1 - Notebook1 - Pipeline1 - SemanticModel1

Why it is incorrect: It assumes that the target is replaced by the source (a mirror). Deployment pipelines do not delete target items that are missing from the source, so Lakehouse2 and Notebook2 stay in Workspace_TEST.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to deployment pipelines

C. Lakehouse2 - Notebook2 - SemanticModel1

Why it is incorrect: It assumes nothing new is copied. Unpaired items from the source (Lakehouse1, Notebook1, Pipeline1) are created in the target during a deployment; only items that are paired are overwritten.

  • Official documentation: Understand the deployment process

D. Lakehouse2 - Notebook2 - Pipeline1 - SemanticModel1

Why it is incorrect: It copies Pipeline1 but forgets Lakehouse1 and Notebook1. All supported items in the source stage are deployed, so they must also appear in Workspace_TEST.

  • Official documentation: Understand the deployment process

Statement 1, Yes: according to the table in the question, DF1 is a Dataflow Gen1. Deployment pipelines support deploying dataflows between stages, so DF1 is deployed to Workspace_TEST when Pipeline1 runs.

Statement 2, No: deployment pipelines copy item metadata and definitions (table schema, relationships, DAX measures, Power Query queries and model settings), not the data loaded into the semantic model. After deploying Model1 to Workspace_TEST, the model has no data until a refresh is run in the target workspace.

Statement 3, No: although Model1 has a scheduled refresh policy configured in Workspace_DEV, refresh schedules are not copied between stages during a deployment; they must be configured in Workspace_TEST after the deployment.

q159.stem:
-

You have a Fabric warehouse that contains two tables named DimDate and Trips.

DimDate contains the following fields.

Trips contains the following fields.

You need to compare the average miles per trip for statutory holidays versus non-statutory holidays.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First box (the MilesPerTrip expression): (sum(t.tripDistance)/count(t.tripID))
  • Second box (the clause before d.IsHoliday): group by

Why it is correct: First box: (sum(t.tripDistance)/count(t.tripID)). Average miles per trip is the total miles travelled divided by the number of trips. sum(t.tripDistance) is the numerator (tripDistance holds miles per trip) and count(t.tripID) is the denominator, evaluated for each group. The result is one MilesPerTrip value per value of IsHoliday. (Both operands are integers, so T-SQL performs integer division; in a real solution you would cast one operand to decimal or use avg(t.tripDistance), but among the options this is the correct formula.)

  • First box (the MilesPerTrip expression), (sum(t.tripDistance)/count(t.tripID)): average miles per trip is total miles divided by number of trips, evaluated per group: sum(tripDistance)/count(tripID).
  • Second box (the clause before d.IsHoliday), group by: GROUP BY d.IsHoliday produces one aggregated row per IsHoliday value, and every non-aggregated SELECT column must be in the GROUP BY.

Incorrect options:

  • First box (the MilesPerTrip expression), (count(t.tripID) / sum(t.tripDistance)) — Why it is incorrect: count/sum is inverted: it returns trips per mile.
  • First box (the MilesPerTrip expression), Sum(t.tripDistance)/t.tripID) — Why it is incorrect: it mixes an aggregate with a non-aggregated column (t.tripID): invalid without grouping and it would give each trip's distance, not the average.
  • Second box (the clause before d.IsHoliday), order by — Why it is incorrect: order by only sorts the output; with aggregates and no GROUP BY the statement would fail.
  • Second box (the clause before d.IsHoliday), where — Why it is incorrect: where would filter rows leaving a single day type; it does not produce the two groups to compare.
  • Official documentation: GROUP BY (Transact-SQL), SELECT - ORDER BY clause (Transact-SQL)

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named LH1 and a warehouse named DW1. LH1 contains a table named signindata that is in the dbo schema.

You need to create a stored procedure in DW1 that deduplicates the data in the signindata table.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First box (after AS): BEGIN
  • Second box (after SELECT): DISTINCT

Why it is correct: First box: BEGIN. The procedure body is delimited by BEGIN ... END, and the statement ends with the END that closes it. BEGIN opens that statement block, which is the syntax that pairs with the final END.

  • First box (after AS), BEGIN: the procedure body is delimited by BEGIN … END; BEGIN opens the block closed by the final END.
  • Second box (after SELECT), DISTINCT: SELECT DISTINCT PersonID, FirstName, LastName returns each unique combination once, deduplicating without modifying the source table.

Incorrect options:

  • First box (after AS), BEGIN DISTRIBUTED TRANSACTION — Why it is incorrect: BEGIN DISTRIBUTED TRANSACTION starts a distributed transaction (MSDTC) and does not open a block the END can close; it is also unnecessary because the lakehouse is in the same workspace.
  • First box (after AS), SET — Why it is incorrect: SET assigns options or variables; it does not open a block or pair with END.
  • Second box (after SELECT), GROUP BY — Why it is incorrect: GROUP BY goes after FROM, not right after SELECT, and would only make sense with aggregates.
  • Second box (after SELECT), TOP (100) PERCENT WITH TIES — Why it is incorrect: TOP (100) PERCENT WITH TIES does not remove duplicates (it returns all rows) and WITH TIES requires ORDER BY.
  • Official documentation: T-SQL surface area in Fabric Data Warehouse, SELECT clause (Transact-SQL), GROUP BY (Transact-SQL)

q161.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant.

You are creating a Fabric Data Factory pipeline.

You have a stored procedure that returns the number of active customers and their average sales for the current month.

You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream activities of the pipeline.

Which type of activity should you add?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Lookup

Why it is correct: The pipeline has to run a stored procedure in a warehouse and hand the values it returns (number of active customers and average sales) to the downstream activities. The Lookup activity can retrieve a dataset from any supported data source, including a Fabric warehouse, and it can run a stored procedure as its query. Its output (the first row, or the whole result set if "First row only" is cleared) is exposed as activity output, so later activities reference it with expressions such as @activity('Lookup1').output.firstRow.ActiveCustomers. That is exactly the "returned values must be available downstream" requirement. Note that the plain Stored procedure activity runs the procedure but does not return a result set to the pipeline, which is why Lookup is the right choice here.

  • Official documentation: Use the Lookup activity to look up data from a data source and How to use Stored procedure activity
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Get metadata

Why it is incorrect: Get metadata returns metadata about data (for example file or folder names, sizes, last-modified dates, structure, column count, existence). It does not execute a stored procedure and cannot return the business values (active customers, average sales) that the procedure computes.

  • Official documentation: Use the Get Metadata activity to look up data from a data source

B. Switch

Why it is incorrect: Switch is a control-flow activity that evaluates an expression and runs one of several branches of activities depending on the value. It does not connect to a warehouse and does not execute stored procedures or return data.

  • Official documentation: Activity overview - Microsoft Fabric

D. Append variable

Why it is incorrect: Append variable adds a value to an existing array-type pipeline variable. It is a way of storing something that already exists in the pipeline; it cannot run a stored procedure in a warehouse or produce its result.

  • Official documentation: Use the Append Variable activity in Fabric

You have the following T-SQL statement.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Statement 1 (returns Region values when a Sales item has a RefundStatus of Refunded): Yes
  • Statement 2 (only returns TransactionDate values that occurred during the current year): No
  • Statement 3 (the TotalRevenue calculation aggregates SalesAmount values that have a RefundStatus of Refunded): No

Statement 1, Yes: the WHERE clause filters only by the transaction year (YEAR(TransactionDate) = YEAR(GETDATE())) and does not exclude records with RefundStatus = 'Refunded'. The refund filter is inside the CASE WHEN in the SELECT list, not in the WHERE, so refunded items remain part of the GROUP BY ProductCategory, Region groups and their Region values are returned in the result (contributing 0 to TotalRevenue).

Statement 2, No: although the WHERE restricts processing to transactions of the current year, the SELECT does not include the TransactionDate column. The query returns only three columns (ProductCategory, Region and TotalRevenue), so it returns no TransactionDate values.

Statement 3, No: SUM(CASE WHEN RefundStatus <> 'Refunded' THEN SalesAmount ELSE 0 END) uses the inequality operator: it only adds SalesAmount when the status is not 'Refunded'; for refunded records it assigns 0 instead of adding their amount.

q163.stem:
-

You have a Fabric warehouse that contains the following data.

The data has the following characteristics:

  • Each customer is assigned a unique CustomerID value.
  • Each customer is associated to a single SalesRegion value.
  • Each customer is associated to a single CustomerAddress value.
  • The Customer table contains 5 million rows.
  • All foreign key values are non-null.

You need to create a view to denormalize the data into a customer dimension that contains one row per distinct CustomerID value. The solution must minimize query processing time and resources.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Join with SalesLT.SalesRegion: inner join
  • Join condition with SalesLT.Address: A.AddressID = CA.AddressID

Why it is correct: the denormalized view must return exactly one row per CustomerID, minimizing query processing time and resources. The full statement is:

CREATE VIEW DimCustomer AS
SELECT
    C.CustomerID,
    C.CustomerName,
    C.CompanyName,
    SR.SalesRegion,
    A.City,
    A.StateProvince,
    A.CountryRegion,
    A.PostalCode
FROM SalesLT.Customer C
INNER JOIN SalesLT.SalesRegion SR ON C.SalesRegionID = SR.SalesRegionID
INNER JOIN [SalesLT].[CustomerAddress] CA ON CA.customerid = C.customerid
INNER JOIN [SalesLT].[Address] A ON A.AddressID = CA.AddressID
WHERE CA.AddressType = 'Main Office'

  • Join with SalesLT.SalesRegion, inner join: the statement guarantees a single SalesRegion per customer and non-null foreign keys: INNER JOIN returns the same rows and lets the optimizer reorder joins.
  • Join condition with SalesLT.Address, A.AddressID = CA.AddressID: CustomerAddress (CA) is the bridge table: after joining Customer with CA, CA is linked to Address through its primary key A.AddressID = CA.AddressID.

Incorrect options:

  • Join with SalesLT.SalesRegion, full outer join — Why it is incorrect: full outer join also keeps regions without customers (CustomerID NULL), breaks one row per customer and is the most expensive join.
  • Join with SalesLT.SalesRegion, left outer join — Why it is incorrect: left outer join returns the same rows, but forces preserving the whole left side (5 million) and limits plan reordering.
  • Join condition with SalesLT.Address, C.AddressID = CA.AddressID — Why it is incorrect: Customer has no AddressID column: it would raise an invalid column error.
  • Join condition with SalesLT.Address, C.CustomerID = A.CustomerID — Why it is incorrect: Address has no CustomerID column; the relationship with the customer goes through CustomerAddress.
  • Official documentation: FROM clause plus JOIN, APPLY, PIVOT (Transact-SQL), Performance guidelines in Fabric Data Warehouse, Views in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse

q164.stem:
You have a query in Microsoft Power BI Desktop that contains two columns named Order_Date and Shipping_Date.

You need to create a column that will calculate the number of days between Order_Date and Shipping_Date for each row.

Which Power Query function should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Duration.Days

Why it is correct: In Power Query, subtracting two date values ([Shipping_Date] - [Order_Date]) returns a duration value. Duration.Days extracts the days component of a duration as a number, so a custom column such as = Duration.Days([Shipping_Date] - [Order_Date]) yields the number of days between the two dates for every row.

  • Official documentation: Duration.Days - Power Query M and Duration functions
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. DateTime.LocalNow

Why it is incorrect: It returns the current local date and time as a datetime value; it takes no column inputs and does not compute a difference between two columns.

  • Official documentation: Today's date in Power Query custom columns

C. Duration.From

Why it is incorrect: Duration.From converts a value (for example a number or text) into a duration. It does not calculate the difference between two dates, and it would not return the day count as a number by itself.

  • Official documentation: Duration functions

D. Date.AddDays

Why it is incorrect: Date.AddDays adds a number of days to a date and returns another date. The requirement is the opposite: obtain the number of days between two dates.

What should you use?

answer.correct:

  • Option D: Tabular Editor

Why it is correct: Object-level security (OLS) restricts access to tables and columns of a semantic model through table/column permissions on roles. The Power BI Desktop and Fabric service interfaces let you create roles and define row-level security, but they do not expose the table and column permission settings needed for OLS. B. Microsoft Power BI Desktop

C. ALM Toolkit

Why it is incorrect: ALM Toolkit is a schema comparison and deployment tool for semantic models (it compares and merges metadata between models). It is not an authoring tool for defining role permissions such as OLS.

q166.stem:
You have a Microsoft Power BI semantic model that contains a measure named TotalSalesAmount. TotalSalesAmount returns a sales revenue amount that is translated into a selected currency.

You need to ensure that the value returned by TotalSalesAmount is formatted to use the correct currency symbol.

What should you include in the solution?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: a dynamic format string

Why it is correct: A dynamic format string lets a measure carry a DAX expression that decides its format string depending on context. For a revenue measure converted to the currency the user selects, the format string expression can return the proper symbol and pattern (for example "€#,0.00" or "$#,0.00") based on the selected currency, so the value is shown with the correct symbol without changing the value itself or creating text measures.

  • Official documentation: Create dynamic format strings for measures
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. a field parameter

Why it is incorrect: Field parameters let report users switch which fields or measures appear in a visual (for example swapping the axis or the measure). They change what is shown, not how a measure's value is formatted.

  • Official documentation: Use field parameters in Power BI

B. a linguistic schema

Why it is incorrect: A linguistic schema defines synonyms and phrasing for Q&A natural-language queries over the model. It has no effect on number or currency formatting.

  • Official documentation: Create dynamic format strings for measures (formatting is controlled by format strings, not by the linguistic schema)

D. the WINDOW DAX function

Why it is incorrect: WINDOW returns a range of rows within a partition and is used for window calculations (running totals, moving averages). It does not control how a result is formatted.

q167.stem:
You plan to use Fabric to store data.

You need to create a data store that supports the following:

  • Writing data by using T-SQL
  • Multi-table transactions
  • Dynamic data masking

Which type of data store should you create?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: warehouse

Why it is correct: The three requirements point to a Fabric warehouse: it is the store that supports writing data with T-SQL (full DML and DDL), multi-table transactions (ACID transactions that span several tables, with snapshot isolation) and dynamic data masking to obfuscate sensitive column values for non-privileged users.

  • Official documentation: Transactions in Warehouse tables and Dynamic data masking in Fabric data warehousing
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. KQL database

Why it is incorrect: A KQL database is queried with Kusto Query Language and ingests streaming/time-series data. Data is not written by T-SQL DML, and it does not offer multi-table T-SQL transactions.

  • Official documentation: Kusto query set - Microsoft Fabric

B. lakehouse

Why it is incorrect: A lakehouse is written with Spark. Its SQL analytics endpoint is read-only for the Delta tables (you can create views and security, but cannot INSERT/UPDATE data in tables through T-SQL), and multi-table transactions are a warehouse capability. Dynamic data masking is configurable on the endpoint, but the write-with-T-SQL and transaction requirements rule the lakehouse out.

  • Official documentation: Microsoft Fabric decision guide: Choose between Warehouse and Lakehouse and SQL analytics endpoint of the lakehouse

D. semantic model

Why it is incorrect: A semantic model is an analytical layer for reports and measures (DAX); it is not a data store you write to with T-SQL and it has no T-SQL transaction support.

  • ② Configure the rule that changes Date1 in Test: Deployment rules icon of the Test stage

Why it is correct: Why they are correct: in Fabric deployment pipelines, the flow to create the test environment with the standard naming and parameterize the Model1 semantic model has two steps:

You have two Microsoft Power BI queries named Employee and Retired Roles.

You need to merge the Employee query with the Retired Roles query. The solution must ensure that duplicate rows in each query are removed.

Which column and Join Kind should you use in Power Query Editor? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Column: Division (the matching column between Employee and Retired Roles; in the Merge dialog it is the column highlighted in the Employee table)
  • Join Kind: Inner (only matching rows)

Why it is correct: Column - Division. A merge requires one or more columns with the same meaning in both queries. Retired Roles exposes Division (and Role) while Employee contains Division, Role, etc.; Division is the matching column for this merge.

  • Column, Division: Division is the column with the same meaning in both queries (Employee and Retired Roles) and serves as the matching column.
  • Join Kind, Inner (only matching rows): Inner keeps only the rows that match in both tables; it is the accepted option (see the note: it does not remove duplicates by itself).

Incorrect options:

  • Column, ID — Why it is incorrect: it does not exist with the same meaning in both queries.
  • Column, Title Detail — Why it is incorrect: it is not a common column of both queries.
  • Column, Role — Why it is incorrect: it also appears in both, but the accepted column is Division (see the note: Role would be a second matching column).
  • Column, Department — Why it is incorrect: it is not a common column of both queries.
  • Column, Department Number — Why it is incorrect: it is not a common column of both queries.
  • Column, Division Number — Why it is incorrect: it is not a common column of both queries.
  • Join Kind, Left Outer (all from first, matching from second) — Why it is incorrect: it keeps all Employee rows, including unmatched ones.
  • Join Kind, Right Outer (all from second, matching from first) — Why it is incorrect: it keeps all Retired Roles rows, including unmatched ones.
  • Join Kind, Full Outer (all rows from both) — Why it is incorrect: it keeps all rows from both tables; it does not remove unmatched ones.
  • Join Kind, Left Anti (rows only in first) — Why it is incorrect: it returns only unmatched rows of the first table, the opposite of keeping the intersection.
  • Join Kind, Right Anti (rows only in second) — Why it is incorrect: it returns only unmatched rows of the second table, the opposite of keeping the intersection.

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but an inner join does not by itself remove duplicates, and the dialog also shows Role as a second matching column (Retired Roles shows Division = 2, Role = 1). Inner is the closest option offered; removing duplicates properly would need a Remove Duplicates step before merging. Check it against the linked documentation.

q171.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1 and a user named User1. Workspace1 contains a warehouse named DW1.

You share DW1 with User1 and assign User1 the default permissions for DW1.

What can User1 do?
options: Build reports by using the default dataset.
Read data from the tables in DW1.
Connect to DW1 via the Azure SQL Analytics endpoint.
Read the underlying Parquet files from OneLake.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Connect to DW1 via the Azure SQL Analytics endpoint.

Why it is correct: When you share a warehouse and leave all the optional check boxes cleared, the recipient only gets the default Read permission on the item. In a Fabric warehouse this permission is the equivalent of the SQL CONNECT permission: it lets the user connect to the warehouse through its SQL (TDS) connection string, which is the SQL analytics endpoint (the option text says "Azure SQL Analytics endpoint", which is a loose reference to it), and nothing more. The user does not get SELECT on the tables, does not get access to the files in OneLake and does not get the right to build on the semantic model. Those capabilities require additional permissions chosen at sharing time (for example Read all data using SQL / ReadData, Read all OneLake data / ReadAll, or Build reports on the default semantic model / Build), or a SQL GRANT executed afterwards.

  • Official documentation: Share your warehouse and manage permissions - Microsoft Fabric and Connectivity to data warehousing in Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Build reports by using the default dataset.

Why it is incorrect: Building reports on the default semantic model is controlled by the separate Build permission, which is an optional check box in the sharing dialog ("Build reports on the default semantic model"). It is not part of the default Read permission, so User1 cannot build reports on the default dataset until that option is granted.

  • Official documentation: Share your warehouse and manage permissions - Microsoft Fabric

B. Read data from the tables in DW1.

Why it is incorrect: This is the tempting answer chosen by some commenters, but the default Read permission only allows connecting to the endpoint (like CONNECT in SQL Server). Reading table data requires the additional Read all data using SQL (ReadData) permission selected during sharing, or granular SELECT permissions granted with T-SQL. Without them, User1 can connect but queries against the tables are denied.

  • Official documentation: Share your warehouse and manage permissions - Microsoft Fabric

D. Read the underlying Parquet files from OneLake.

Why it is incorrect: Access to the underlying Delta/Parquet files in OneLake is granted by the Read all Apache Spark / Read all OneLake data (ReadAll) permission, which is also optional and not part of the default permission. Without it, the user cannot access the files directly through the OneLake endpoint.

  • Official documentation: Share your warehouse and manage permissions - Microsoft Fabric / OneLake overview

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • DBUser can read the data in Lakehouse1 by using the: OneLake endpoint
  • DBUser can query the data in Lakehouse1 by using: OneLake file explorer

Why it is correct: Analysis of the exhibit: DBUser was granted access to the lakehouse with only one additional permission, Read all Apache Spark. Read all SQL endpoint data and Build reports on the default semantic model are not selected. Also, DBUser has no access to the tenant (no workspace role), so everything depends on the item-level share.

  • DBUser can read the data in Lakehouse1 by using the, Tabular Data Stream (TDS) endpoint — Why it is incorrect: the TDS endpoint is the SQL analytics one and would require Read all SQL endpoint data, which was not granted.
  • DBUser can query the data in Lakehouse1 by using, a KQL queryset — Why it is incorrect: a KQL queryset queries KQL databases (eventhouses), not lakehouses.

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1.

You have three groups named Group1, Group2, and Group3.

You need to assign a workspace role to each group. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege and meet the following requirements:

  • Group1 must be able to write data to Workspace1, but be unable to add members to Workspace1.
  • Group2 must be able to configure and maintain the settings of Workspace1.
  • Group3 must be able to write data and add members to Workspace1, but be unable to delete Workspace1.

Which workspace role should you assign to each group? To answer, drag the appropriate roles to the correct groups. Each role may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Group1: Contributor
  • Group2: Admin
  • Group3: Member

Why it is correct: Group1 - Contributor. Group1 must write data to the workspace but must not add members. The Contributor role can create, edit and delete content and write data in the workspace, but it cannot manage membership. The Viewer role is read-only, so it is not enough, and Member or Admin would grant more privilege than needed (they can add people), which violates least privilege.

  • Group1, Contributor: Contributor writes and edits content but cannot manage membership: least privilege for Group1.
  • Group2, Admin: configuring and maintaining the workspace (settings, permissions, delete or rename) is exclusive to Admin.
  • Group3, Member: Member writes content and adds members with lower roles, but cannot delete the workspace.

Incorrect options:

  • Group1, Admin — Why it is incorrect: Admin grants more than needed and can add members.
  • Group1, Member — Why it is incorrect: Member can add people; Group1 must not add members.
  • Group1, Viewer — Why it is incorrect: Viewer is read-only: it cannot write data.
  • Group2, Contributor — Why it is incorrect: Contributor cannot change workspace settings.
  • Group2, Member — Why it is incorrect: Member cannot manage workspace-level settings.
  • Group2, Viewer — Why it is incorrect: Viewer is read-only.
  • Group3, Admin — Why it is incorrect: Admin can delete the workspace, which Group3 must not be able to do.
  • Group3, Contributor — Why it is incorrect: Contributor cannot add members.
  • Group3, Viewer — Why it is incorrect: Viewer is read-only; it can neither write nor add members.

What should you use to add the data?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: shortcut

Why it is correct: The requirement is to make a CSV file stored in an Azure Storage account outside of Fabric available in Lakehouse1 while minimizing development effort. A OneLake shortcut to Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (or Blob-compatible storage) creates a pointer in the lakehouse Files section to the external location. No pipeline, code or transformation needs to be built, no data is copied or duplicated, and the file is immediately visible to Fabric engines. It is just configuration with a connection, so it is the lowest effort option.

answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. copy job

Why it is incorrect: A copy job does move the file into the lakehouse, and it is simple, but it still requires creating and configuring a job (source, destination, mapping, schedule) and it duplicates the data. A shortcut needs less effort because there is nothing to copy or run.

  • Official documentation: What is the Copy job in Data Factory for Microsoft Fabric

C. pipeline

Why it is incorrect: A data pipeline with a Copy activity can load the CSV into the lakehouse, but it is orchestration tooling that requires more design and maintenance (activities, connections, parameters, triggers). It is more development effort than a shortcut for a simple file.

  • Official documentation: Microsoft Fabric decision guide: choose a data integration strategy

D. Dataflow Gen2

Why it is incorrect: Dataflow Gen2 uses Power Query to extract, transform and load data. It is meant for transformations and is the heaviest option for just exposing a CSV file; no transformation is required in this scenario.

You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Table1. Table1 contains the following data.

You need to create a T-SQL statement that meets the following requirements:

  • Outputs the item name of each item and returns a null value if the item name is longer than 20 characters
  • Outputs the PurchaseDate value in the format of МММ dd, yy

How should you complete the statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • ItemName: ,try_cast(item_name as varchar(20))
  • PurchaseDate: ,convert(varchar, purchase_date, 7)

Why it is correct: ItemName. The requirement is to output the item name and return NULL when it is longer than 20 characters. TRY_CAST is the "safe" conversion: instead of raising an error when the conversion cannot be performed, it returns NULL, and among the offered options it is the best fit for the requirement. convert(varchar(max), item_name) simply returns the full value with no length restriction, so it does not satisfy the requirement. convert(varchar(20), item_name) truncates or fails rather than returning NULL by design.

  • ItemName, try_cast(item_name as varchar(20)): TRY_CAST returns NULL when the conversion cannot be done; it is the best fit among the options (see the note: strictly it truncates silently).
  • PurchaseDate, convert(varchar, purchase_date, 7): CONVERT style 7 produces Mon dd, yy (for example Apr 20, 22), the requested format.

Incorrect options:

  • ItemName, convert(varchar(20), item_name) — Why it is incorrect: convert(varchar(20), …) truncates the value instead of returning NULL.
  • ItemName, convert(varchar(max), item_name) — Why it is incorrect: convert(varchar(max), …) returns the full value with no length restriction.
  • PurchaseDate, convert(varchar, purchase_date, 109) — Why it is incorrect: style 109 produces Mon dd yyyy hh:mi:ss:mmmAM (four-digit year with time).
  • PurchaseDate, convert(varchar, purchase_date, 112) — Why it is incorrect: style 112 produces yyyymmdd (basic ISO, no separators).

⚠️ Heads-up: The study source marks this answer, but strictly speaking TRY_CAST(x AS varchar(20)) does not return NULL for strings longer than 20 characters: explicit conversions between character types silently truncate, and TRY_CAST only returns NULL when the conversion fails (for example, an invalid format). A true NULL-if-too-long result would need CASE WHEN LEN(item_name) > 20 THEN NULL ELSE item_name END, which none of the options offers, so try_cast is the best available choice. Check it against the linked documentation.

You have a Fabric warehouse named Warehouse1 that contains a table named dbo.Product.

dbo.Product contains the following columns.

You need to use a T-SQL query to add a column named PriceRange to

dbo.Product. The column must categorize each product based on UnitPrice. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • If UnitPrice is 0, PriceRange is "Not for resale".
  • If UnitPrice is less than 50, PriceRange is "Under $50".
  • If UnitPrice is between 50 and 250, PriceRange is "Under $250“.
  • In all other instances, PriceRange is "$250+".

How should you complete the query? To answer, drag the appropriate values to the correct targets. Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • PriceRange = CASE
  • Before '$250+': ELSE
  • Last target (after '$250+'): END

Why it is correct: Analysis. To categorize each row by ranges of UnitPrice in a query, you use a searched CASE expression. It starts with CASE, evaluates each WHEN ... THEN ... branch in order, falls back to ELSE for "all other instances" (UnitPrice of 250 or more, giving '$250+') and must be closed with END.

  • PriceRange = ___, CASE: CASE starts the searched expression that categorizes UnitPrice by ranges.
  • Antes de '$250+', ELSE: ELSE covers “all other cases” (UnitPrice of 250 or more) and returns '$250+'.
  • Último destino (tras '$250+'), END: END closes the CASE expression.

Incorrect options:

  • PriceRange = ___, BEGIN — Why it is incorrect: BEGIN delimits statement blocks; it does not open a column expression.
  • PriceRange = ___, ELSE — Why it is incorrect: ELSE only makes sense inside an already open CASE.
  • PriceRange = ___, END — Why it is incorrect: END closes; it does not open.
  • PriceRange = ___, IF — Why it is incorrect: IF is flow control and cannot return a value in a SELECT column.
  • PriceRange = ___, WHILE — Why it is incorrect: WHILE is flow control and cannot be used in a column expression.
  • Antes de '$250+', BEGIN — Why it is incorrect: BEGIN is not valid before the final value of a CASE.
  • Antes de '$250+', CASE — Why it is incorrect: CASE is already open; repeating it here does not cover “all other cases”.
  • Antes de '$250+', END — Why it is incorrect: END would close the CASE before the '$250+' branch.
  • Antes de '$250+', IF — Why it is incorrect: IF cannot be used inside a column CASE expression.
  • Antes de '$250+', WHILE — Why it is incorrect: WHILE is a loop, not a conditional CASE branch.
  • Último destino (tras '$250+'), BEGIN — Why it is incorrect: BEGIN opens a block; it does not close CASE.
  • Último destino (tras '$250+'), CASE — Why it is incorrect: CASE would open another expression instead of closing the current one.
  • Último destino (tras '$250+'), ELSE — Why it is incorrect: ELSE was already used before '$250+'; it does not close the expression.
  • Último destino (tras '$250+'), IF — Why it is incorrect: IF does not close a CASE expression.
  • Último destino (tras '$250+'), WHILE — Why it is incorrect: WHILE does not close a CASE expression.

You need to add an activity that will execute the stored procedure in a warehouse. The returned values must be available to the downstream activities of the pipeline.

answer.correct:

  • Option B: Script

Why it is correct: The Script activity in a Fabric Data Factory pipeline runs SQL (including EXEC of a stored procedure) against a warehouse and, when the script returns a result set, exposes that result in the activity output (result sets and rows affected). C. Stored procedure

Why it is incorrect: The Stored procedure activity does execute a stored procedure in a warehouse, but it is designed to run the procedure (for example to perform data modifications) and does not surface the values returned by the procedure as an output usable by downstream activities. Since the requirement is that the returned values must be available downstream, the Script activity is the one to use.

D. Get metadata

Why it is incorrect: Get metadata retrieves metadata of data (files, folders, tables, structure) from a data store. It does not execute stored procedures.

You have a Fabric workspace that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

Warehouse1 contains the following data.

You need to create a T-SQL statement that will denormalize the tables and include the ContractType and StartDate attributes in the results. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • Include attributes from matching rows in the Contract table.
  • Ensure that all the rows from the Employee table are preserved.
  • Return the total number of employees per contract type for all the contract types that have more than two employees.

How should you complete the statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Join type: LEFT OUTER JOIN
  • Filter on the aggregated count: HAVING

Why it is correct: Join type - LEFT OUTER JOIN. The query starts from Employee AS e. The requirements are to include attributes from matching rows of Contract and to ensure all rows of Employee are preserved. That is the definition of a left outer join with Employee on the left: every employee is returned, with ContractType set to NULL where there is no matching contract. INNER JOIN would drop employees without a contract, RIGHT OUTER JOIN would preserve Contract rows instead of Employee rows, and CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product with no join condition, which makes no sense here.

  • Join type, LEFT OUTER JOIN: LEFT OUTER JOIN with Employee on the left keeps every employee and includes Contract attributes when there is a match (ContractType NULL otherwise).
  • Filter on the aggregated count, HAVING: a filter on an aggregate (COUNT(DISTINCT EmployeeID) > 2) goes in HAVING, which filters after grouping.

Incorrect options:

  • Join type, CROSS JOIN — Why it is incorrect: CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product with no join condition.
  • Join type, INNER JOIN — Why it is incorrect: INNER JOIN would drop employees without a contract.
  • Join type, RIGHT OUTER JOIN — Why it is incorrect: RIGHT OUTER JOIN would keep Contract rows, not Employee rows.
  • Filter on the aggregated count, CONTAINS — Why it is incorrect: CONTAINS is a full-text predicate, not a clause for filtering aggregates.
  • Filter on the aggregated count, LIMIT — Why it is incorrect: LIMIT is not T-SQL syntax (T-SQL uses TOP).
  • Filter on the aggregated count, WHERE — Why it is incorrect: WHERE filters rows before grouping and does not accept aggregate functions.
  • Official documentation: FROM clause plus JOIN, APPLY, PIVOT (Transact-SQL), HAVING (Transact-SQL)

q179.stem:
-

You have a KQL database that contains a table named Readings.

You need to query Readings and return the results shown in the following table.

How should you complete the query? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • First box (computing the previous values): | extend
  • Second box (final column list): | project

Why it is correct: First box - extend. prev() is a window function that returns the value of a column in a previous row of a serialized row set; sort by Datetime produces a serialized set, so prev(MeterReading) and prev(Datetime) can be used. Adding new calculated columns (PrevMeterReading, PrevTimestamp) to every row while keeping the existing ones is exactly what extend does. summarize would aggregate rows, evaluate invokes plugins, and lookup enriches a table with another table, so none of them fit.

  • First box (computing the previous values), extend: prev() is a window function over a serialized set (sort by Datetime); extend adds PrevMeterReading and PrevDatetime to each row while keeping existing columns.
  • Second box (final column list), project: project selects and orders exactly the output columns: City, Area, MeterReading, Datetime, PrevMeterReading, PrevDatetime.

Incorrect options:

  • First box (computing the previous values), evaluate — Why it is incorrect: evaluate invokes plugins; it does not add calculated columns.
  • First box (computing the previous values), lookup — Why it is incorrect: lookup enriches a table with another one; it does not compute values from previous rows.
  • First box (computing the previous values), project — Why it is incorrect: project selects columns; it does not compute new ones with prev().
  • First box (computing the previous values), summarize — Why it is incorrect: summarize would aggregate rows instead of keeping them.
  • Second box (final column list), evaluate — Why it is incorrect: evaluate invokes plugins; it does not select columns.
  • Second box (final column list), extend — Why it is incorrect: extend adds columns instead of selecting and ordering the output ones.
  • Second box (final column list), lookup — Why it is incorrect: lookup enriches from another table; it does not limit the column list.
  • Second box (final column list), summarize — Why it is incorrect: summarize would require an aggregation.
  • Official documentation: prev() function, Use the extend operator, KQL quick reference (project, extend, summarize, lookup)

q180.stem:
-

You have a Fabric workspace that contains a warehouse named DW1. DW1 contains the following tables and columns.

You need to summarize order quantities by year and product. The solution must include the yearly sum of order quantities for all the products in each row.

How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • SELECT ___(SO.ModifiedDate) AS OrderDate: YEAR
  • GROUP BY: GROUPING SETS ((YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate), P.Name), (YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate)))

Why it is correct: the warehouse DW1 supports analytical T-SQL queries over relational tables. To get exactly the two requested levels (quantities by year and product, plus the annual total for all products) without unrequested grand-total rows, the full statement is:

SELECT YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate) AS OrderDate
      ,P.Name AS ProductName
      ,SUM(SO.OrderQty) AS OrderQty
FROM [dbo].[SalesOrderDetail] SO
INNER JOIN [dbo].[Product] P
  ON P.ProductID = SO.ProductID
GROUP BY
  GROUPING SETS ((YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate), P.Name), (YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate)))
ORDER BY OrderDate

  • SELECT ___(SO.ModifiedDate) AS OrderDate, YEAR: YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate) extracts the year and matches the GROUP BY expressions.
  • GROUP BY, GROUPING SETS ((YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate), P.Name), (YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate))): GROUPING SETS computes exactly two levels: year+product and the annual total across all products, with no grand-total row.

Incorrect options:

  • SELECT ___(SO.ModifiedDate) AS OrderDate, CAST — Why it is incorrect: CAST requires the target type with AS; CAST(SO.ModifiedDate) is not valid and does not extract the year.
  • SELECT ___(SO.ModifiedDate) AS OrderDate, CONVERT — Why it is incorrect: CONVERT requires at least two arguments (type and expression); CONVERT(SO.ModifiedDate) is not valid.
  • GROUP BY, CUBE(YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate), P.Name) — Why it is incorrect: CUBE also generates the per-product total across years and the grand total, which were not requested.
  • GROUP BY, ROLLUP(YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate), P.Name) — Why it is incorrect: ROLLUP adds a grand-total row () that was not requested.
  • GROUP BY, YEAR(SO.ModifiedDate), P.Name — Why it is incorrect: a plain GROUP BY only returns year and product, without the annual summary across all products.
  • Official documentation: GROUP BY clause (Transact-SQL): GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP and CUBE, YEAR (Transact-SQL), CAST and CONVERT (Transact-SQL), T-SQL surface area in Microsoft Fabric

q181.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains multiple semantic models, including a model named Model1. Model1 is updated by using an XMLA endpoint.

You need to increase the speed of the write operations of the XMLA endpoint.

What should you do?
options: Delete any unused semantic models from Workspace1.
Select Large semantic model storage format for Workspace1.
Configure Model 1 to use the Direct Lake storage format.
Delete any unused columns from Model1.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Select Large semantic model storage format for Workspace1.

Why it is correct: Model1 is written to through the XMLA endpoint (for example by Tabular Editor, SSMS, ALM Toolkit or a deployment pipeline). The way to make those write operations faster is to enable the Large semantic model storage format. With this format, the service uses a different, optimized storage layout for the model, which is what improves the performance of XMLA write operations (processing and metadata changes) on big models, and it also removes the 10 GB model size limit. The setting is applied per semantic model (in the model settings) or as the default for the workspace, so selecting it for Workspace1 covers Model1. Nothing in the other options changes how data is written through the endpoint.

  • Official documentation: Large semantic models in Power BI Premium and Fabric and Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. Delete any unused semantic models from Workspace1.

Why it is incorrect: Semantic models in a workspace are independent items. Removing models that nobody uses frees capacity memory and tidies the workspace, but it does not change the storage format or the way XMLA writes to Model1 are executed, so the write speed of the endpoint is not improved in a meaningful way.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint

C. Configure Model 1 to use the Direct Lake storage format.

Why it is incorrect: Direct Lake is a storage mode that reads Delta tables from OneLake directly into memory. It is a different way of loading data into the model, not a way to speed up XMLA write operations, and it would force a redesign of Model1 (data must live in Delta tables in a lakehouse or warehouse). Large semantic model storage format is the setting the documentation ties to faster XMLA writes.

  • Official documentation: Direct Lake overview

D. Delete any unused columns from Model1.

Why it is incorrect: Removing unused columns reduces model size and can speed up refresh and queries, but it is a modeling optimization, not a configuration of the XMLA write path. It also means changing the model design, whereas the requirement is simply to speed up the endpoint writes, which the large model storage format addresses directly.

  • Official documentation: Large semantic models in Power BI Premium and Fabric

q182.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1.

You need to create a semantic model named Model1 and publish Model1 to Workspace1. The solution must meet the following requirements:

  • Can revert to previous versions of Model1 as required.
  • Identifies differences between saved versions of Model1.
  • Uses Microsoft Power Bl=I Desktop to publish to Workspace1.
  • Can edit item definition files by using Microsoft Visual Studio Code.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
options: Save Model1 in Power BI Desktop as a PBIT file.
Enable users to edit data models in the Power BI service.
Save Model1 in Power BI Desktop as a PBIP file.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Enable Git integration for Workspace1.
  • Option D: Save Model1 in Power BI Desktop as a PBIP file.

Why it is correct: The four requirements split into two needs.

  • Version history, revert and compare versions are source control features. Enabling Git integration on Workspace1 connects the workspace to a Git repository (Azure DevOps or GitHub), so every change to Model1 is committed, you can compare versions through diffs and you can revert to a previous commit.
  • Publishing from Power BI Desktop and editing item definition files in Visual Studio Code require the model to be saved as a Power BI Project (PBIP). A PBIP stores the semantic model and report as a folder of text-based definition files (TMDL/TMSL for the model, PBIR/JSON for the report), which are readable by humans, diff-friendly and editable in VS Code. Desktop can still publish the project to the workspace, and the same folder structure is what Git integration in Fabric understands.

Together, PBIP gives the editable text-based files and Git integration gives history, diff and revert.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects (PBIP) overview, Power BI Desktop projects and Git integration and Manage Power BI content in version control
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

B. Save Model1 in Power BI Desktop as a PBIT file.

Why it is incorrect: A PBIT is a Power BI template: a single packaged file that contains the model and report definition but no data. It is a binary-style container, not a folder of editable item definition files, so it cannot be edited properly in VS Code, and it provides no version history or diff of saved versions. It is meant for sharing reusable starting points, not for source control.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects (PBIP) overview

C. Enable users to edit data models in the Power BI service.

Why it is incorrect: This tenant/workspace setting lets people edit a model in the browser (web modeling). It has nothing to do with saving versions, comparing them, publishing from Desktop or working with definition files in VS Code, so it covers none of the requirements.

  • Official documentation: Manage Power BI content in version control

q183.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that is assigned to a newly created Fabric capacity named Capacity1.

You create a semantic model named Model1 and deploy Model1 to Workspace1.

You need to publish changes to Model1 directly from Tabular Editor.

What should you do?
options: For Workspace1, create a managed private endpoint.
For Capacity1, set XMLA Endpoint to Read Write.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: For Capacity1, set XMLA Endpoint to Read Write.

Why it is correct: Tabular Editor connects to a semantic model through the XMLA endpoint of the workspace. By default the endpoint of a capacity is Read Only, which lets client tools query but not change the model. To deploy or save changes made in Tabular Editor to Model1 you need read-write XMLA, and that is configured in the capacity settings (the XMLA Endpoint option, set to Read Write) in the Fabric admin portal or the capacity settings. Because Workspace1 is assigned to the newly created Capacity1, this is the setting you have to change.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint and Manage semantic models with the XMLA endpoint
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

A. For Workspace1, enable Git integration.

Why it is incorrect: Git integration synchronizes workspace items with a repository for version control. It does not open a write channel for third-party tools such as Tabular Editor; those still need the XMLA endpoint to be read-write.

  • Official documentation: Power BI Desktop projects and Git integration

B. For Model1, enable external sharing.

Why it is incorrect: External sharing controls whether guest users from other organizations can consume content. It is unrelated to how Tabular Editor connects to and writes to the model.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint

C. For Workspace1, create a managed private endpoint.

Why it is incorrect: Managed private endpoints are used for outbound secure connections from Fabric workloads (for example Spark) to data sources. They do not configure the inbound XMLA endpoint that client tools use, and they do not enable write operations.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model connectivity with the XMLA endpoint

You are creating a report and a semantic model in Microsoft Power BI Desktop.

The Value measure has the expression shown in the following exhibit.

Use the drop-down menus to select the answer choice that completes each statement based on the information presented in the graphic.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • A [answer choice] was added to the Value measure: dynamic format string
  • The Value measure can return values formatted as: percentages or whole numbers

Why it is correct: Analysis of each selection:

  • A [answer choice] was added to the Value measure, dynamic format string: the Format dropdown shows Dynamic and the formula bar holds a SWITCH returning a format string: it is a dynamic format string; the measure still returns its numeric value.
  • The Value measure can return values formatted as, percentages or whole numbers: the SWITCH branches give "#" (integer), "0.00%" (percentage) and "#,###" (integer with thousands): only integers or percentages.

Incorrect options:

  • A [answer choice] was added to the Value measure, calculation group — Why it is incorrect: a calculation group is a separate table with calculation items; it is not what the screenshot shows.
  • A [answer choice] was added to the Value measure, data category — Why it is incorrect: a data category only classifies a field (URL, city…); it does not change formatting.
  • A [answer choice] was added to the Value measure, synonym — Why it is incorrect: a synonym is an alternative name for natural-language questions; it does not format.
  • The Value measure can return values formatted as, percentages only — Why it is incorrect: percentages only: the other metrics are integers.
  • The Value measure can return values formatted as, percentages or decimals — Why it is incorrect: percentages or decimals: no format shows decimals except inside the percentage.
  • The Value measure can return values formatted as, whole numbers only — Why it is incorrect: whole numbers only: Gross Margin % is a percentage.
  • Official documentation: Create dynamic format strings for measures and Use custom format strings in Power BI Desktop

q185.stem:
-

You have a Fabric lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

You have the data sources shown in the following table.

You need to ingest data from both data sources into Lakehouse1. The solution must minimize maintenance and development time.

What should you use to ingest the data into each data source? To answer, drag the appropriate options to the correct data sources. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Datasource1: A pipeline with a Copy activity
  • Datasource2: An eventstream

Why it is correct: according to the Fabric decision guide, each tool fits a different volume, latency and development-effort pattern, and the requirement is to minimize development and maintenance:

  • Datasource1, A pipeline with a Copy activity: Copy is the low-code option for moving large volumes (500,000+ rows, 20 GB per day) from Azure SQL with CDC to a lakehouse, with historical and incremental loads.
  • Datasource2, An eventstream: an eventstream connects directly to Azure Event Hubs and writes to Lakehouse1 with no code or streaming jobs to manage.

Incorrect options:

  • Datasource1, A Dataflow Gen1 — Why it is incorrect: Dataflow Gen1 is the legacy Power BI architecture and does not write directly to a Fabric lakehouse.
  • Datasource1, A Dataflow Gen2 — Why it is incorrect: Dataflow Gen2 is for transformation at low-to-medium volumes; for large daily loads Copy is recommended.
  • Datasource1, A notebook — Why it is incorrect: a notebook requires developing and maintaining code, which contradicts minimizing development.
  • Datasource1, An eventstream — Why it is incorrect: an eventstream is for streaming data, not batch loads from Azure SQL.
  • Datasource2, A Dataflow Gen1 — Why it is incorrect: Dataflow Gen1 is not suitable for streaming ingestion from Event Hubs.
  • Datasource2, A Dataflow Gen2 — Why it is incorrect: Dataflow Gen2 is a batch engine; it does not consume an Event Hub continuously.
  • Datasource2, A notebook — Why it is incorrect: a notebook (Spark Structured Streaming) requires code and checkpoints to maintain.
  • Datasource2, A pipeline with a Copy activity — Why it is incorrect: Copy moves data in batches; it is not a continuous streaming solution.
  • Official documentation: Microsoft Fabric decision guide: copy activity, dataflow, or Spark, Copy activity in Data Factory for Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Fabric eventstreams overview, Add a lakehouse destination to an eventstream

q186.stem:
-

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that uses the Premium Per User (PPU) license mode and contains a semantic model named Model1.

Large semantic model storage format is selected for Model1.

You need to ensure that tables imported into Model1 are written automatically to Delta tables in OneLake.

What should you do for Model1 and Workspace1? To answer, select the

appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Model1: Enable OneLake integration.
  • Workspace1: Change the license mode to Fabric capacity.

Why it is correct: Analysis of each selection:

  • Model1, Enable OneLake integration.: OneLake integration automatically writes Import tables to Delta tables in OneLake; it is enabled per model (with large model storage).
  • Workspace1, Change the license mode to Fabric capacity.: OneLake integration needs a workspace on a Fabric (F) or Premium (P) capacity; PPU is not supported, so the license mode must change.

Incorrect options:

  • Model1, Enable query caching. — Why it is incorrect: query caching only stores results to speed up report loads; it does not write to OneLake.
  • Model1, Enable query scale-out. — Why it is incorrect: query scale-out spreads queries across read-only replicas; it does not write to OneLake.
  • Workspace1, Create a workspace identity — Why it is incorrect: a workspace identity is for access to external sources; it does not enable the Delta export.
  • Workspace1, Enable authentication by using OneLake user-delegated SAS tokens. — Why it is incorrect: OneLake user-delegated tokens give temporary data access; they do not enable the model's Delta export.
  • Official documentation: OneLake integration for semantic models, Large semantic models in Power BI Premium and Fabric and Power BI semantic model scale-out

q187.stem:
-

You have a Fabric eventhouse named Eventhouse1 that contains a table named Weatherdata. A sample of the data in Weatherdata is shown in the following table.

You plan to use a KQL queryset to manipulate the data in Eventhouse1. The result set must have the following columns.

You need to build the query.

Which four KQL statements should you use in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate statements from the list of statements to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Step 1: Weatherdata
  • Step 2: | sort by Datetime asc
  • Step 3: | extend Delta_temperature = Temperature - prev(Temperature)
  • Step 4: | project Datetime, Lat, Long, Temperature, Delta_temperature

Why it is correct: in KQL, computing differences between consecutive rows requires this order in the pipeline (|):

  • Step 1, Weatherdata: every tabular KQL query starts with the source table through which the following operators flow.
  • Step 2, | sort by Datetime asc: prev() only works over serialized rows: sorting by Datetime ascending guarantees the previous row is the earlier record in time.
  • Step 3, | extend Delta_temperature = Temperature - prev(Temperature): extend adds Delta_temperature = Temperature - prev(Temperature) while keeping the existing columns.
  • Step 4, | project Datetime, Lat, Long, Temperature, Delta_temperature: project leaves exactly the five requested columns, in order, and excludes Pressure and Wind.

Incorrect options:

  • extend … next(Temperature,1) — Why it is incorrect: next() takes the following row, not the previous one: it inverts the requested logic.
  • extend … prev(Temperature,2) — Why it is incorrect: an offset of 2 compares with two rows back, not the immediately previous one.
  • summarize … by Datetime — Why it is incorrect: it groups and drops needed columns; prev() cannot be used inside an aggregation.
  • Official documentation: prev() function (KQL), Window functions overview (KQL), sort operator (KQL), extend operator (KQL), project operator (KQL), next() function (KQL), summarize operator (KQL)

q188.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains an eventstream named Eventstream1.

Eventstream1 reads data from an Azure event hub named Eventhub1.

Eventhub1 contains the following columns.

You need to add a continuous percentile calculation to the Payload column. The solution must minimize development effort.

What should you do?
options: Add a KQL queryset to Workspace1.
Add a Group by transformation to Eventstream1.
Add a Manage fields transformation to Eventstream1.
Add an Aggregate transformation to Eventstream1.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Add a Group by transformation to Eventstream1.

Why it is correct: the Fabric eventstream no-code editor includes built-in operators to process data in transit with minimal development effort. The Group by transformation calculates aggregations over events within time windows and is the one that offers the continuous percentile function the question asks for, so the calculation on the Payload column is solved visually inside Eventstream1, with no code or extra items.

The Aggregate transformation, on the other hand, only offers sum, minimum, maximum and average, so it cannot calculate a percentile.

  • Option A, KQL queryset: it is used to query a KQL database on demand with code (for example, percentile()); it requires an extra KQL destination and code to maintain, and it does not calculate continuously inside Eventstream1, increasing development effort.
  • Option C, Manage fields: it lets you select, rename or change column types and apply built-in functions, but it does not perform time-window aggregations or percentiles.
  • Option D, Aggregate: it only supports sum, minimum, maximum and average; it does not include the continuous percentile.
  • Official documentation: Eventstream transformations, Microsoft Fabric eventstreams overview, Process event data with the event processor editor
